div.p: tOR ALL PASTRY Mc DOUCALL'S PATENT SELF RAISING FLOUR IS UNRIVALLED. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6, 1913.
was quite the best night work ever done by the battalion, and everyane was playing .the game to the very best of his ability. -- • •
Old , ~;,:c, .. .._. . •P ft a „..„... ar „ CHICALA .. ~., . ' A DRY FEED FOR CHICKENS

The battalion 'returned to the bivouac and ,hot coffee at. four a.m., marched back to camp to it substantial breakfast, and in .two hours marched out again to a long brigade field day, getting back to camp early in the afternoon of Wed- nesday. The Colonel met the farmer later on in Denbigh and he told him he would not find even a cigarette end on his field. He • said: "No compensation 'claimed by me. No, in- deed." So keen were the Scouts, cyclist's, offi- cers and N.C. officers that on several :nights after a long day's work they went out volun- tarily to practise various kinds of night work. The men were, many of them, also ready and anxious to go out, too.
Brigade Field Days.

Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday were brigade field days. On Wednesday, after the bivouac, two cap- tains (Captain Cary and Captain Roberts) were examined for their Major's certificate. The former commanded the 9th Liverpool in the field, and the latter the 10th Liverpool (Scottish) and both passed their examination successfully. Thursday the brigade advanced, under the Brigadier, to the attack, and first practised ad- vancing in small sectional columns at irregular intervals through the artillery zone, the ,enenr.y being represented by screen targets. The brigade then re-organised, and again advanced against an enemy, but this time undclrl oimed rifle fire against a very strong positi9n. On Friday the brigade marched out towards 13odfari (the2,4tli being in reserve) against an enemy represented by the six machine guns if the brigade and a line of screen targets, repre- senting Infantry in an entrenched position. The 4th were ordered to reinforce the 9th Liverpool on the right, .and were led along .a deli) 1-tne, affording excellent cover from fire and View, by the Colonel, whence they emerged right on to the enemy's position. On Saturday the battalion represented the White Force, which was Welsh, and which had been defeated by a Brown InVading. Force and was being driven back into the mountains. The 'objects of White (commanded by Col-on.l Fair.. his attention clough) *Eire to 'hire on the Brown Force under STY entrenched Tied Fried FpCoo:linOitnmioe,ln alnolacnic,fiewa),hilpig:ococi:apoyusintiOntgl ea there, with the remainder of the Ffirce to scupper Brown's convoy, which, it eventually turned out, was "Parked" at Pripm, being protected. by a.company of the Scottish. While Colonel Fairclough successfully accom- plished his- object, the Force he sent against the convoy had not located it when the "Cease Fire" sounded. Brown advanced rapidly against White, driving back all his seOuts and advanced troops, and eventually made a flank attack upon the mountain with the Scottish, covered by the fire Of the machine guns and the 9th Liverpool. The Scottish went up the hill, which was 1,100 feet high, in splendid style, and many of them had gained the first crest when the "Cease Fire" sounded, and were engaged with White on the mountain.- The attack was also reinforced by two companies of the 9th, who prolonged the Scottish right. A pow-wow was held by General Lindsay at Priom cross-roads, when he criticised the oper- ations and told the Commanding Officers that he hoped they would give special attention to sectional training before camp next year.

Machine Guns, Scouts, Cyclists, Signallers, &c. ;During most of the time the machine guns of the brigade were trained by a Regular Officer. The 4th machine gun sections, under Lieutenant lienshall, won the Silver cup, kindly presented for competition by the Brigade Machine Gun Officer (Captain Paris), and, from all accounts, they most thoroughly deserved the cup. Their range-finding, the condition of their harness, &c., were specially worthy of praise, though they were examined on 10 points and led on most.

Scouts and cyclists, under Lieutenant Robert- son, worked very well both during preliminary training and maMeuvres, and the Commanding Officer was on all occasions most admirably served with information. ,

, . The signallers, under Lieutenant Seymour- Jones, did very good work, and every man passed the examination herd in .camp, which speaks volumes for their Work and training. . The band was trained as-stretcher-bearers by Major Adams, and on the 'Friday- in the second week -put their:work into practice'-by attending tottlie casualties, to whom they gave first-aid in the field. .2
The March Discipline of the Battalion.

_ This improved ILIA year, but it was this year, after the first day or two, almost perfect. The covering off was excellent, the dressing by the flank by which the battalion was marching very good. Distances were well kept, and although the Commanding pfficer controlled the battalion almost entirely by the whistle and hand signal, these were instantly responded to by all ranks. This, and the great advance- in individual train- ing, were, perhaps the most conspicuous im- provements•made ;luring the training, which was brought to a conclusion on Sunday:morn- ing, when the battalion returned to Warrington and Newton-le-Willows, looking hardy and well bronzed. _

The band and drums brought great credit to their_ battalion in a way that must have been some reward to Mr. Wainwright (the band- master) for all his devoted work in their behalf. The Social Side of Camp.• The Mayor and people of Denbigh gave the 'brigade a very warm welcome. They presented a silver cup for,the sports, got fip concerts (free), made officers honorary members of: Golf and Tennis Clubs, and the men of the Political and Social Clubs in the town. The brigade tried to repay this kindness by giving a torch-light tattoo on the first Saturday night, in which the whole of the' drums and pipers and the. brass band Of the 9th Liverpool and some 300 toreh- bearers took part. Each battalion in turn sent their band to play in the Market Square in the evenings, and on. two occasions the 4th beat Tattoo and Last Post, accompanied by torch- bearers, and on the first occasion had the band, as well as the drums. There was an enormous and enthusiastic crowd on both occasions. The battalion won on events in the brigade sports, but was beaten by the Scottish on points, they securing three places in the 100 yards, and also doing well in the half-mile. The -4th won the tent-pitching tug-of-war, and marching competition. It was a great -treat to see the marching section, under Sergeant Rot- tomley. The section kept its dressing :perfectly the whole time, and to see it wheel round the corners as one man was splendid. Every man was in full marching order, with water bottles filled, entrenching tools, &c. The battalion sports were confined to an inter-' company football competition, eventually won by "A " Company, who beat the band in the final. This company also won the Brigade Cup for the best company in the brigade. Lieutenant Frost was unwearying in the close attention he gave to the football competitions and to the brigade sports, and nearly the whole of his spare time was devoted to the-One or the other.

Captain Elgood, Adjutant. • Towards the end of camp everyone began to realise, to his great regret, that this was pro- bably the last camp which Captain Elgood.would spend: with the battalion, and on Saturday afternoon he was asked to go into the Sergeants' Mess, in order that his health might be enthu- siastically drunk with musical honours. While this was going on, the men, discarding an offi- cer's chair, produced one of their own manufac- ture, and when Captain.Elgood showed his face outside ttheir Mess a rush was made for him, which he evaded • for a time. • He was soon captured, however, and hoisted into the 'Chair of Honour., borne by some stalwart soldiers on poles resting on 'broad shoulders.

Both brass bawl and drums were waiting, and he was played round .and round the battalion lines, the whole of the officers and men falling in in fours behind. He was cheered to the echo again am! again, MA only by his own battalion, but also by the 9th and 10th (Scottish) on the flanks. After many attempts at escape he eventually gave in and made a short speech, in which he said he had done his best for the battalion which he had made his own while with it. He said that the three years of soldier- ing he had done with the 4th were the happiest of his life, And that the thought of having to. part iiith the battalion was very bitter to him. Thus the battalion tried to show Captain Elgood bow much all ranks appreciate! his hard work for the battalion during the time he. had been Adjutant and their affection for him' personally.
- No Adjutant has ever received so sponfaneous anti enthusiastic- au Oration.

div.head: ELECTRIC CHICKENS.
div.p: ELECTRIC CHICKENS.
New Method of Forcing Young Birds
for Market.
READY IN FIVE WEEKS.

Ingenious experiments have been made in the effect of electricity upon growth, both of plants and animals. Beyond question young poultry respond to . electrio stimulus with astounding rapidity. They surpass the best .on record in speed of growth at the itime of year, they keep their health in crowded conditions, and become almost independent of the season. In the South of England, on the largest poultry farm in the world, an experinient.of this nature has been completed,..Eight'hUndred chickeris, in equal groups of 400, were nurtiked on the in- tensive system—that is, in flat, almost. trays, one above the other. One group of ,460 was treated by this electric system, and so charged were the chickens with electricity that the shock could be distinctly felt if the finger was put to the beak' of a chicken. The chickensin this 400 grew to a marketable size_ in five weeks, and 'of the' .400 only six, and those were weaklings in the beginning, .died. Of • the other 406 nearly half died—it being late in the year for healthy growth—and the survivors took three months to reach the marketable size.

div.head: GROWING CHICKENS.
div.p: GROWING CHICKENS.

All young stock should now be making good progress. and should receive unremitting.atten- tion. .Satisfactory growth of frame, -muscular development, and a superabundance of vigour are what successful poultry-keepers strive for. Keep up a plentiful supply of gm/en !clod and arrange for scratching exercise and fresh soil; renewed as ofterr as possible. Road dust will be'. found:very:acceptable during the dry weather,, and Will form- an excellent substitute'for..fresh ground. Lime should be !freely used at all seasons of the year to check disease.. FREEDOM FROM INSECTS.

If chickens are to be healthy and strong they must bp kept scrupulously clean. The presence of insects, although not a disease in itself, is responsible in a large measure for many ef The diseases from which" fowls suffer. Fleas, lice and red mites are the most „tronb'e- some of the insect pests that prey upon Poultry. To keep them in check'the interior of the coops end houses should be dressed with Hale or creosote preparation, while the loose nesting material should be burned and renewed at least twice a month.

Lice live upon the birds, and insect powder dusted among the feathers is the best thing to deal with them. Bed mites live In the Cracks and i:revic?s. rJ the houses, and are, perhaps, the most tr.-:u1-1--. some of all poultry pests. . "i'Lle rnly way in which to keep them in check is to dress all the woodwork, outside and inside, with. limewash or creosote, and to spray it into the cracks'.

Broodiness is the prevailing note in !tie r..pert just to hand of the tenth montli,of this cOmpe- Wiwi. 'ln Spite of this-and the mauai.?,.2r,- Mg. F. W. Rhodes, states that no less a-an fifty of the birds are affected—the egg Sieid for the month (four weeks) shows a slight increase- -7,884 eggs, as 'against 7,831 eggs fast month. This amounts to an average of thirteen eggs pa- bird for the ,twenty-eight days—by no means poOr for the time ot year. The Manager also draws attention to the fact that the white Leg- horns have considerably improved their posi- tions this month, but a study of the table of results to date would seem to show that it is unlikely that in the remaining three month's (twelve weeks) they can so improve their posi- tions as to hold leading places at the Close of the competition on October :14th; at the same time they should be able during, the period to. maintain a distinct advantage over the broody varieties.

As regards positions, there is little .:hange from last month. Pen 60, 'white Wyandottes, still hold the first place, with a total record of 1,062 eggs, (value £5. 4s. 7A-d.). • This score gives them a very. ,substantial lead over pen 86, Buff Docks, which led for so many months, but now; take second place, with a total score of 947 eggs (value .24 19s. Id.). Pen 32, white Wyandottes, hold third place, with a totabscore of 992 eggs (value £4 14s. llfd.). The highest record for the month has been made by pen 7, .white Leg- horns, 'with a score of 125 eggs (value 11. s. 1/d.). The health of the birds Vas been quite satis- factory.
MOVABLE CIIICKEN PENS ON STUBBLI7.S.

I want to point out, says a writer in "Farm and Home," an excellent opportunity that pre- sents itself to farmers, ,Of adopting a system of poultry-keeping that is, a hundred times more up-to-date and likely to prove profitable than the average farmyard method of poultry-keep- ing. I refer to the Movable house system. It can be started now, with the twoods of growing chickens ; you cannot (except- .at the cost of infinite trouble) alter the habits of fully-grown 'poultry, and persuade them to give up roosting in the barn and t 9 sleep instead in open-fronted pens, -ant in the fields; but you can manage this rearrangement so far as chickens are con-, cerned, and now is the very best time to do it. The fields are becoMing clear of crops, there is abundance Of food to be got at no cost at all; and the poultry—young and -old, alike—ought, during the next few weeks, to do wonders, both as regards growing and laying. Let-the farmer get his movable pens Out, then, or if be has none let him buy a few old packing cases, and Set the carpenter to convert them into mov4le rooSts. being moved' a foot or 'two every. second or third dayi. so that there will, no.need of cleaning out. 1.4 'each Such *robsrbe large enough to accommOdate a ffoz.t.n full-sized fowls, and when put into position, let each be made the home of twelve, or fifteen growing chicks,.which can be kept in place by the use of ii wire run, attached to the house for a couple of days, after which they will need no further restraint, but will go to roost according as their owner intends. There is, of course, just. one danger to lie thought Of, and that is tfie danger of visits Cron) foxes of the district; but there are plenty of ways of dealing with them. One plan is to put a sheet of coarse wire netting across, the bottom of the roost, so that they find if they try to scratch out hole underneath, that their progress is barred that way; the netting to be used in tne front Should be strong, and if a number of stout' wooden bars, or portions of old iron hurdles be brought into use as well, there need be no fear of an irruption through the netting. I need say no more. This is a subject that wants to be brought under the notice of farmers noW and again, with particular emphasis. Those who are ready to adopt it can till in the rest for themselves.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
BONE MEAL AS MANIME.

This is the best-known bone manure, says a writer in "Farm and Home." It consists of the raw bones, after the mere extraction of fat, ground into meal. Various degrees of fineness are to be had, from the 4-in, and Fin. used by gardeners for fruit trees, down to more or less tine meals. It may be said at once that nothing but fine bone meal should be used, as even this is quite slow enough in becoming available. In the old daysr it is true, roughly crushed,bones in very coarse condition were employed, but as much as a ton or more per acre was applied, and the result expected to last twenty years. Bone of this nature did much to build up the famous dairy pastures of Cheshire'; but it was soon found that tfie finer the bone 'could be reduced the better the result. As a matter of fact, it is impossible to grind raw bone ex- tremely tine, on account of the tough nature of the cartilage. It is for this reason. and because of the very slow decomposition of this cartilage in the soil, that bone meal is slow in action. It should, thereto:ire, always •be applied in autumn or. early winter. When applied to pas- tures more effect may be expected in the second and subsequent years after the dressing than in the first, and the beffefit'is long lasting. Gener- ally speaking, boneinealls a better manure for grass land than•fOr .arahle:. .• • . Bone meal is both nitrogenous and phos- phatic. A good sample should contain at least 3.30 per cent. nitrogen and 45 per cent. phos- phate Of lime. The nitrogen is generally held out as a great advaritage, but, as a matter of fact, it is of dotibtfilit.bgn6K. because it has to be paid for, and; ''considering that it is very slow-acting organic nitrogen., it .is generally valued too high. However, bone meal is rather cheaper than it used to be, and it is quite worth buying for light land pastures that are too sky for slag with potash, and too deficient, in lime for superphosphate. An average dressing is -4.ewt. per acre..

LINSEED CHAFF DANGEROUS FOR SHEEP. In the " Transactions " Of the Aberdeen Col- lege Foriner Students' Association, Mr. C. Michie, Upper Balfour, Durris, gives a warning of the danger of using linseed chaff as a food for ewes at lambing time. He says: Having a small flock of ewes, and wishing to supplement their turnips after the new year with some 'dry feed, hay being a short;crop in the-locality as in many other places, I was advised to give linseed chaff a trial, as something bulky to make up a mixture with some dried grains and light oats. • The proportions, roughly, would have been linseed chaff • two parts, dried grains one part, and light oats one part, with one part of ,bran added after the: ewes. Commenced to drop their lambs. The •ewes ate it readily from the start., and, with a trough feed of t-lb per head of the mixture'(which proved bulky in propor- tion to weight.) before 'their turnips, seemed to winter well. A fortnight or three weeks after .lambing one or two of the strongest lambs were lound•dead, wool ball being suspected; but, a few more following, the stomach in each case was examined, and ample traces of flax fibre, quite sufficient to set up irritation, and cause death, were found. The trough feed was;.dis- continued at once, but the after effects on the lambs continued for arfortnighl. The deduction. to be drawn is that, although linseed cfiaff may be a safe food for ewes, it should be discon- tinued .at lambing time, as it is sure to give trouble. Linseed chaff, Which is imported mostly from Russia and the Continent, shows an analysis of '2.3 per. cent: of oil; and is used for the greater plirt in a mixed ration for dairy cows .as a, substitute for draff .when Mat com- modity is scarce. HINTS ON CHEESE-MAKING.

• A good duality cheese ,cannot be made from milli which is tainted.or o.verripe. _lt is there- fore necessary to have pure fresh milk to deal with. Milk Of this description may be ripened to the correct extent-by the cheesemaker. When unclean or sour milk is received at the dairy, the best quality products cannot lie made from. it.

For most •hinds of hard-pressed cheese suffi- cient rennet is used to. produce re,' curd of, the right consistence in from :forty-five to sixty minutes. The right renneting temperature must • be: adopted, as this, has a considerable effect upon the resulting curd. Too low a tem- perature produces a weak curd that readily parts with its fut. • When the milk is too warm at the time of setting,. a hard curd which is difficult to cut is the result.

. It is imperative that the curd be cut skilfully, so that the übes; are uniform in size ,other Wise there will be an uneven drainage, and Come- „ . . qnently the Cheese will not be of uniform quality throughout. This is one cause of cheese going bad in parts.. The whey retained ip the large pieces of curd ferments when the cheese should be ripening normally. A very important point in cheesemaking is to stir the curd very gently at first, or.a lot of fat will be lost, resulting in a hard cheese that will not be mellow when ripe. The cheese yield will also be low, as the finished product should con- tain toughly about 30 per cent. of fat. The card is usually stirred by hand, but where a large vat of milk is dealt with, a, wooden stirrer is often made use of.

• In scalding curd the temperature must be raised very slowly at first, no quicker titan. at the rate of .1 deg. F. in three minutes. The maximum temperature of the scald will depend upon the variety olcheese being made, and the state of the Milk. • Scald higher with an -acid: milk, and towards the end of the season ,when the milk becomes richer in quality.

The ripening of the curd is also- of great im- portance, as upon the State of the curd when vatted will depend very largely • the '-quality of the ripened cheese. An unripe curd often re- sults in a weak cheese, which ferments wrongly when in the curing room. There are several methods of ripening turd, and. the one adopted should be that which is easiest carried opt under the axisting conditions.—" Farm and home."

We had our correspondent in camp and he has sent us interesting reports of the leading events of the training.
This week we are enabled to give a bird's eye view of the whole fortnight's work, written specially for us by a highly placed military expert. -
As will be seen, he has very little but the highest praise for the Warrington men, who turned up in great force and remained the strongest battalion to the end of the camp.
Whole Training Reviewed by a Military Expert.

Sion of each day's operations he •gave on the ground, to the whole battalion, his criticisms, which were very much appreciated by all ranks, and for which he was thanked, on behalf of the battalion', by the Commanding Officer. He had particularly noted the excellent bit of good scouting mentioned above, the individuals concerned being called .out by him and com- mended to the rest of the battalion.

The schemes were, however, car- ried out jnat as if it had been fine. The gorse

div.head: BIVOUAC.
div.p: THE BIVOUAC.

manded by General Lindsay, reached Denbigh early in the afternoon of Sunday,- August 17th. The training of the Division was carried out this year by brigades. The Liverpool Brigade trained first, being succeeded by ;the North Lancashire Brigade, followed in turn by the South Lancashire Brigade on ..August 17th. This brigade had trained for years early in August, always going into camp on the Sunday before the August Bank Holiday. The change of date bore very hardly upon many of the eni, ployers; and also upon many of the officers and men, and it seems a great pity that it was found necessary thus •to add to the many' difficulties of the Territorial Force'. The Officer Commanding the sth South Lanca- shire Regiment found it impossible to take his battalion to camp oo August 17th, so he Was allowed to train as .a siipernumary battalion with the North Lancashire Brigade, incidentally carrying away the silver cup given by the Mayor and COrporation of Debigli for the brigade sports. Not Withstanding f be. diffic:ilties inentioned above, the 4th South Lancashire ,was the strong- est battalion in camp. and took a very much larger proportion of its strength to camp than either of the other two battalions. During the *second week this advantage was considerably increased, as the 4th had only a net loss of 50 men, while the other two battalions lost three figures. Cleanliness of Camp.

! The 4th took over a standing camp from ow of the battalions of the. North Lancashire:Bri- gade, which they left in a filthy conditiOs. This being also a much weaker battalion- added to the difficulties of the Quartermaster (Lieutenant Ingram), who had hastily to erect more tents, and requisition for the necessary additional camp equipment, kte. • In a very short time the camp was thoroughly cleaned up, and the Quartermaster was able to show a camp quite Up to the standard of battalion, which is noted for ti spotlessly clean camp. - The men were fed in two half-battalion marquees as last year.•
and heather on the mountains were glorious, and their beauty was some consolation for a wet skin.

The battalion was formed into four double companies and carried out three individual schemes and one collective practice, under the supervision of General Sir W. Mackinnon, Major Allan (Inspector of Musketry), and sev- eral other staff officers from the Western Com- mand at Chester. As long as these officers were on the range they criticised each section after it had fired, which was very useful to all con- cerned..
. _ The first practice carried out was an indivi- dual one and. was done by a: double company, under-aptain Layton. Range: 300 yards.

Object: To teach men the difference in -cover from view and corer . from fire, reservation of fire, and mutual understanding as to -targets to be fired at, 'practice at moving targets: • The firing was supervised- by the Company Commander, hut the Itetual firing Was I.carried' out by the section. commanders. Each section ,advanced in turn to the 300 yards range,- where slight Cover Was improvised. Figure targets, representing an enemy's scouts, passed to and fro and kept dropping down, sometimes behind a bush. which was cover from view only, and sometimes behind • the • cover from fire. One section had 20 hits on the figures,. which was quite gOod shooting. This section oncentrated its fire on a scout _known to be in cover behind the bush, and therefore 'Stationary. The seoond PractiCe was also an individual one and was carried out by another double com- pany, under Captain Cary.
Firing•took place sit an unknown range across ,the valley at Tiles. representing a squad in pairs.

Object: To interest men, teach observation and impress the value of the first hit. The third practice was also an individual one and was carried out by another double com- pany, under Major Crosfield. Firing was car- ried out by sections at Tiles across the valley at three paces inter Val. • Object: A deinonstration to test. individual skill when shooting at an unknown range and to .nick out the best military shot in the sec- tion. Distance proved to be 459 yards. The last practice parried out was a collective one and was done by a 4th double company, under Captain Roberts.
Range, 600 yards: targets, four groups of figures on the hill side above the butts. Object: An elementary squad practice in fire direction and control.

The shooting throughout was quite good, and as the whole of the battalion not engaged in firing at the moment was in a position from which it could observe all that was going on, the day, from a musketry point of view,)vas very valuable to all concerned.

. Night Work ,and Night Operations. Tuesday and Wednesday, August '26tli and 27th, were, perhaps, the two -.most strenuous days of the training. • Oa Tuesday morning the battalion marched out to a bivouac about three miles along the Bettwys-road. On arrival in the field, as pre- viously arranged with the farmer, the battalion settled down individually to cook its own din- ners in the mess this, .officers helping to add to the stock of firewood -by-collecting loose sticks and brushwood for the men.

The battalion fell in about two pan. and practised by daylight an advance and a rush on a strong position which it was going to carry out during the night. This was carried out in absolute silence and With the close touch neces- sary in the dark, and the value of this pre- liminary work was very evident when the advance was so admirably carried out at two a.m. the following morning. After returning to the bivouac the men had tea, and all ranks, except the guard, dossed down under their one blanket.

At one a.m. the Commanding Officer sent out Major Appleton. the Sergeant-Major, one scout (lance-corporal) and a bugler on to the position to be attacked. The night was a very still one, and although nO. moon and few stars were visible, a veryl light one—in fact, an ideal night for the. watching piquet. The battalion had to: traverse in fours . a very stony lane, go through. a water-splash. aboat 'a foot deep,. get across an open field, go through a very stony gateway, itrici..then deploy in two lines of half- battalions on to the position. The first sound hoard by the piquet was -a slight ramp over stones, when a "G," as previously arranged, was sounded on the bugle. Next was heard a tramp or thud of feet on the ground, then voices at the foot of the hill (which must have come from a civilian), then a man's repeated cough, but although all the piquet werk listening with all their ears it was most. difficult to hear any- / • thing. and although it was evident that a force was deploying at the foot of the position it was impossible to see-theta until Some 15 yards dis- tant, there being an admirable background of trees behind the bnttalion. The. Commanding Officer was wily enough, not to cross the open field, as he had d'ohe'liV daYlight, but led his battalion along the hedges, getting very goo(' cover thereby. It would have been impossible for an alert sentrx. to realise that a whole bat- talion was advancing against his position. This

div.head: Manceuvre Areas.
div.p: Manceuvre Areas.

The country,round Denbigh, is very beautiful. The ,manceuvre areas were mostly close agri- cultural ones, and as very few of the cereals were cut, it was constantly necessary to move round growing crops. The areas were, )iow- ever, only a mile or so away from camp, so that it was only a short road march ,to reach any of them. This is a very great advantage, since so little time need be wasted in long and dreary road marches.
Sectional and Company Training

--- - The prevailing idea of this year's traiaing was to give a very careful individual trainin,f; to follow on with careful sectional and comp. Any training, supervised by Company Com- manders', the'brigade and battalion staffs. This FS surely very sound, and the ieSult was SOOR apparent, in the 'great increa‘e in efficiency in detail. If this is once attained it follows that when called upon to work as a battalion, a bri- gade or a division, the work of these units A ill correspondingly be increased in efficiency. The individual became more interested, learned himself to take better advantage of cover, &c.; the sectional commander got more. hold of his section, and the company com- mander and his half-company commanders found, as the result of their work, the general efficiency of their commands very considerably increased.

Inter-Company and Battalion Training. Company training was followed after the first few days by inter-company schemes. These had been most carefully drawn out, previous to camp, by Lieutenant-Colonel, Fairclough and the Adjutant (Captain G. Elgood), and proved most interesting and instructive. On Saturday, the 23rd, each company in turn took part either in the attack or defence of a convoy, iome of them in both, from which most valuable lessons were learned. On Monday, the 25th, one company_ and a skeleton. force,. under Captain Layton, with screens 'representing firing lines, tot* up in succession two defensive positions, being attacked by the rest of the battalion, under the Commanding Officer. ' These also proved most interesting and in- structive, and were; especially noted for a Very : smart piece of work by the Battalion Scouts, sent out by the Commanding Officer, one of whom crept up quite close to Captain Layton's: position and heard his dispositions for a retire_! ment to his next defensive position. The .pre- sence of the scout was eventually betrayed by his hand. Major Green's Interest. Major Green, commanding the South Lanca- shire Regimental Depot at Orford Barracks, who was present in camp as the guest of the aScers, mice more displayed his great interest in his sister battalion, and, at the invitation of Colonel Fairclough, acted during the *Saturday and Monday as chief unwire. At the conclu-

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT. Manager of Pawnshop Charged. CASE ADJOURNED. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. W. Roberts (in the chair) and other magistrates, Joseph Thomas Dolan, of respect- able appearance, 141, Lovely-lane, appeared in answer to four charges of embezzlement from his former employer, Mr. Benedict Tyrer, a well-known local pawnbroker. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted and Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defendant.

"Mr. Browne said was formerly the manager of Mr. Tyrer's Orford-lane shop. Some time ago it was found that there was a deficiency in the stock and the man was dis- missed. Certain examinations had been made of different accounts, along with the defendant's books, and they had picked out four specific charges, which they could prove up to the hilt. Prisoner had received no less than 27 payments and had not accounted for them in any way. Mr. Jenkins at this point announced his. in- tention of applying for a remand. Ile had only been instructed that morning and they had had no time to arrange the defence. As they had learned, there were a series of Offences charged aghinst the prisoner, to which he had stated he had a complete answer. If that was so, he should have the opportunity of prepar- ing his defence. Ile had been with. Mr. Tyrer for seven years and was starting in business on his own- account in opposition to. his late em- ployer. He had "put his stock in the shop, which was ready to be opened. The prisoner was exceedingly unlikely to do that were he not conscious that he had committed no wrong. The man had four children, the youngest of whom was seven years of age, and his family were exceedingly respectable people. Prisoner asked for a week's adjournment, and Mr. Jenkins asked for bail to be allowed. Mr. Browne said he had no objection to the remand, and no objection to bail, if it was high enough. The case was adjourned for a week, and bail was allowed in two sureties of 0f.:20. each.

Patrick did .not go, and was seen several times loafing about by the police. He was again ordered to appear in Court, did not do so, and sentence of 14 days' imuisonment was passed upon him in his absence. Green, referring to Alfred Brown, living in I lodging-houses, and charged with begging.—The Chief Constable: The witness is 'a Yorkshire- man, and the fact that he did not understand Brown's language shows it must have been some- what remarkable.—Five shillings, including costs, said the Mayor, and Brown understood that 'language, for he went below smiling hap- pily. AN ENERGETIC WOMAN.--r-It took a policeman and four. young men to convey Margaret Belliel ! from 9, Edward-street, where she was, fetund drunk and disorderly, to the Police Station in the early hours of Sunday morning.--4 The Chief Constable said that Margaret had struggled so violently that the. young. men were quite ex- hausted when they got her to .the lock-up.— Fined 109., including costs, or seven dais.

A WINDOW SMASHER.—John Loyden, 8, Orchard,street, was ,fined ss. and costs for hav- ing been drunk and disorderly.--It was stated that Loyden had smashed 20 panes of glass and all the woodwork out of the back windows of the house. ALL OVER TEIE Dni.NE:--4oseph and Thomas Caddick . (father and son), 5, Watkins-street, were charged with assaulting . and beating Catherine Caddick, wife of the younger pris- oner.—Both pleaded guilty in self-defence."— , The. Clerk: In self-defence of a woman !—The Chief Constable said that on Saturday after- noon the parties had been drinking, and they gave! the Woman a smaller amount than she thought she should have had. She remon- strated, and they struck her, bruising her face and arms very badly.—Prosecutrix said she had no desire to press the case. The whole of the trouble was caused through drink. • She was as much to blame as anyone.—Both prisoners said they were sorry.—The Chairman said that un- questionably a great amount of brutality had been used. She had pleaded on their behalf, as women generally do, and the prisoners would be ordered to pay 30s. and costs or in deflt one month's imprisonment. TROIZBLE OVER A LOAN.—Ellen Murrill, 4, Stoney‘yard, was charged with assaulting Mary trey, .2,• Stoney-yard, by striking her on the head with a jug on Monday.—The Chief Con- stable said that on Friday last complainant lent the prisoner threepence.. On Monday 'Mrs. trey went for the threepence, and prisoner failed to return it. The latter went into the house. but afterwards came ,out with a jug and smashed it across Mrs. Urey's forehead. The woman fell to the ground and lost a large quan- tity of blood. She was removed to the Infirm- ary, where three stitches were put in the wound. Wen charged. prisoner said, "I did it to defend myself.' The doctor had said there was no grave danger, but it was necessary that the case should. be adjourned for a week,— Prisoner said it was he.. who lent the other woman -fourpence. . Complainant, struck her first,—The case was adjourned for a week. CRUELTN• TO A • ITORSE.—ThArty Davies, 83, Bee- five-street, oil Earl-road, Liverpool, was sum- moned for having ill-treated a horse on August 23rd.—P.C. Cameron deposed to seeing prisoner in charge of a grey mare attached to a furni- ture float, belonging to Herbert Moores, 107, Park-road, Liverpool. He was in a striking attitude, and he (the officer) saw that the hind part of the horse was bleeding. there being about 20 or 30 small punctures. Defendant had produced a broken whip stock, from the end of which a small steel rod- was pro4.,,ruding. In the officer's opinion the punctures had been *caused by this stock. Defendant had - admitted strik- ing the horse, but said the punctures must have been caused by the curry comb.—lnspector Dee said the horse was in good condition, but the punctures were numerous, and the parts affected were very much swollen.—Defendant denied ill- treating the horse. He had knocked two heat lumps off with the curry comb, and that had caused the punctures. He had not been used to the horse, and had hit it to keen it from going to the wrong side of the road into the other traffic.—He was fined 20s. and costs, or in de- fault one months' imprisonment.

The husband had been working for Mr. Smith, a Warrington contractor, and after he had drawn his wages he went away and had not •re- turned: neither had he. communicated with his wife. NOT COMING TO WARRINGTON.

is so thoroughly discredited that although this is the "silly season" when editors are on the look-out for sensational news, they are not able to manage a single scare headline from all North-East Ulster. The rest of Ireland treats the "leader" with absolute indifference,. know- ing full well that the only people to suffer in the long run from acting upon his advice will be the men he, in his misguided judgment, seems to imagine he is serving by his pantalooning.

The question of Ulster women coming to Warrington when "shot and shell" begin to fly in the Northern Province of Ireland was mentioned by Mr. Sanders, Liberal agent, at the meeting of the Progressive Labour League at Bridge Foot on Monday evening. I find, said Mr. Sanders, that, after all, you People will not be troubled with the Ulster women in Warrington. From the Ulster papers I learn that the women have decided to stay alongside their husbands in the Carson "War." They are therefore not going to send, as Mr. Harold Smith said, 500 women to Warrington; they .are not even going to send half-a-dozen.

Perhaps ,you saw that at the -garden party at Walton Hall the "Examiner" had been referred to as a comic cuts. Well, we have seen nothing comical in the paper, except it be Mr. Harold Smith's- speech. (Laughter.) If you have read the speeches of Lady Greenall .and Mr. Harold. Smith.. you will say they are. :very. comical, stuff: (Hear, hears and applause.i They- are about The silliest. 'speeches any. Tories -have eve!' made,- and even the, Tories in Wai- ringfon, are disgusted with them.

Didyou notice that Lady Gr-e-e-n- all had got up on the public platform and said that if she thought any Liberal liked her she would be ' thoroughly ashamed of herself? We are not ashamed of .outselves as Liberals, and she need ! not feel any shame on our behalf. . When they say what they have said it shows thrit., the Tories are becoming afraid of us. The 246' votes' by which Mr. Harold Smith got in will be wiped off. • (Applause.) lam con- vinced that when an election comes in War- rin.gton there will be such a majoritk for the Liberal cause that Mr. Harold Smith will never feel fit tp fight again, and he himself will have to 'find 'fresh lOdgings. (Laughter and loud ap- plause.) I see the Tbries in Ulster have formed an Army Advisory Board. They will very likely give Captain Craig one of the most responsible positions, but you know they have not got an Army yet.. (Loud laughter.) The only man with any experience of war was a man of the name or Captain Ricardo ; probably this man was given in along with the dununy rifles com- ing from Italy. :(Loud laughter.) ! • '

Recruits from Germany. Sir Edward Carson has gone to Germany ,to try and get recruits. Captain Craig sent him his hest wishes, and he now calls Sir Edward "Prince Von Carson," or -something like that. Great. laughter.) As soon as the first shot is fired in Ulster, says Captain Craig, I will join you in Germany. (Laughter.) We have had Lady Greenall and Mr. Harold .Smith making speeches, and I defy any intelli- gent person •to find in these.- speeches one 'sensible argument. They are absolutely slang from beginning to end. They called us the "astounded party." Well, we are astounded at the silty things they have uttered, and they will be the astounded party when the result of the next election is declared. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: HUMBUG FROM HOMBURG.]
div.p: HUMBUG FROM HOMBURG.]
Warrington Irishman's Criticism of Sir Edward Carson.
STORIES FOR HORSE MARINES.

Sir Edward Carson, from his retreat in Hom- burg, writes to the London " Times" that, while he is not inclined, without inquiry, to agree With the Unionists of Derry that the police were responsible for the recent trouble in that city, Still he believes that because of the nearness of Rome Rule, the majority of the Protestants in the force will retire! We can imagine the omazement of the Protestant County and Dis- trict Inspectors—who form a number entirely, ont of proportion to the total of their co-reli- gionists in the force—on reading the statement that it is their intention to relinquish their Present very liberal salaries and settle down on pensions long before the time had arrived for stepping out of harness. And when this is Most unlikely to occur amongst the superior officers, it can be asserted with safety that the resignation mania being fostered by Sir Edward Carson will never affect the men in the ranks.

div.head: POLICE FORCE UNDER HOME RULE.
div.p: POLICE FORCE UNDER HOME RULE.

But Sir Edward is emphatic. The chiefs a Ids intelligence department, who must be- de, scendants of the. once-famous Marines. have Placed shim .in• a position .to write to that most veracious organ of puhlie opinion; the London: r, Times;" that : 'Protestants will not enter the Force which is destined to be engaged in the coercion of theirs co-religionists, and I believe, from the informa- tion furnished to me, that if the Home Rule Rill is put upon the Statute Book very many Of the Protestants will resign from the Force hither than place their services at the disposal of ati Irish Parliament and Executive."

Strange things are said and done every day. Nothing, however, is more remarkable than that declaration of Sir Edward's in the London "Times" on Saturday, that "it is absolutely certain that the proportion of Roman Catholics *to Protestants in the Force will daily increase," ,for, while the statement is intended to convey a !treat deal, it really means nothing new, as the `Proportion " of Catholics to Protestants in the Force has always been greater, everything Oonsidered, although no one would think that tile Catholics were in the ascendant to judge .from the shameful way the promotions have heen arranged in the past. His other statement that -When Home Rule comes the Protestants Will leave the Force, has in it, first, the adrais- 'Rion that ,a Native Parliament is certain; and, 'secondly, a declaration of a runaway policy Which does not fit in *ith the warlike utter- flee e of the more fierce of the 'leaders" 'friends.

- THE LAWLESSNESS OF BELFAST. New; if we were directing operations in the LI-nit:nista' ranks, we should, first of all, see that the Protestants in the Force did not clear out And leave the entire field to Catholics. This, .of course, is what any ordinary "leader" ICO4, ld give " instructions"' to have carried out; •Int, then, Sir Edward Carson is ',not a, leader, e 8 not possess the most elementary 'quartfica- Imes. and will land his Force into a morass, as Unionists will find out before they have done with him. A 8 to the character for lawlessness which he ime given the Orangemen of Belfast in his "tter to the " Times, it certainly goes beyond

div.head: SIR EDWARD AND THE CHURCH.
div.p: SIR EDWARD AND THE CHURCH.

With the taking • over of the control of the North-East under his Provisional Government, he has also included, it would appear, the man- agement of the Protestant Church, thus super- seding the Primate, for he has written "That as the 28th -September falls on a Sun- day this year, Ihope the clergy of all denomina- tions will think it proper to hold services speci- ally fitting to commemorate the day on which we- entered' into our Solemn Covenant. I am confident all Covenanters will he anxious in. this most solemn way to emphasise the seriousness of their action." One might naturally expect that edicts in connection with the services of a Christian Church should come from dignatories directly identified to control the Church, as well as the Custom House, the Volunteers, and everything else to be found within the confines of the North-East corner. One wonders, moreover, whether Sir Edward missed his vocation or not. At least, that is the reading to be taken from Sir Edward Carson's letter; but, then, there are many Protestants who resent his interference— and rightly—in this connection, just as strongly as others of the-same religion do, in his attempt to cause lasting hate bettween the Catholics and Protestants of Ireland. One of the former, who signed himself " A Loyal Churchman," wrote as follows to the "Irish Times" of irAdnesday, August 27th : " Sir,—lt is time r•icst some protest should be raised against politi.-4 leaders and party organ- isations arranging tor Church services. In the Church of Ireland, September 28th 'happens to be the 19th Sanday after Trinity, and the ser- vices are fully provided for; but Sir Edward Carson wishes it to be observed as Ulster Day, and to have the Covenant commemorated, and ft is to be feared that some at least of the clergy will think they are bound to follow Sir Edward's request Will the clergy of the Church of Ire- land please to remember that they cannot, at their will, or the will of any political leaders, alter the character of the prescribed services? Within a certain limited area the bishops may issue directions, and until they do so in this it is to be hoped every 'loyal' clergyman rill refuse all, outside interference."
Iftwe

So' that it. iitrquite possible the. clergy of the Church of Ireland may resent as vigorously all Interference by Sir Edward Carson as does " the Loyal Churchman" who has written to the Dublin Unionist paper. Burden?

div.head: BETTER TERMS CONCEDED.
div.p: BETTER TERMS CONCEDED.
Councillor Gough's Successful Motion in Favour

Gas was the main theme discussed at the monthly meeting of Warrington Town Coun- cil on Tuesday, and for two hours the mem- bers talked gas. The position of consumers through the auto- matic meter was fully discussed, and it was proposed to allow them a special discount of sd. per 1,000 feet. Speakers on behalf of the Gas Committee argued that the slot meter customers were being fairly treated, when the extra cost of such meters and the extra work in collecting were considered. Finally the proposal, which was made by Coun- cillor Gough, to allow the sd. discount, was carried by ten votes to nine. Alderman Tin- nion referred to this as "a stupid and foolish" act on the part of the Council. He argued that if these cencessions were made, the rates would increase Is. in the £ neat year.

For two hours gas was the subject- debated at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday night. The matter was raised by Councillor GOUGH, who moved "That all- slot meter gas consumers in the borough he allowed sd. per 1,000 cubic feet on all gas consumed on and after 30th September, 1913. "That all slot meter gas consumers in the borough pay a rent; of is. 6d. for each 3-light meter, and for each 5-light meter shall pay rent of 3s. per annum. "The discount allowed by the Corporation to the consumer 'shall he returned each quarter, or each time the slot meter is emptied of money. The meter rent shall be paid each quarter, or a quarter's rent kept out of the discount allowed by the Corporation by the collector each quar- ter, or each time the meter is emptied. "That all slot meter gas consumers in the borough, on and after the 30th September, 1913, shall pay a rent for all slot cookers or grillers supplied by the Corporation, who have not pur- chased them."

SLOT METER GAS CONSUMERS. Councillor Gough asks for a Concession. Councillor Gooon said the profits which were being produced by the manufacture of gas, not only by that Corporation, but in a great number of towns and cities scattered over the country, had been occupying the careful consideration of many Town Councils during recent years. The democracy were forcing the question to the front. Had Corporations a right to make large profits on the manufacture of gas to relieve tile rates? Whether local governing • authorities would have the wisdom to adjust that anomaly, or whether Town Councils, by holding back, would force the democracy to call upon their Parliamentary representatives to voice their grievance in the House of Commons, was not for him to say that night. For years past the Corporation had been trading with two classes of consumers of gas on a different system of pay- ment. To one customer, the ordinary gas con- sumer, vela() paid 2s. 7d. per 1,000 cubic feet, the Corporation, on purpoee to ensure prompt pay- ment on a given date, allowed a discounCof 6d. per 1,000 cubic feet of gas, which reduced his gas to 2s. id. per 1,000 cubic feet. The Corpora- tion, in order to develop the gas consumption of the borough and adjoining districts, and to meet a long-felt want of the working man, adopted, like other Corporations, a system of payment by slot meters. By the introduction of these slot meters the working man was able to get 28 cubic feet of gas for a penny. By that system the Corporation had been obtaining from the slot meter consumer 3s. per 1,000 cubic feet of gas. About four or five years ago the Corporation made. what the officials called, .a great concession. It. increased the number of cubic feet of gas for a penny from 28 to 31. where the Corporation supplied the fittings. and 33 Where the gas fittings belonged to the land- lord or tenant—it concession of fd. -per ~1,000 cubic feet. That meant that the slot meter consumer was new paying 28. Old. net for every 1,000 feet of gas he consumed.
of eoor Gas Consumers.

have to pay 41-d. per quarter for meter rent, but in return would get from the Corporation (like the ordinary consumer) sd. discount for every 2s. 6d. he paid for gas. If he burnt 4,000 cubic feet in one quarter he would get in discount Is. Bd. off 10s., the price of gas consumed. It was only natural that some member of the Council might ask: ." Suppose the Council adopt your motion to-night, how will it affect the estimate given on the 31st of March, which pro- poses to set aside‘ £13,000 to relieve the rates?" He did not think it would materially interfere with the sum set aside. From meter rents they would produce £962 9s. 6d., and from slot cookers and grillers £.724 17s. 11d. They would only require to make up the differenee,v.iz.,Xl,634, which was a small concession to ask the Col:fl- ea to grant to slot meter gas consumers, seeing .that. they contributed last year £3,320 175.. pro- fit over and above the ordinary gas consumer.

div.head: CRUX OF THE QUESTION.
div.p: THE CRUX OF THE QUESTION.

That was the crux upon which the difference between the ordinary gas consumer and the slot meter consumer hung. For years the Cor- poration had been doing a grout injustice to the working man gas consumer. he had to pay before he got the gas, and the Corporation had been making him pay 2s. Ceid. for every 1,000 feet of, gas he consumed. The ordinary con- sumer, the man who was well able to pay, and ought to pay the most, itany,class should pay more than the other, only paid 2s. Id. for every 1,000 cubic fe9t of gas he consumed. The slot meter consumer not only had to pay the price of the ordinary gas consumer, but an extra profit. Mr. Howard's statement, with which each member of the Council had been furnished, gave a vivid comparieop of both gas consumers, the number of eiibiefeet"btant and the price paid, by the slot meter gas consumer last year; also the same number of cubic feet of gas, which, if consumed through the ordinary meter, at the ordinary consumer's net price of 2s. id. per 1,000 -cubic -feet, would only have realised £14908 les. 4d. That statement clearly showed that tbe -slot tr consnmer jaw% a. profit of .23,320 17s. over and -above the 'ordinary gait ' consuiner'e irtfit for'tffo sainii-ntrniher Of cubic feet of gas. He was aigking far no favour. All. he asked for was administration of righteous- ness and justice. These were the foundation of all good government. He had heard, a good, deal of talk during his examination of the question about the gifts, benefits and favours which the Corporation had bestowed upon the slot meter consumers. Some said they were allowed free gas meters, without rent charge, but those statements would not stand the test of examination. One question would expose the fallacy of such an assertion. Why do the Cor- poration give 40 cubic feet of gas to the ordinary gas consumer for a penny, and only 33 cubic feet to.the:elot meter consumer for a penny? What did they stop seven cubic feet of gas for? Again, the Corporation said that if they charged Is. ed. for a 3-light meter and 3s. for a 5-light meter, it would produce for last year in meter rents the sum of £962 9s. &I. His motion proposed to give slot meter gas consumers 40 cubic feet of gas for a penny, and to let them pay meter rent.

div.head: 'ANOTHER GIFT OR FAVOUR.
div.p: 'ANOTHER GIFT OR FAVOUR.

He asked the Council to examine another gift, benefit, or favour, which the Corporation .allowed some slot .meter gas.consumers, to have. There were 3,081 persons using gas . cookers without paying -a rent charge, and ..he. submitted that these Were.as•well.ahle. to. pay .as the ordin- ary gas consumer for gas cookers. -It..was self- evident they had something to cook. There were 9,000 slot Meter gas consumers who did not use gas cookers, and 'only required gas for light- ing purposes; and it might be they were 80 poor that they had little or nothing to cook. It was ultra vires and unreasonable to ask these 9,000 poor slot meter consumers to pay a proportion for the 3,081 who were able to pay. If the Council confirmed his motion they would get the Corporation out of this. quandary by making those who used slot cookers pay a rent charge, , which ought to bring into the treasury of the Corporation an equivalent for depreciation and interest. ,

In his motion for the adjustment /of the anomaly that at present existed between the ordinary gas consumer and the poor slot meter consumer, he proposed that the Corporation should allow a discount of sd. for every 1,000 cubic feet of -gas consumed to all slot meter gas consumers in the boroukh. That would put both slot meter and ordinary meter consumers on an equal payment for 1,000 cubic feet of gas. That was 2s. 1(1. It ought to be obvious to every member who had given the subject an hour's _consideration, that the slot meter gas consumer must gain by that change of system. He would

div.head: TO DEAL WITH INEQUITY.
div.p: TO DEAL WITH INEQUITY.

Councillor PEACOCK seconded. He said it was five years since he advocated a similar system of dealing with the inequity in the supplying of gas to the slot meter consumers. Ho then sug- gested that a discount might be given when the inspectors went round to collect. It was stated that such was undesirable, and in the same words as the Gas Committee still used, he was told "It can't be done." He could not see why the discount could not be given. It would be no trouble to the collectors. The slot meter consumers got a smaller supply of gas, although they paid cash for it before delivery, while the ordinary meter consumers got two or three months' credit and discount. Such was most unfair. (Hear, hear.) In that case they were punishing the poorest of the poor, and now the way they were dealing with the cookers Seemed to relieve the difficul- ties which faced the question when he first pro- posed it. He would like the Council to con- , sider the poorer people, and if they did so, they would also do something to mitigate the smoke nuisance, for by encouraging the people to use more gas, it would tend to lessen the smoke. and he was sure. if Alderman Bennett had been present, he would have supported him, if only on the ground of lessening the smoke nuisance. In regard to a suggestion to give more gas by altering the wheels of the slot meters, they knew what that would mean. Six years ago they had promised to do so, and it took two years to have the work done. Alderman Tixriios : No.

... Councillor PEACOCK: I asked two years after the work had been started, and they said it WAS not done. but they were doing it as quick as they could. (Laughter.) It is very expen- sive to alter the meter wheels. I ask you to consider the poorest of the poor, who have to buy gas by the pennyworth, and at least give them the same advantages as you give to people who can afford to pay more.

FORTY FEET FOR A PENNY. Councillor WILSON expressed regret that he could not support the motion. Five or six years ago he had brought forward a_motion to allow- discount- to slot meter users, and it was defeated: In place a that it as said they were going to give more gas for a penny. The present- motion did not show either that they were going to give 40ft. a penny, or were going to place the slot meter consumers upon the same footing as the ordinary consumers. It was all very well to offer a discount of 5d., but they were going to make a five-light slot meter pay rent of 3s. a year, and he did not think that was fair. He would go all the way with Coun- cillor Gough if he would bring forward a motion at the next meeting to put the slot consumers on preeisely the• same 'footing as the ordinary consumers of _gas.

Councillor Grout:in: That is what I want to do. Councillor WILSON added it was not what was being done. He was sorry he would have to oppose the motion, because he considered the poor ought to have some consideration. He thought the happiest way out of the difficulty would be to enlarge the meter wheels and give ,401 t. of gas for a penny, and allow a discount on the same footing as was allowed to ordinary meter consumers.

CHANGE BADLY NEEDED. Councillor HhirriiouN thought most of them must feel that a change was badly needed in the method of charging for gas to the slot meter users. Many felt a great injustice was being done to those people who paid ready money, and were charged almost half as much again as the ordinary consumer. He could not altogether support the motion, because of the method by which it was proposed to make the re-adjustment.

11. thought it would be better to give more gas for the penny than to allow discount. The committee said that gas should be sold at 25., and the slot meters would have to pay 2e. 2d. even if they got the sd. discount, and that would still put them on an inequality with the other consumers. There would be great diffi- culty in carrying out the suggestions mid' by Councillor Gough, and he thought the time had arrived when the slot meters should have more gas for the penny.
COUNCILLOR 7 OSBORNE'S METHOD TO EQUA-LISS.

:Councillor aSomme said that, while agreeing Councillor .Gougb in his desire to give the slot meter, RAI*, fair play. he could not sup- port his resolution, because he did not think that he had submitted the 'beet method of: equalising between the slot 'meter users and the ordinary users. The tendency should be not to put a rent on meters, but to take it off. The Electricity and Tramways Committee had abol- ished meter rent for all installations of ekc- tricity for lighting purposes, and each con- sumer was now supplied with one meter free of rent. Why should the usets of electricty be treated differently from the lasers of gas? The statement prepared by Mr. Howard, the assist- ant secretary of the Gas Department, and accepted by the committee, did not, in his opinion, present a fair comparison, andzif the committee had based their suggested reduction on that, he thought it was unfair to slot meter users" Mr. Howard had adopted the principle of rent as the basis for arriving at his results in the first instance, and had then changed it to one of ' depreciation and interest. He did not agreo with that course.

-Having once adopted the principle of rent, it would have-been better if he had not departed from it, as he, was far more likely to arrive at ,a fair comparison that way. Take, for instance, the-manner in which he had dealt with thaaddi- tional net east of slot. meters. Slot meters cost more than ordinary.-meters, and it. was only fair, of-course, that: some eharze -should be made •for the additional capital expenditure'. It was not lair, 'however, to charge ten per cent. depre- ciation—which, after all, was. rent in-this Case— and four per cent. interest. If the life of a slot meter was considered to be only ten years, as compared with 20 to 25 years for. an ordinary meter, then the rent would naturally have to be more. But the only difference between the two meters, so far as he had been able to ascer- tain, was in the automatic contrivance attached to the meter, and that, no doubt, often got out of order and needed repair.

div.head: NOT AN EQUITABLE CHARGE.
div.p: NOT AN EQUITABLE CHARGE.

'Faking all that into account, it was certainly not equitable to charge anything like £1,448 17s. lid, on the extra expenditure. He next criticised the amount allowed for cost of cookers. He noticed that a sum of £1,827 lie. 6d. was put down— as 'cost • Of 'fixing, and taken into account. But the cookers on rent, .puichase 'rent, and to purchase, are fixed free to 35ft. piping, and therefore it was not fair to debit the slot meter users for any portion of that which ordinary meter users received for noth- ing. No allowance was made in the statement for the amount received for entering names: on I.the list for grillers, is., and cookers, 2s. If they

looked at the comparative statement they would find that instead of there being a deficiency of £472 14e. lid., it was easy to show that there was a surplus of .t5OO in *favour of slot meters. Then it should be remembered that people who were less able to bear the expense were being taxed most, and something should certainly be done to remedy that. He thought the slot meter users, even from the statement which had been prepared by Mr.. Howard, were paying far more than the ordinary users, and that should be remedied.

Elementary justice *should secure that if the large gas consumer, was able to get special treat- ment, if the user of an ordinary meter was allowed a discount on his consumption, the user of a prepaid meter should it least be consid- ered, and it did seem to him-an anomaly that no matter bow much gas a person used through a slot meter he had to pay the same rate as the smallest consumer.

div.head: "THE CORRECT POLICY."
div.p: "THE CORRECT POLICY."

Alderman .I'isxfox said. the policy of the Gas Committee was 'to charge every c(ansumer fair and equitable prices arm they should not charge one more than another because he received his gas in a •different way. In the opinion of We Gas Committee and the Engineer, Coun- cillor'S • Gough's resolution: was certainly •• not the best way. It was hardly a pradical way of meeting the difficulty, if .the difficulty existed.. The collection expense S-were already high and when. a collector went round—he was casting no reflection upon the collectors—what guarantee had they that the discount would get into the proper hands. Unfortunately the responsible. person was not always at home to receive the cash discount. He 'contended that to give such a discount; was not the proper .way to deal with the matter. .

In his opinion, when they supplied gas to a consumer. in whatever form he wanted it, the gas should be supplied at a cost which in- cluded everything,. and meter rents should be abolished._ They should have .one charge— so much per 1,000 feet, and do away with fancy charges. (Hear, hear.) The question became: Was the ratepayer or the gas consumer to be considered first? The ratepayer was the re- sponsible per-son; the gas consumer was not. A gas consumer to-morrow might adopt elec- tricity and shut off the gas, but the ratepayer was responsible for the Gas Works, and when he took that risk he should have the, profits. Councillor Gough had not made out what he intended. He (the speaker) denied in toto Mr. , Cough's statement. that his was the' proper way to deal with the matter. - It was =businesslike, and what he had suggested was altogether an improper method of handing money back. He would, not like to multiply the meter charges; he would rather decrease them or wipe them out altogether. It would be unfair to give the slot meter users the same quantity of gas they gave the ordinary consumer, because the cost of' delivery of the article to him was 'so much greater. The mechanism of the meter was also different. He asked the Council not to com- plicate matters, and whether the Council agreed or not that the slot meter user was unfairly charged, his own opinion was that he was fairly and reasonably charged. If there was an opinion that the charge was unfair, the method suggested by Councillor. Gough was not the proper method to adopt to put; the matter right. He trusted that Coun- cillor. Cough would see his way to withdraw the motion. "TO GET A PROFIT OUT OF IT."

Alderman BOLTON said the only way to handle a business was to get a profit out of it. He. found the slot meter users had a" grievance, because they only got 33 feet for a I.enny, in- stead of 40 feet, but evidently in regard to other things somebody had got hold of a mare's nest and had been mixing up capital expenditure with something else. They would have to pay £5Bl for cellectors and 4.212 for clerks—XB93 for collecting more than at present. Councillor (-)1301iNE: You are taking the debit and credit and adding them; you must deduct them: Alderman BOLTON: lam not. The clerks' wages have to be put down— Councillor OSBORNE: They should_ not be put together. Alderman Boutos, continuing, said everyone knew that as far as fittings were concerned, slot meter cost more, and needed more_careful handling and consideration than an ordinary meter. He did not wish to say that because a working man put a penny into the slot for his gas that he was not as much entitled to con- sideration as other consumers, but he believed that if the Council would leave the matter in the hands of the Gas Committee they would, if they.eould see their way to do So, help the One who brought in the most rmenue, and thus keep capital expenses down. • Every million feet of gas consumed meant that the capital expenses were reduced. The question which ought to be asked was, "Is the Gas Committee dealing equitabl with men as with anybody else?" The Gas Committee said they. were. They could always get outsiders who could tell them more about their business than they knew themselves. The gas was the best asset the Corporation possessed, and it was only through the gas that they could: get any profit out of the people out Side who bene- fited from their enterprise. , • • CONFUSED.THE ISSUE.

Councillor ROBERTS said Alderman Bolton had confused the issue. An injustice was un- doubtedly done to the slot meter consumer, as he did not get so much for a penny as the other consumers. The only way to have peace is to wait for the other fellow to begin the trouble. Crumbs of comfort don't always materialise from casting our bread upon the water. When you feel that you have the world at your feet, be careful that your foot doesn't slip. It takes more courage for a man to admit that he is wrong than to insist that lie is right. A Half and Half Bridge. Much amusement is being caused in Burton- wood- by the present state ef Causeway Bridge, which, according to the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, is "an 'absurdity." The bridge is on the bound- ary of the Warrington Rural District Council's area and that: of Newton.' -Recently the New- ton authorities painted their half of the bridge, and the other half was left, as Mr. Mitchell put it at the monthly meeting of the Rural District Council on Wednesday, in all its -"beautiful blackness." Mr. Newcombe, the 'Council's sur- veyor, stated that the matter would be put in hand at once, and the Burtonwoodites wills no doubt, rejoice When the WhOle-beidge sports its • new paint. •.

Liberal Van Lodgings. A wag suggests that the, Liberal van might be utilised, when the time comes, as a lodging- house for the women yefUgees from Ulster. Possibly the van would provide ample accom- modation for all the women who will -cdrae from Ulster to Warrington.

A Novel Tea Party. • One does not generally associate a drunken man with a lea party, but nevertheless a pris- oner at ,the COunty• Petty Sessions on Wednes- day stated that he had been to. a tea party, and got a lot of (kink. Natulifily enough; the curiosity of the Clerk was groused, and, in reply to .his question, the prisoner said it was a Labour Club ten party, and.there was a lot of free beer. The Clerk's final warning was, "If you go to Labour tea .parties you must drink tea." •

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6th, 1913.
LABOUR AND LEGISLATION.

Mr. W. J. DAVISv in his presidential address to the Trades Union Congress, made: a thoughtful and weighty defence of the value of the vote to Labour interests, as against the ,point of view of those who assert that Labour has little or nothing to gain from legislation. lie probably had in mind almost exclusively ,what, Jun), ,be called the Syndicalist view, which puts, all ,its, faith in the instrument of the strike and 'sneers at Parliamentary action. / - But his' discourse 'excited the indignation of the. "Times," which proceeded to read Labour a. lecture for condemning Itself to impotency by, its political associations. Certainly, some of the remarks made by the President of the Trades Union-Congress were calculated to pro- voke the great Tory journal. For instance, Mr. Divis said to his fellow-trade unionists:—
"With the Tory party neither you nor I can deal except by denunciation; it opposes all reforms except as matters of poljtical expedi- ency

"The insidious Tory- attack." Mr. ()Avis says, " to re-establish the tyranny created Ely the Taff Vale decision required all the ener- gies of. the Labour party to keep the Progres- sive forces united." When the "Times," joining hands unconscioAy with the Syndicalist cause, suggests that the Labour party has come to disaster through meddling With Parliament, there is a good deal of explanation required for the reCord of sOciat legislation which has been carried through_ since the Liberal ,party came into ofik*-,- and the Laliour party into eistenc.e, in 1906. That record includes Old Age Pensions; the Trade .Boards Act (for coin- bating: sweating, 'National. Insurance/Labour Exchanges, the Small Holdings Acts, and a Miners' Eight Hours Day. All this has been done without any additional burden of taXation upon the necessities of life. The Tory party makes it a condition of any social reform that the workers should consent to a bread-and- butter tax.
WHAT EVERY ELECTOR ,KNEW. The demand for a special General Election on
the Irish question is, if honest, sheer lunacy. AS Mr. Binami. says, "There was not an elector in Bristol or anywhere else who was riot aware that the approval at the polls of the
Parliamnt Bill meant the immediate introdue-

lion and the probable passing into law of a Bill setting up an Irish Parliament and Executive 'subordinate to the knperial parliament Suppose you.had a General Election to-morrow, who is to guarantee' that the Irish question will ic ,the sole, or even a chief, issue? In my belief, Home Mile was far more an issue at the last General Election than it would be .at any . election:that could now -be held."
