the statement- by Councillor Osborne that the Gas Committee had not only. made sufficient :profits to pay ; for the, purchase of .the gas. undertaking, but.. that they had, in the years 1910 and 1911, paid more in relief of the rates than they had made in proffisilfose years. The question .of adjusting the relative claims of tne gas consumer and the ratepayers to the bene- fits from 'gas profits is a " nice " one, into which many questions enter.

TERRITORIALS IN CANIP. From the ,report ,we give Jo today's " Examiner " of :the• annual encampment of the local Territorials—a report written by a' mili- tary expert—it Will be seen that the Battalion have well maintained their reputation. There are just two causes for regret. One is that there should have ,been a misunderstanding ahout the rations, an episode which appears to have been exaggerated out of all recognition; and the other is the fact that ,Warrington nowadays can find so few men to join the Bat- talion. However, we must not allow the short- cqmings of those who were not at Denbigh to detract from the praise due to those who were. They did .their duty:, well,, as will be seen from our expert's .critiiism, and it is to be hoped that their example may be a standing induce- ment to their fellows to imitate them. Lord Haldane's New Model is deserving of every sup- port. if only for the reason that it is the one effective_ barrier we have- to conscription. •

OUR MORIBUND DEBATING SOCIETY. We regret to hear that the Parliamentary Debating Society, v.-hich was established in such promising conditions a feW year ago, is in extrends. What exactly is the cause for the falling off that has taken place' in the more recent years of its existence is not known, riut some have been inclined ,to blame the political tone that necessarily accompanied• all its doings. Be that as it May, there is need in every ebm- munity for some centre at which the art of Public speaking may: be cultivated, and the Debating Society should survive in one form or other. An effort is being made to keep the organisation alive, the suggestion being that it should be run on general lines. If such an ar- rangement could be made, there is little doubt the 4society Would' continue to flourish—until the new style became old, when another fresh start could be made. For immediate purposes the question is: Are there a sufficient number of ambitious young men in Warrington to maintain such a 'useful and even necessary organisation?'

SMOKE PLAGUE. An article published in this week's' "Examiner " on the smoke plague as it affects America; makes the stock arguments of those who are afraid, or who pretend to be afraid, of tackling, the question, look extremely ridiculous. To those who put up their hands and knit their brows as an accompaniment to the declaration that smoke is necessary if we are to keep our trade, comes the reply that trade can be car- ried on without that excess of smoke which reckless manufacturers insist 'an throwing into the air for consumption by an innocent coun- tryside; those who say that 'smoke is not in- jurious are 'provided with a scientifically stated list of the constituents of smoke—carbon, tEir, acids and other minor things not Ordinarily regarded in the light of tonics. 'The deleterious' effect of smoke on -health' and vegetation is, clearly stated, as are' the means ready tp the hands of the•public for, ridding themselves of a pest which can be eradicated, and ought to be eradicated; -A cor,nmunity, like an individual, 'receives, -generally, Speaking, the treatinent it deserves; if '‘'VaiTington,consents to continue to- live •under elOud of smoke and breathe aeid-charged. air .when it: could ''easily 'live in clear sunshine and enjoy the delights and, ad- vantages of a Pure atmosphere, Warrington will hate only itself to blame.
• BY THE MOUNTAINS AD THE SEA. Here by the mountains and the sea Life grows healthy and sane again; All its worries and fevers flee, All its dragons of doubt and pain.
What is the worth of its minted gold Seen in the fight of these sunset skies, Or the rarest gems in its markets sold— Its blood-red rubies and pearls of price?
Where is the .organ whose deepest tone Can maieli the Music to? grand for speech When the waves by the wandering winds are thrown In a thunderous manner on yonder beach?
Above me,. eastward, the great sun glows, An altar On.!;the:mciuntaints.crest, • As the golden breeze of the morning blows And the waves creep up to kiss my breast.
I lave my limbs in the stream that leaps From the heart of the heather with shouts of mirth, Or under the hanging harebells peeps As I hail my mother, the green old Earth.
Here, where the amber waters drop Down to the depths of the dewy dale, ,Over the towering mountain top, Hiding its face in a silver veil.
No one present but 'God and I, How can I choose but pause and pray? EVety Ifichnitain 'touches Surely.' heaven Is "hear to-day I
There is calm in the sweep of yonder hills, There is strength in the silent peaks afar, There is peace in the sunset light that fills The purple arch where the planets are.
What if the friends I trust should fail? The everlasting mountains stand— What if the roaring storms assail? The stars are steadfast, the,sea is grand;
And I softly smile as I sing my song. For I know that the best must surely be: And life grows sweeter, and God seems strong, Here by the mountains and the sea. ARTHUR BENNETT.

div.head: WHO SHALL BE MAYOR?
div.p: WHO SHALL BE MAYOR?

There was a long discussion at the special Meeting 43.1‘ ttie Town Cbtinell'on 'Thesday night, when the question as to who should be Mayor for the ensuing year came up for consideration. It was proposed by Alderman Tinnion, who had first claim to the honour, but declined for busi- ness reasons, and seconded by Alderman Bur- ton, who was also asked to accept, but refused, that Councillor Peaco& be the Mayor. Plead- ing that seniority should not be overlooked, and also scenting a "political dodge," Councillor , Broadhurst proposed Alderman Bennett, who was seconded by Councillor Craik. Gradually the list grew until ,it also contained the names of Alderman John -Evans, Alderman 'James Evans, and Councillor H. Roberts. It was de- cided to wait upon these five gentlemen, and to submit the names of those willing to stand to a -futUre-' vote: of the Council. As to the Aldermen, it was somewhat hastily, at the end of what 'is described as a weary meeting, de- cided to Support the re-election of those who retire in November—Aldermen Smethurst, For- shaw, James Evans, John Evans and Bolton.

TIIE HOME .R.La.ERS OF ULSTER.. . As some people speak of the "woinen of War- rington " when they mean an insignificant sec- tion of the women of Warrrington, so they speak of Ulster, when they mean a minority of the people of that province who make up by Arrogance- and boisterous intolerance—not to say the thrOWing.of nuts and bolts at unoftend- ing workmate—what they.-lAck in--numbers and political' sagacity. ,From what .oile hears ocea.: stormily about Ulster., -one might, be inclined to believe that Ulster -Was against Home Bute to a man, and that a .grent, solid and menaced community -was combining to fight against a common enemy. But the fact is that in Ulster itself there are more M.P.'s returned to demand Home Rule- than of the kind who shout so vehe- mently against it. Even Belfast that, makes all this noise to make Ulster appear to be what it is not,- has its Nationalists. We have before us an Ulster paper which is full of Home Buie sentiment and ridicule of Sir Edward Carson and all his associates. The greatest part of last Saturday's "Ulster Guardian," in fact, is great, fun. There are articles on the ," Last bitch," "Ulster Day in Germany," the " Ree.og.: nition of the Ulster Provisional Government by the kaiser," "The Church of Carson," and the "Dummy War Office "—" a conglomeration of colonels and captains reinforced by three civilians, who scarcely know one end of a wooden gun from the _other, form the Board which is to give the British War Office .its quietus." There is Much dreadfully dangerous talk of this description. The imagination reels in the act of attempting to realise what will happen to the "Ulster Guardian" people when the Provisional Government has got to work, and the city is under martial law.
ARE THE,WONIEN COVENANTERS GOING
TO DESERT?

The greatest punishment will be reserved, we. should think, for the writer, of a column. entitled " Without 'Prejudice." This gentleman has read of the Walton Hall speech, to which a week ago we drew attention, and. prejudice or no prejudice, nothing less than boiling oil will meet his case when he comes to be sen- tenced. He reminds his readers that the Union- ist women signed the &Ileum covenant .to stand , by their Male relativeslo,_the last, and to shape their.- danger—yet the suggestion was made not by wicked Radicals or Nationalists, but by 'sound Unionists, that the women were no; .goinik•to desert. • Speaking at Warrington. continues the writer. Mr. Harold 'Smith, Nr.p.:• we..forbear; all our readers know What, he said '.abont;-theliroposal .to.dump Orange wompen- and children upon 'Warring_ ton. We give the •writer's comment; however, "Without Prejudice" sayS: Now I ask, -is this playing the game? Hay. jag won .our admiration for their ptudo resolve to stand by the men to the last, the Women-Linienists try to evoke our tears by drawing a pitiful spectacle of them flying as soon as there is trouble, to England fo; safety, "so that the men may be free." What a Warring-town will Warrinton be then! He then has something to say about the ,way these women-Covenanters are displaying their "wonted energy 7- before they leave an Army Corps of grass-Widowers behind them in Ulster —the energy taking the form of excluding, all from a certain -.bazaar who .were .not •..bf their. way of 'thinking, We could ''go' on indefinitely :finding. amusement from the pages, of the " Ulster Guardian," but we only desire to show that there is just breathing room in Ulster for a few besides the Ulster men of the blood and thunder and dummy gun variety.

div.head: GAS-COAL AND OTHER.
div.p: GAS-COAL AND OTHER.

It is a long while since so .much time was expended upon one single subject as wtfs spent upon the question of gas at the Council meet- ing on Tuesday night. Whether the sugges- tion, made by Alderman Tinnion, that we are getting near to the. November elections, had anything to do with the outbreak, we cannot tell, but it seemed at one period as though every member present was destined to join in the -fray, but _fortunately .we .Were spared that extreme infliction. Alderman Tinnion made a comparison between .the gas spoken .and the gas spoken- about; but some useful -information was laid before the 'Council 'with reference to the most. profitable .undertaking "owned by the town:. 'The- -question divided itself naturally into two parts, one as to. whether the.slot meter gas user is -"paying through the no" • as is so often alleged, and the other whether the gas consumer generally is paying an excessiVe price in order that large sums may be devoted to the reduction of rates. A Lively Episode Between Councillor Jenkins and Alderman Bolton.

The Cemetery • Committee recommended : "That the Cemetery gravediggers and attendants in the employ of this department, whose duties and remuneration are already fixed to cover Sunday work, be excluded from the scope of the resolution passed by the Council on the Ist July. 1913, with reference to the payment of a. rate not less than time and a half for such work." -

Clerk about the• matter, but now found they had been under a misunderstanding. The men were paid 245. a week, and 3s. a day for Sunday work. The 3s. was above the time and a half rate, and he thought in giving it the Cemetery Committee were, acting most generously to the gravediggers. Councillor DIcKENsoN said whe,n the men went off ill they got also a month's wages. COUREinOr BIRTLES said the 3s. was above time and a half rates. The MAYOR read the following letter received from Dr. Fox in reply to the resolution of sym- pathy passed at the last Council meeting in reference to the death of Dr. E. A. Fox :

_ "Dear Sir,—ln accordance with y—our request I have communicated to the other members of my family the terms of the resolution passed by the Town council at their last Meeting, with reference to the death of my father; Dr. Edward Austin Fot. I shall be glad if you will convey' to the Town Council on behalf of my family and myself our most sincere thanks for their: public expression of regret for the loss we have sus- tained and for their generous appreciation of my father's life and 'work. Although private rea- sons rendered advisable his residence in New Brighton during the last few years, all his interests and hopes were centred in Warrington, and shortly before he died he expressed his gratitude for the many kindnesses he had re- ceived from the people of Warrington and for the matiy happy and strenuous years he had lived in their midst, and-an earnest hope for the continued happiness and prosperity for .the people and town he 10-red_ so sçelL

div.head: LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
General Condition of Local Workers

div.head: to be Inquired into.
div.p: to be Inquired into.
TRADES COUNCIL BUSINESS.
BY A WORKER.

There were many interesting items of busi- ness brought forward at the monthly meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday night, several of which were of it private nature, but all went to prove that the interests of the trades unionists in the town are the dominant note. The .President (Mr. S. H. Smith) occupied the chair, and was supported by Mr. C. Dukes, secretary.

The Dublin Strike. In referring to the strikes at Dublin,.' Mid- Cornwall and Devonshire, the CHAIRMAN said he was sure their, sympathy would be extended to the strikers, especially in regard to the treatment which . had been meted out by. the pdlice. At the meet;ing of the Trades Congress on Monday a resolution had been adopted deprecating such conduct, and he felt that as a link in the chain of the trade unionists it would . . no doubt be thetr wish to endorse a similar one. The SF,CRETARY then submitted the resOlption, which read as follows :—" That this Colincil condepins, in a most. emphatic manner, the Goverriinent and the Lord Lididenant of Ireland for their action in prohibiting the holding of meetings in Dublin, and for the brutal manner in which the citizens of that city were treated by the police, which resulted in the hiss of two lives and injuries, to several hundreds' of people, and calls ,upon the Chief Secretary to re-establish at onee the right Of public 'meet- ings; And to institute a rigid: inquiry into the conduct of the police. We also view -With concern the growing tendency of pollee inter- ference in strikes • before their services are re- quired, knowing that inquiries into their con- duct never 'result in the responsible persons being made to suffer for their misdeeds."

The Police Methods. In moving this resolution, Mr. Dukes com- plained bitterly of the methods adopted by the police in their attitude to the men who under- took to'do picket duty during strikes. The Act of Parliament allowed such a practice to be carried on under certain conditions, and he contended that it was part and parcel of a con- stable's duty to be well informed of such things, whereas they were, in a large number of cases. not aware of the full privileges of the Act. After' citing_ instances Of unfair police 'actions; including the Dublin and Mid-Cornwall riots. Mr. Dukes said if instead of. allowing the re- sponsibility for the conduct of the strikers to fall on the leaders, who, in the majority of cases, were better able to handle the men, the authorities were going to arouse a turbulent 'spirit, by the action of the police, then they could only lay the blame on the shoulders of the Watch Committee. Mr. PUNSTON seconded and stated that the attitude of the police in Ireland was 'worse tha7 that of England. He hoped the day was not far distant when the police would receive adequate instruction in the duties of picketing. The resolution was carried, and the Secretary was instructed to forward copies to the heads of the various departments of the GOvernment. Labour Representation. The SECRETARY read a letter from Mr. Arthur HendersOn,,ln!which it was stated 'that in view of the forthcoming conference on the Trades Union Act, it was desirous that local organisa- tions Should discuss the question of Labour representation. It was 'very urgent that inter- est should be stimulated on this point.

Consolidating Local Trades Unionism. A discussion took ..place .on the; question of consolidating the various trades unionist bodies, many of whom were xiot, as yet, affiliated to the Trades Council, and, with this object In view, a delegation .was appointed to wait- upon the various .organisations, and-, place ,before :them the neCessity. for- combined unity.

General ,Conditions.:ot the Workers. The SECRETARY said he had. been in touch with. many influential men, who had placed before him the facts that large numbers of the workers lived under conditions that Ought not to .exist In •-Warrington.- He suggested that a com- mittee should be appOinted lo.,investigale into the housing (sanitary and . otherwise), rent, wages and food, and other conditions surround- ing the workers. It wag very important and they wanted to focus public opinion on these things. They wanted to prove to the workers and the townspeople generally that there Was an outside as well as an inside to the workshop. He was .sure it would have a good effect, and result in bringing more happiness into the lives of their fellows. After a discussion, the suggestion was adopted; and a committee was formed. The ArinnolAlfeeting. The CHAIRMAN announced that at the next meeting the annual business of the Council would provide the agenda. The nominations for the various offices Were then dealt with, and the following were pro- posod president, Mr. S. H. Smith • vice-presi- dept Mr secretary, fr cDue, treasurer,. Mr. J. Haley; Executive Committee (Seven), Messrs. J. Morris (Co-operative em- ployes), E. Bandies and T. Millar (Gas Workers and General Labourers), T. Mitchell and S. Howard (Stove Grate Workers), R. Whitby (Crane Drivers and Enginemen), Quinn (Ham- per Workers), A. Eden and H. V. Wakefield (Wire Drawers), and J. E. Shummin (Postal Workers).

div.head: CONSTITUENTS OF SMOKE.
div.p: CONSTITUENTS OF SMOKE.

1. Carbon in a finely divided state.—This, as is well known, is lamp black, the basis/of4nost black paints, and has a great covering power. It has the power of absorbing the corrosive acids which are produced by the combustion of coal containing sulphur. _

2. Tar.—lt is common coal tar which makes the soot cling tenaciously to everything with which it comes in contact. Tar 'contains car- bolic acid, and a large number of ,other com- pounds of an injurious nature. •

3. Acids.—Sulphurous acid, sulphuric acid, hydrogen sulphide, hydrochloric acid, to- gether with a number of organic acids. These acids corrode .and tarnish all the common metals. They attack many of the stones and building materials, especially limestones. Draperies, paper, paints and other decorative materials suffer to no less' extent. In burning the sulphur in the coal, the relatively inactive sulphurous acid is for th 9 grgater., part pro- duced, but this soon becomes oxidised in the air to the far more active and corrosive sul- phuric acid. These acids are also poisonous and detrimental to health.

4. Ash.—This is the ,least injurious of all the constituents of smoke, and may be, for all practical pUrposeS,;cOnSifiered as common dirt. , The amounts of these constituents of black smoke vary between the widest possible 'limits, depending 'upon the cOmposition of the coal, methods of firing, amount of air, temperature of the 'ficnace, Sro. Whon soot is. produced, a large percentage of the, .acid- is occluded in: the soot. 'where ,it is more injurious than- if allowed to escape alone into the -414 r. The soot Coming in contact with' metal, stone, decorations,. Szc., is made to adhere firmly by means of its tar content, in reality covering the surface with a coat' 'of' black paint. -The acid is. not readily Washed away by the rain, but continues to act.until it is used up. Interior draperies and paper are soiled much quicker in a smoky city than elsewhere. The acid in the soot attacks draperies, rendering. them useless in a short time. The extra wear of 'cleaning shortens the life markedly.

In a smoky atmosphere the sunshine is less intense, the short wave length of. blue light suffering the greater depletion. Daylight, which' Often 'depends entirely upon dirfutSed' light, is depleted by smoke in greater propor- tion than direct sunlight. 4.

The Chief Constable's ,Holiday. „ . The Chief Constable of Warrington, Mr. Nichols, resumed his duties on Monday, after his annual vacation. He spent a pleasant holi- AO -at Ithyl.

div.head: Successful Warrington Esperantist.
div.p: Successful Warrington Esperantist.
Miss D. E. Parsonage, the secretary of the Warrington Esperanto Society, has passed, with honours, the preliminary examination of the London British Esperanto Association.

div.head: Harvest Festival.
div.p: Harvest Festival.

Harvest festival services are announced to be held to-morrow by the Spiritualists in the Druids' Hall. The speaker is Mrs. Richardson, of Northwich. A public tea, followed by a social, is to be held on Monday evening.
Sale of Furniture. Mr. Frank Hickman, auctioneer, announces an important sale of furniture, %, modern and antique, to be held in the OM Music Hall, Market Place, on Wednesday, September 176.

Progressive Labour League. The speakers at the meeting of the Progressive Labour-League at Bridge Foot on Monday even- ing will be Mr. P. M. Oliver, prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, and Mr. E. Wynne Jones. Mr. James Elwell, jun., will be chairman.

div.head: Assistant M.O.H.
div.p: Assistant M.O.H.

A month ago we announced that Dr. Lumb, the assistant medical officer of health, had been selected for appointment as the School Medical Dfficer.for-,Jarrow. Dr. Lamb has decided not to Accept the ,Appointment, but Will remain in Warrington.

div.head: Footballers at the
div.p: Footballers at the

The playing members of the 'Warrington N.V. Football Club visited ' the Hippodrome night, upon the kind invitation of Mr. T in' the manager.—The committee of the ltcalusbhuarvPereceived an invitation to attend the opening of the Runcorn N.U. Club's new ground to-day.

div.head: Scourge of Summer.
div.p: The Scourge of Summer.

There were seven deaths recorded in Warring- ton last week from the scourge of summer— diarrhwa. These deaths were of infanta, the spell of warm weather being the primary cause. Three died in each of 'the past two weeks, and two the week before, 15 thus having died from this disease in four weeks. Six new cases of scarlet fever have been reported.

Lawn Tennis Matches. Crosfield's Lawn Tennis Club' defeated Ash- ton on Saturday, at Ashton, by seven events to five, 17 sets to 14, and 163 games to 148. The Crosfield team, against Newton, at Hood-lane to-day, will he: Misses A. Jackson, E. Jackson, ilazlett, C. Jenks, S. Jones and F. Bennett; Messrs. W. Barlow, A. S. Percival. (captain), J. Snelling, G. Evans, H. Sandy and E. Yeadon.

div.head: More Births Than Deaths.
div.p: More Births Than Deaths.

There were six more births in Warrington last week than deaths. The births numbered 33 (14 males, 19 females), and the deaths 27 (15 males, 12 females). The birth-rate was equal to compared with 31.9 for the same week 234. last year; the death-rate was 18.9. With the exception of Wigan and Oldham, Warrington had the highest death-rate in Lancashire last week.

div.head: Visit of Mr. Francis Neilson, M.P.
div.p: Visit of Mr. Francis Neilson, M.P.

A great open-air mass meeting will be held under the auspices of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association at Bridge Foot on Friday. The speakers will be Mr. Francis Neilson, M.P. for Hyde, and Mr. J. B. Martindale, prospective 'Liberal candidate for Widnes. Mr. C. E. Parker will be chain:Attu, and, should the night ,prove- wet; The meeting will beheld in the Co- operative Hull.

Junior Conseyvative Women at Bowls. r On Thursday the annual bowling main for the lady friends of the members of the Junior Conservative Club took place in favourable 'Weathei.. There were 88 competitors, including Mrs. J. Holbrooke,_who is 74 years of age; and -a I member of• a noted • local bowling family. Tea. as provided by Atkinson 's Cafe. The first prize winner was Mrs. G. Gilks and the second prize winner, Mrs. T. Clare. Junior Liberal Fete.

• The Warrington Junior Liberals are holding a,: garden fete and sale of work at Lodge-lane, Bewsey, this afternoon, in the grounds of Major Crosfield. The fete will be opened by Mrs. E. C. Osborne, the hon. secretary of the Women's Liberal Association. Sports will play a, pro- minent part in the afternoon's programme, and Mrs. Peter Peacock is to present the prizes. Special attention has been given to the attrac- tions, and a thoroughly enjoyable time should be spent. Tea will he provided in a very spacious tent, and a band will play at intervals during the afternoon.

ThefProphets Went Astray. Warrington shared in the exceptionally high tides which visited the Mersey this week. The wat,er,rose on each tide three feet higher than the prophets Who compile the tidal almanac, predicted. The exceptionally high tides caused the roadway beneath the Arpley railway bridge to be flooded, and had the river happened to be in flood, instead of being very low, owing to the drought, some damage might have been -done. As sit was, the,work at the, Bridge was hampered by the high state of the tides.

div.head: Old 'Warrington Musician Dead.
div.p: Old 'Warrington Musician Dead.

It is With regret that we record the death of Mr. Reuben Weston Manning. at 23, Dixon's Green, Dudley, Staffordshire, on Thursday week. Mr. Manning will be remembered by older Warringtonians as the conductor and leader of the Court Theatre orchestra in Mr. Joseph Potters day. He was 71 years of age, and was well known in Warrington as a cap- able violinist.

Co-operative Employes as Bowlers. The Warrington Co-operative einployes, on Thursday, visited the Stamford Arras bowling green, Bollingtein, in. order to play .the semi- final and final. rounds for the ' Tryiner Cup and 'gold. medal.. - ,The preview round.s were played at the Verniers' Arma, ..Vearnhead. the senii-final E. 'Eyes_o3) beat J. Ilardirig and A. Waring (13) beat S. Appleton T 9): In the final Eyes defeated Waring 13-7. In a consolation • main, in which 16 prizes were awarded, the first, place was secured by A. Gleave, who beat W. Mann, 13-3.

div.head: Singular Fire.
div.p: A Singular Fire.

_ The Warrington Fire Brigade received a somewhat singular call to a fire on Wednesday night. Near, the "Griffin,": on the outskirts of Bold, 17 bales of cotton, which were being conveyed from Liverpool to Shaw, Oldham, had caught fire. Sergeant Monks, with nine men, was quickly on the scene, and the flames were eitinguished, but not before much damage had been done by fire and water. The lurry was " standing " for the night and the cotton was being conveyed to the Trent Manufacturing Co., .Shaw, near 'Oldham.

Display of Fancy Dancing.

patronised by the Mayor and Mayoress, a pretty display of fancy dancing was given in the 'Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening by the juvenile pupils of Miss Gertrude Brown, whose classes are held in the Hall Cafe, Stock- ton Heath. There was a good attendance, and the exponents of the terpsichorean art were loudly applauded. A capital programme of dances was gone through, and at intervals Miss Clarice Newall gave pianoforte solos in an ex- pressive manner. Miss M. Southerden executed the fan dance in an exceedingly graceful man- ner, and Miss M. White danced the Highland fling in truly Scottish fashion. The fascinating Italian dance, " Tarantella," was given in an artistic manner by the Misses M. Southerden, D. Tyrer, and H. Doraville. A pleasing spec- tacle was the gavotte, in which the Misses M. White, H. Doraville. L. Hough, D. Tvrer, M. Houghton. M. Newa.ll,ll. Deakin and M. South- erden took part. As "The Ragtime Coons," the Misses M. Houghton and M. White were a decided success.

div.p: TIIE EXAMINER,
WORKERS AND EDUCATION
The Claim of the Democracy to University Instruction.
LAST NIGHT'S W.E.A. MEETING.

Interesting information concerning the 'Wcirlorrs' Educational Agas, "CleliC4las.,given,to a meeting held in the Warrington Technical Institute last night, for the object of forming a branch Af the association in Warrington. Mr. J. Wore Murray preside, and Congratu- lated the organisers of that meeting on the suc- ceBs they had achieved in getting such a large number interested in the movement. The local authority would cordially wOcerne the formatiorr of a branch'. LEISURE-HOUR EDUCATION.

. . . Professor Weiss: expressed on beralt of the Manchester University their hearty good wishes, for the success of the Warrington undertEtking. Inquiries were now being made by committees: faosundto w.thhaet:ori;drnsg:v.mwernrei.:rtvriooucllid4iligkeai!n, ththeedw:o‘ry of further higher 'instruction. For the first time in the history of university education they and asking 'for admittance:. The workers were now .managing their own association branches, and asking for the particular courses they Ete. sired. They wanted to give; the workers a radical change of thought arid occupation for their 'leisure hours, such as a stbdy of music, art.. literatures and natural! science.. He be- lieved the man. who had the power. to throw ITimself fully 'and heartily into guar a hobby, which might mean serious studr,--was. the hap- pier man than the one vvilo had, perhaps:, More leisure-, but no. hobby, to extend. his educational and -physical energy... They. wanted to eduCate Those men who were concerned in making taws and those who elected' the taw Maker's. They. wanted a thinking, educated, Cultured commu- nity. and until we had that we should never be: out of our troubles. If the workers were eduL- cated he felt sure that we need not fear any- thing for the country. He hoped that -War- rington, which was the home of learning in the past, would have, a splendid association. They looked to the Warrington Academy with great reverence, and awe, because they did a greater educational work when Manchester, in that respect," was in its infancy. They looked to Priestley and other Warrington educationists as beacon lights of the past, and they hoped Warrington would not belie them at (he present time. ,(Applause.)

Mr. frookwaY Shid they wanted to get at those workers who strove for tile general' up- lifting and success, of the State. On the proposition of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Mr. J. Jarman, it was decideil to form a branch, and a provisional committee was appointed.
THE WORK OF THE ASSOCIATION.
"An Old journalist" writes

Last evening's meeting to inaugurate a War- rington branch of the Workers' Educational Association, made me long for space in which to enlarge, from my own knowledge, of the achievements Of that excellent institution. As Mr. Mansbridge, its founder and inspkrer, once observed, the need of the times is not a system by which a few clever boys and girls may be prepared for scholarships and helped to rise to places in the Government service or offices, but a system by which every man and woman. in their own vocation and industry—labourers and servants, as well as professors and cap- tains of industry—may be able to do their 'work with intelligent interest, and enjoy Abair leisure with satisfaction to 'their .being., The .N,V.E,A. is admirably calculated' to 'meet this want. The,lasktimal: met Mr, 'Flookway-;. trie oropising'•segretary of the.North-Western dis- trict (who. at:dressed:the Warrington meeting), he made special reference to the development ,of.. a higher type orserious studie.s fji work-. people in the _tutorial (-111S.ses, Which were. re- ,garded,- be Said, .by some eminent .ediication- alists as the highest. type .of adult 'education" that England had ever seen. The subjects were chosen by the students themselves. The greater nisabe9. of those now being held dealt with economics and industrial, history, but classes had also:been.held -in such subjects as philosophy, 'natural science and English. litera- ture. At,each meeting Of the-class there was an 'hones teaching, followed by an hour's dis- cussion. and in addition library facilities were offered by the University. and additional pro- vision, for , the continuation, of the students studies either at Leeds University or one of tht ancient Universities of Oxford or Cambridge. Mr. llookway further Mentioned that in four years the number of tutorial classes had in- creased to 110. with an average attendance of 30 students, thus bringing within the realm of Univer§ity education over 3,000 working .nin,Tl and women students. I can personally testify to the excellence of the work accomplished by this means.

div.head: SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6, 1913.
div.p: SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 6, 1913.
MR. E. WYNNE JUNES
Accepts the I `astorate of Zarlestown Bapt, .st Church'
-- A POPULAR PREACHER.

div.head: MR. E. WYNNE JONES
div.p: MR. E. WYNNE JONES

so well knOwn as a public speaker,, but better known as a first-class preacher, after having resisted two previous invitations to accept pas- torates,- has' consented, owing to. its unanimous and pressing nature, to accept-the invitation of the Earlestown Baptist Church to -become their lay pastor. "Mr. "Jones has -preached at Earles- town at least: thirty- times,- and the " ctill,"-after so full an experience, is especially gratifying. The church -at Earlestown- has-good premises, with excellent School accommodation, 'and there being a. fairly large number in attendance, the opportunity provided for Mr. Jones is distinctly -promising. Mr. Wynne Jones- has preached in almost every Free Church in Warrington and district, and is well known as a Brotherhood speaker, not only here, bid in, many Lancashire and Cheshire tOwns. Considerable pressure was ,hrougtit to.hear upon him in his earlier years to enter the Ministry,- and although he obtained an application form for admission to the Theo- logical College, and still 'possesses it, he felt that he was unable to go forward at the time. He has been actively engaged, at GOlborne- street Church, Warrington, for 'many years, both as an officer. of the church and president of the adult class. He intends to continue to reside in Warrington, and, so far as he is con- cerned, the change will merely mean that in religious work he will concentrate, instead of serving so many churches, as in the past.

div.head: "WARRINGTON DAY." Festival at Liverpool Exhibition.

The Mayor, Dr. Joseph, and several, members of the Warrington Town Council, are to be present, on the invitation of the manage- ment.
• Bands from Warrington will figure largely in the ,programme, of ,the day. The ,Pioneer, the Borough and the League of. the Cross

Band's are.-to compete for -a handsome, silyer cup. Irhas long been a mocit point as 4o which of the. trio were entitled to rank as *the premier band of the town, and this contest should lead' td'a 'definite regult. The band con- test, otight to prove an attractive feature. A singing _competition has- been arranged, and in this ,WarringtOn choirs will. he the com- petitors. 'Amongst the entrants are Bewsey-, road Wesleyan, Bold-street Wesleyan, Bank- street Mission and Stockton Heath Wesleyan Choirs. The Mayor will 'present the prizes in the spacious carnival hall at 6 p.m. . The band .at the exhill4,on, next week will be that of H.M. Grenadier:GUards, under the Con- ductorship of Dr. Williams, the skilled band- master. The Exhibition Cencert Party are to give a special programme for the Warrington Day, andlheir repertoire will include items of much interest to Lancashire folk.

div.head: TERRIERS TROUBLE.
div.p: TERRIERS TROUBLE.
A Misunderstanding which upset the Denbigh Camp.
HUMOROUS POSITION.
It was with fear and‘trembling that one went - to Inca the Warrington Territorials upon their home-coming on Sunday. After the alarming

reports thaE the men had mutinied, one ex- pected to find at least simile of the men absent, and to learn that they lay corpses on the soil of Wales in consequence of the mutiny. - All, bronzed and jovial, returned, note even a little bugler was mis Sing. , The trouble which arose on the second last day in camp 'seems to have been the &Income a misunderstanding. One day in- camp, the men; according to regulations, were to haire half rations only, just as might happen in actual warfare. In past camps this was ,ang- niented by supplies provided wit' of the batta- lion fund; MA on this occasion the old cuStotn for some i.'earoM or other was not adopted, and the men, u'ho VP ere in the main not aWare of .the nature.,,oi the regulation .which .order: half rations, thonght ',they were Unfairly' depinved of a full breakfasG and they, good humouredly made their protest. , "The whole trouble :trose," spid one of the. men, "through the. men -.not being aware of the regulation which placed them on half rations of preserved food for breakfast.' The messing ar- rangements had also • a good deal to do with the matter. Up till -two years ago eight or nine men would"mess together in one tent, but now We mess-in a. large tent. There were long tables and those at-. the -ends nearest the serving orderlies. got the greater share .of -I-he food- and others at the top got, precious little. Each of us were served out .some army biscuits and .a tiny. bit of tinned salmon.

div.head: CALLED FOR BREAD
div.p: CALLED FOR BREAD

"This was supposed: to tie the quantity allowed, but as the men did not understand the rule they called for bread. In ,the ordin- ary rations we were allowed 11b. of bread each. Some bread was brought, but it was promptly commandeered by the men at the foot of the tables, and those at the top got some biscuits and about . a square inch of salmon. Ido not think live-Sixths Of the men got even the proper. half rations. _

"The men decided that they would not work upon the small allowance of food, and. when the orderly officer came round he was greeted with sarcastic cheers. Td him the men, said they would not go out. There was no actual leader amongst them; all were agreed they would not do further soldiering on the small breakfast- received. Finally, after the Colonel had reported that the men would not parade, we 'got a second brealaast. "For a time the situation was more humorous than serious. Some one struck up an extem- pore song, rhyming the words 'Bread, bread, give Us bread,' to the tune of 'Lead, kindly light.' The men took up the chant, and for some time it was heartily sung in both of the messing tents. Finally, we got the bread.. "All the week there was a feeling amongst the men that they were not getting full rations. ('hat feeling was caused by messing the men together in a large marquee. If, as was done until two years ago, eight or so m6n fed in small tents,Jhey''Would have been able to check the quantity of food.

div.head: "THAT IS ALL NONSENSE."
div.p: "THAT IS ALL NONSENSE."

"I see a local paper said that the food in :Amp: was better than the -average nian'got at ;low. That is all nonsense,:.and rubbish. If it was so, how Came it there whs a deeided im- provement in the; food immediately -after -the trouble?. The -diriner--we- got on' Friday was the .best given the whole time we were in camp,. but even that was .not equal to what the ordin- ary ,inan gets,. at home:. Just before the Camp. broke -up . there were .sorne. lively doings. The adjutant, whO ,was extremely popular with the men, had pleted his term of office and was retiring. The men decided to "chair" him, acCording to camp custom. He was invited into the N.C.O. tent., while the Iwo bands and , the men stealthily assembled- , outside. . A chair was' fixed, upon a ,stretcher.

div.head: HUNTED TIIE ADJUTANT
div.p: HUNTED TIIE ADJUTANT

.When the adjutant rose to depart, he saw the trap into which he had been enticed, and sought to .avoid it by running round the tents. An exciting chase followed. Nearly all' the bat- talion, in al.l states of dress and undress, gave hunt, and after a few minutes they succeeded in capturing the adjutant and fixing him in the chair. He was carried shoulder high round the camp, the bands playing lively music, and nearly every. "Terrier" in the camp taking part in the procession. After the adjutant had been deposited. at•his tent'it• cOrtibral' was'hoiSted into- the' Oak .arld carried through the lines. All the way he was heartily' bombarded with pillows. .

The new motor fire engine, which Leyland Motors, Ltd., Leyland, are about to deliver to the Warrington Corporation, is of the firm's standard_ size and is similar to the one they have supplied in grqat numbers of late to various municipalities, including the L.C.C.,. Hobart, Shanghai, Calcutta, &c. It is fitted with their powerful 55 h.p. engine, and Bees' Floturbo turbine pump, and is cap- able of delivering 450 gallons at 1201 b.• per square inch,' 580 gall Ons at 801 b. per square inch, and 380 gallons at 1601 b. per *square inch. It has a maximum lift of 2811., and is capable of attaining a speed. of 40 miles pef. Nur. It is arranged for fitting a large " Ajax " escape' and telescopic ladder, as seen in the photograph. It is also fitted with a 40-4allon capacity first-aid attachment, besides additional hand fire extinguishers. • The tyres have been made by the St. Helens
ICable and !lubber Company, so that the , machine throughout is made practically in thol, I Warrington district.
ST. HELENS CABLE WORKS TYRES
The massive rubber tyres Used on This vehicle are Of the very latest type.

They are an example of .the enterprise of local firm—the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company, Ltd.—and are the invention of !heir Works Manager (Mr. E. Seymour). They are like other heavy motor tyres in appearance, but otherwise they are .quite dif- ferent. The patented feature consists of inserting in the body of 'the tyre a specially- shaped layeAopad of absolutely pure and soft indiarubber, whiCh adds greatly to the resiliency. ,The Cha.sis and :niachinerY are thus largely relieved 'of the destructive strains due- to road impact mad vibration, with

resultant economy of upkeep. There are six tyres in all, those on the back wheels -beng "twins." V s Distributed in this way they carry the load much better, as • well as counteracting any tendency, to skid:** They weigh not less 'than six cwt., and cost nearly £lOO. They are moulded under a hydraulic pressure of about 100 tons, to give the greatest possible homo- genity, and every care is taken to make thein .absolutely reliable. This,' of course, is a matter of great importance with such a vehicle as a fire engine. .' They are of exaCtly the same type as used so successfully on the War- rington motor 'buses. .‘ The St. Helens Cable Company repqrt that this tyre is meeting with such unexampled approval all over the country that. they are finding it necessary to set down plant to enable them tq double their already very large output:

div.head: "MISS HOOK OF HOLLAND."
div.p: "MISS HOOK OF HOLLAND."
Musical Society's Opera to be Presented Next Month, THE CAST: SOME NEW PRINCIPALS.

I With the approach of autumn, and the com- ing of the longer nights, one's thoughts turn naturally .to the events .which the opening musical and theatrical season Inay have in store tor us. . One of the brightest of the pioneer..fix- tures that we have been taught to look forward to is the Warrington Musical Society's annual venture into\ther,palnis-sof nu)siCal comedy and light opera.. That the management of the society's opera section has this year chosen "Miss Hook of tkiiland ." for presentation at-the Royal Court Theatre in' the- nifddle 04 October Will, we feel sure; be matter for public con.: gratulation; for the Warrington public having already made thy acqVaigunce of "Miss Hook" and evinced a Ng* apptecfation of its charms, the conviction thaf members- of the MUsicat Society's Opera Cosupany would do well to undertake the perroMonte of this favourite work his, we believe', often been expressed.. From Mr: Bond, the honorary secretary cit the Misled, Sociefy'S Opera contingent, we learn that thelgettliiig up of sMisS Hook"-is now crell al divantkdy, thanN toa uilinber of rehearsals- which are always- entered upon in the early summer. These' practices;, Ssi.Wended for holi- days &witty the, niorttli! of August, have, we understlantkbeen)already resumed in all serious- ness, for,, at this-point,-the onesTas work of Mr. •Lomax, the coach and stage manager, begins- to supplement the equally respouSible training: of Mr. Crustey, the society's Muilical director and condlittior.. -

Speaking in "The Play. Pictoriar of the in- ception of "'Mass Hook,", and of PL/... Paul A. Rubens, the composer of the music and also the librettist hal collaboration with Mr. Austen Hurgon, Mr. M. W, Findon is warmly apprecia- tive of the story and the locale of the work. He says: "Mr. Paul Ruben% has an emtremely nimble gift, both. PanGical and lyrical, and it has never been displayed to more advantage than in the "Dutch, Musical Incident ' which is now nightly filling the Prince of Wales' Thklatre (London). Many have been the countries that have been taxed tasupply the colour scheme,Lor the musical plays• retent years, and it was a happy-thought orb the part Of Mr. Paul Ruhens to place his action in a country that has been closely identified with Englaild in the past„ and Which has sci presenved -its national 'Character- istics as Holland. . . Immediately on the rise of the curtain the eye is pleased with. the quaint charm of the, costumes and the pictur- esque environment of the Cheese Ivlarket at Arndyk. Forthwith a pleasant sense of satis- faction takes possession of the spectator and holds him fast in its 'thrall what time he is on the borders of the Zuyder Zee, or in the interior of the Liqueur Distillery at Amsterdam." At this point .it is apropos- to. note that much &Rends upon the scenery and the costumes for adequate presentation ''of. "Miss Hook." H is reassuring, therefore, to record that the Musical Society's Opera Committee Will furnish their performances with scenery from a .well-known expert in these matters, Mr. T. Robinson; of Liverpool, whose "-fit up" is the most admired thing of its kind in the provinces in regard'to its .completeness and its wealth of realistic and artistic detail. The society's costumiers :for "Miss Hook "—Messrs. B. J. Simmons-arid Co., of. :London—are "also similarly' recognised as authorities in, theatrical dresses, for they almost invariably' dO 'the costuming 'at, the initial Lon- don performances. - - The Musical ,Society's cast for " Miss Hook of Holland" discloses the names of 'new candidates for stage honours, along with, those of gonie old- time, favourites.. Miss: Mullins in. the .character_ of, the vivaeious "Mina," Mr. F. Fieldhonse as' the shrewd 3r4 genial " Mr; Hook," Mr. J. Babbitt in the guiSe., of the energetie and fascinating "Bandmaster Van Vuyt," and Mr. J. W. Bibby as the dashing officer, "Captain ,Paap," will all be recognised as being placed in positionswhich they are pecu- liarly fitted to fill, and in which, it may be pretty confidently predicted, they Will give a good account of themselves. Amongst the names of new peOple and Of those who have not taken prominent parts in the society's operas for some years back, may be mentioned Miss Nellie Anderton, who will appear as "Miss Hook U; Mr. J. E. Harman, who will portray the part of the mute "Van Eck " ;.Mr. A. Davis, who will become the loafer "Stalks " ; and Mr. S. L. Partridge, who has been entrusted with the part of the lively "Schnapps." It will be seen that some of these are by no means strangers to the business of ilea opera, and high expectations are being .fornied that there will.be some, agree- able surprise's in store for the Musieal Society's. div.head: EillittlNG SCHOOLS.
div.p: EillittlNG SCHOOLS.
Provisions made for Continuation of Study.
MONDAY THE OPENING DAY.

On Monday the evening schools at ths Tech- nical Institute, the Connnercitil Institute, and the Branch Technical Schools will re-open for th 6 coming autunin and winter. A syllabus, which can be obtained from the Direetor of Education, contains full information as to courses, fees*, scholarships, &c. From this syllabus we take thefollowing:—

The Branch Technical Schools have been organised with a view to providing opportun: ities .for boys and girls, who .are not able to attend Secondary SChools, to have the educat tlon they have received in the public elemen- tary schools continued, so that they may be prepared to pass on to. the Commercial or Technical Institutes tb receive their profes- sional training. The Branch Technical Schools fort boys .specialise on the commercial and technical side, whilst.. those for. • girls specialise . on. the domestic training side; and those who Are 'sticCeSsfal :in their .studies will proceed 'Co. the Commercial or Technical Insti- tute. Special 'attention is drawn to the industrial. course at the Beamont Branch Technical School; which is intended for -boys working .at trades who require to gain manual dexterity and at the same time improve their general knowledge.

The Commercial and Technica) Institutes have been organised so that the requirements of most students will be met.. It is absolutely essential that every student should be properly qualified to take up the course of study. A student who is not properly qualified in the preliminary subjects not only wastes his own time, but wastes, that of his fellow students. Consequently no students will be 'admitted to the courses at the Commercial or Technical Institutes unless .the Principals are satisfied that they are qualified. An entrance examina- tion to the Technical Institute will be held- for all students desiring admission who cannot produce evidence of qualificatioh. • _ -

Stwlents must take the full course of study, attend regUlarly, and take the necessary examinations. The Principals and. Superin- tendents will exclude any student who. does not fulfil these conditions.

Home work.exercises will be set and students will not be allowed to continue in attendance unless they do the home work. Any student finding that he has too much home work set should consult the Superintendent or Principal,

div.head: COUNTRYSIDE Running Water as an Agency for Transforming the Landscape. SOME LOCAL EXAMPLES.
div.p: THE COUNTRYSIDE Running Water as an Agency for Transforming the Landscape. SOME LOCAL EXAMPLES.

The action of running water on the land through Which it passes is very great. After a heavy downfall on the upper reaches of the Mersey 'the :water, 'Which ,surges in Hood as it rushes under Warrington Bridge; is much dis- Coloured by sand and .mud. This has been received from the tributary streams of the drainage atea, and adaed, to considerably by the action Of the inemased velocity of the cur- rent aS it grinds the banks and bed -on its swift journey, seawards. Au instance of the amount oft detritus heia. in suspension by- the flieeded river was seen some months ago at Howley Weir, when,- after a heavy rainstorm, a large sandbank was deposited beibw the weir as the waters abated. Further &Ant) the river, be- yond Fiddler's Ferry and inmorn Gap, the sandbanks assume very large Dportions, and become a feature of the lanclgtave, especially at low tide. Where, may we alic does all the sand come .from?

!ikeilley Makers. On the Cheshire and South' Lancashire coasts, within a few miles of each 4her, three rierrss empty themselves through wide estu- -myths into the sea. The geologicatArmations of their drainage area Consist of new'rted sand- stone,. moilisione grit, carboniferous ifinestone, coulr measures, glacial drift, and gituvium. This areat includes the higher Pennineeflarige,, wheve:the Mersey, Irwell, Dee and Ribble have , their seuraes. AlOng this range of •hills there are •new deep ,cloughs and valleys. We ask , how Amine: they made, and what has become of the sections which once connected these hills? The answtlr is:. The action of the rills, becks and rivers, which now flow from and through [them has effected the marvellous change over a period sufficiently long to be I termed "the ages." The continuous running lof the waters has ground the rocks and minerals which once filled the/ cloughs and valleys into sand and mod, which,. in their have been, gradually, but ceaselessly.* deposited as sand and mud, to become the littoral sand-banks, sand-dunes and mud-flats as we now know them. This assertion does not rest on faetory, but on repeated and ex- haustive microscopic examination of thousands of samples of reeer,berne deposits. by the late Professor Lomas, of Liverpool. .In addition to this evidence ol the expert, it they be seen that the :materiall" brought down by the Reeds and the Alt is of a clayey nature, as seen by the deposits , on' the banks at the mouths of these rivers, whilst that Of the Dee and the Merse7 is sand. This is what to expect from a knowledge of the respective formations through, whit* the rh-ers pass. Why then, we may further ask, do we not find mud- banks in the same proportions as we do sand- dupes? Because hie clays are brought down stream either in a sthte of SOLUTION, or in very fine particles, and the sand in SUSPENSION in rounded grains. The finer particles of the day are carried f4r: out to sea before they are depAiiitti,:. but the sand falls whenever the urrent,' Which carries it exhausts itself. The answer as to the origin of the sand would not be complete Without mentioning the facts that there is also much material brought in by the tides from a distance, and a vast amount of matter Catised by mast erosion. All these factors add their quoth to the solution of the problem. Comp.ensations by the Sea.

• Whilst- it is •true. that the land is being denuded by water, and the coast suffers from 'erosion, there are compensations. What the sea receives from the rivi,rs it gives back in full measure to the land in another way. On the. Edit and South Coasts, find, to a snialler extent, on the West ConsVvery large areas of land are annually washed away by the inroad of the sea. But, takfnwthe results of erosiOn and land formation during the last forty years. there has beep a gain of over thirty thousand acres to-the land.

A 'considerable 'amount of erosion is pro- ceeding op the Cheshfre• coast, more especially between•DbVe Point, near. Leasowe, Where the famous submerged forest is situated, and Wal- lasey. The earliest record of the coast line belongs to the year 1690; when Dove Point was a mile and three-quarters further seaward than it is at -present, and the' erosion is still averag- ing about five yards a year. Fifty years agc. Leasowe Castle was halr a. mile from the sea. now it stands' Close to high-water mark. The old lighthouse at Leasowe; built in 1763, severe hundred yards from the sea, is now only visible at very low tides. Onctlie other hand, on the South-Lancashire coast thrge areas are beinp annually silted up and reclaimed. At Formby the distance from high-water across the sand- hills' to the town is nearly three miles, yet we have historical evidence that in 1690 there were ridSandliOnes at Formby, and that as late as 1715 tivsops.entharked at Formby Pier to quell the rebellion in Scot/arid'. It is common knowledge that Southport is rapidly becoming an inland town, far from the sea. Morecambe Bay is gradually silting up"..

The Fight Between Land and Sea. It is worth while to "seek -the cause of these. changes. Stated briefly; ills somewhat es fol- lows: The rivers bringing down the sand from the uplands flow at an even velocity through their narrow banks, until they reach_the widen ing parts of the estuary, when the .currents become less powerful and the sediment is allowed to settle, forming the sand-banks. As the ,fresh, waters reach the sea the current is overcome and- checked by the tidal currents of ,the sea, and thus the mouths' of the estuaries become glutted by great-quantities of deposited seditnent. That is how the Hoyle Banks at the mouth oI the pee, and the great banks and bar

at the mouth of the Mersey, are formed. Were It mit for the fact that Liverpool has a great shipping trade, and as, year by year the size of the ships become larger, and, in consequence. require a deeper channel, it is possible that the mouth .of the Mersey would be completely silted up. • The trade of the port has saved Atie- waterway. To keep it open two of the largest sand-sucking dredgers in the world are in constant use, pumping the sand from the channels and bar at the rate of 10,C00 ,tons an hour. This is taken out to the Irish Sea alid deposited. A great percentage is washed back by the sea currents tOwards Morecambe .Bay. The Formby and Southport sand is caused 'chiefly by the Coastal currents washing, the estuarian banks of the Dee and the Mersey further north. The sand is washed further and further up the . beach with each tide,- and as it is dried above.high-water mark by the sun, it ,is blown inland lip the faces of the sand- dunes. This-, iS how the.sand-hills are formed. On the East "CdaSt, the same fight between land and sea is going on. The Holdernes Coast of Yorkshire, between Flamborough Head and Spurn Head, is beidk reduced at the rate of seven feet per annum, and as much im 1,904,194 tons of cliff are mashed "away every year, Since the Roman period the sea has encroached upon the land to the extent of three and a. half miles, taking from it 66,600 acres. During this process no fewer than 27 towns-- some of them of considerable size and having an important maritime trade—have been washed -away by the wayes. In the estuary of the Humber seven towns have disappeared in the saine Way. The sand and. silt brought down by the four great rivers—the Aire, Wharfe, Ouse and Trent—into the Humber estuary is enormous, and is carried past Spurn Head, where it is met by a strong shore cur- rent,. which carries the/ sediment down the Lincolnshire Coast. where Dart is deposited., to the Wash, Which is rapidly filling up as a result. Spurn Head itself is being gradually washed away, but as the sand is denuded,from the side it is added to the point which is stretch- ing-further out to sea.
G. A. DUNLOP.

SHALL WARRINuTuN RAVE I DEBATING SOCIETY? Slr,—As one who has only relootly come to reside in the town, tney I crave (he courtesy of your columns to express my :surprise that your local Parliamentary Debating. Society appears to receive such a scant measure of support from the general 'public. My attendance at one or two of the meetings held during last session (which were, I under- stand. occasions of a special 'character), was sufficient to convince me that the handful of enthusiasts who form the backbone of the society were by no means receiving the generous encouragement which their efforts certainly merited. The town boasts a bewildering number of organisations, including an Agricultural Seeley. a Garden Society, a Warrington Society, and a Beautifful Warrington Society, but apparently those organisations which cater for what one might term tie:" beauties",nl 'the mind" are doomed to strugiae' aj9ng. without the syrnpathy and support of the vast majority of the townspeople. I cannot believe that 4 town et,.75,009 people is incapable of .ylekling -sitificierg—ehtlittislesra to tustify the existence ol "a nourishing Debat- ing Sodets (whether it he entirely Parliamen- tary in character or not), and I trust that irtg the ensuing session the society will gain a new lease of life, and an infusion of genuine enthusiasm. Those critics outside We society (experience has taught one that most critieiStn comes from noo-supporters I) would do well to remember that from outside their criticism . is futile, whereas inSide the society 1143'ir criticism may assist in shaping its character, and guiding Its destinies.
MERSEYSIDE.

Sir,—The question a.s to whether Warrington shall have a Debating Society rests entirely with the young men of the town. Such a society does actually exist at the moment, but unless support is forthcoming in the shape of a large accession to its present na.unbership, the society must inevitably cease to be. There is no finer training ground for " budding orators" than that provided by the local society, and for a small subscription all the facilities are offered Which enable young men to "stand at ease" in public and to acquire the art of "thinking. on their feet." Do the. youth of NN'arrington really care for the thing which makes-art appeal to Intellect? Many in this town spend more on football and other amusements in one week than the Debating Society askSlor them for a whole session. It will be interesting to know whether there Is suflicient loyalty among the young men of Warrington to keep alive a society which offers them so much worth tile having at such a trilling cost. Perhaps some of your readers may take up this subject and give to the society the much-needed backing which. it so well deserves.
. . • •' • G. DAVEY-SMITH. 1,5, Victoria-road, Rod:ton Heath.

div.head: CO-ORDINATION IN MEDICAL WORK.
div.p: CO-ORDINATION IN MEDICAL WORK.

. , Sir,--tt is not oftemthat one reads so sensible a .letter on. "Things medical, sanitary and hygienic," as that by "Sanitas" in your last issue. The letter itself is it sign that people are beginning to think that some better organisa- tion of the medical profession than at present exists is necessary. in the public interest. The ideal of the future, pictured by Professor cUshing at the International Congress of Medi- cine, and approved by "Sanitas," is that the hospital should be the centre for co-ordinated effort in medical practice. With this most of -those who have thought on the subject will agree, but it is curious to ob,serve that the ten- dency to this end is seerninglyiess than ever.•.• The latest phase of medical- progress is the campaign itgainSt IIIberCUIOSIS, end the disease lc all its forms ha .4 been made compulsorily notifiable ; but organised effort in the treatment of tuberculosis—for which tuberculous dispen..l saries are being established—stops short at tuberculosis of the lungs. Them is no organ- Ned attempt to treat tuberculosis of the bones, joints, skin, kidney, brain, peritoneum, Re., Ste. These cases are to be left as before, to The care of the voluntary hospitals: The scheme is Obviously incomplete. • The .defect, however, could be partially remedied by attaching the , tuberculosis dispensaries to the general hospi-

This plan would, at any rate, tend to that co-ordina- tion which Professor Cushing looks forward to, and which has been done in that model hospital, the Johns Hopkins, of Baltimore. Sir William Osicr, who is..in ,the: forefront of the present campaign against: tuberculosis, strongly' disapproves of the present tendency to divorce tuberculosis from general medicine and sur- gery. , What. with Insurance Committees, Health Committees, Hospital --Committees, .Education Committees and Boards of Guardians all deal- ing with medical problems, it is almost hope- less to look for co-ordination of effort and unity of aim by their various medical officers. div.head: MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.
div.p: MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.

SitHln answer. 'to 'Mr. Townroe's letter in your last week's issue, may we be-allowed first to express a hope that the interest shown by him is but an index of the minds of the Church laymen of, Warrington. Whether they have eonscientinus :objections :agginst • mtssionB .or not, we do hope that one and all will Pity a. visit to the Missionary Exhibition during the ten days it will be open. And not laymen of the Church .of England only. We shall accord a most heerty welcome to all men of all religious opinions, for indeed, in this great work of -advance, we can meet in fellowship on common ground. - We Churchmen do not for- get the Splendid- missionary ,exhibition held in Parr Hall a few years ago under Nonconformist auspices,- We trust and hope our exhibition may be aii•suecessful. . More definitely to answer Itr. Teiviircie.- The object of, our exhibition is not to prothote:.any fleeting interest in misSforis, but to achieve per- manent results. We may get great croWnt, WO nifty -have great financial success, but unle,ss the exhibition results in more definite interest in the work of the Church abroad and more real work done and more real ,prayer offered for missions in our parishes, we shall count ourselves to have fulled. To this end it may be noted that all OUT stewards (they already number over 1,000) have been studying mis- sionary needs and problems, as well as history and customs of peoples, for many months past. These stewards Will be guided by over 30 depu- tations—those who have laboured in the coun- tries about which they will speak, and who have been face to face with file needs and the problems of those countries'. There will also be some four or five deputations who have not actually been abroad, but who have been, specially trained to deal with the objections to which, I think, Mr. Townroe alludes in his letter.

•In addition to these there will be present each day a Bishop and a prominent layman of the Church, who will deal with the subject of mis- sions in a general way most, likely to_ appeal to the- 'Milking man. We may mention that already file Lord Bishops of .Chester, Liverpool., -Whalley, .Burnley, Adelaide, )31-shop Coyle (of Cores), Bishop Mylnc (of Bombay),. Bishop _Hamlyn (of West Afrita), have promised to-be with us; also Lord Shuttleworth, Lord Wohner, Sir Wm, Mr. W..Collingwood and Mr. Coxon.
FREDEtaC"t". WILLIS. Chairman. F. F. KINILOsY, Hon. See.

ZION CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY.—The Zion Chapel, congregation, Cherry-lane. Lymm, held their anniversary services on Sunday. Mr. R. B. Woods, of Grappenhall, preached, and the at- tendance at both services was good. The collec- tions were in aid of the church funds. PARISH CHIME/I.—The Rev. B. M. Maynard. of St. Cuthbert's, Worksop, conducted on Sunday afternoon a young men's service. He gave an eloquent address, pointing out that young men should be exceedingly careful in choosing their companions, as many were led astray through seeking bad company. Some parents did not exercise sufficient control over their children. and the consequence was when they went out into the world a good many of them drifted into evil surroundings, only to lose all respect Thbey Ltyhe Rev. lici- bort Dunnico, of Liverpool and for themselves and their parents. mm Oongre- g a tCONGREGATIONALjehai Church waseHU EC li . visitedformerly of Wu-- rington, on Sunday. The attendance a: ii•oth services was very good, especially in the even- ing, when many from the other denominations went to hear him. The text in the eveniagV us "And they said unto Him, Rabbi, where dud. lest thou?' He said unto them, 'Come and see." Philosophers said the only world in which a man lived was the world he feels and the world that he hears; also •philosophers said the only things that had any real existence were the things a man feels, sees and hears. The truth, the preacher said, he wanted to force home was, that the world in which a man lived was not so much as what was outside of him as to what there was within. He went on to show how men lived with beautiful things around them, yet could not see the beauty be- cause beauty did not appeal to them. MAy QUEEN COMMITTEE.—The annual general meeting of the Lymm May Queen Committee was held in Hurst's Pavilion on Friday night, when the principal matters discussed were the balance sheet for the last festival and the chil- dren's tea. In, making his financial statement, the hon. treasurer, Mr. A. H. Hudson, gave the income and expenditure of previous festivals. He said a comparison between the present and past balance sheets revealed the fact that, whilst the 1913 result •;svas not all it had been desired, the small profit of " A:2 Is. 74d. was an oncoutaging sign, and- it also showed the con - mit-tee-were working in the right direction when the largedecrease in the amount of subscriptions had been considered. There was still a- deficit of £l3 14s. 101 d. The balance sheet was adopted and Mr. Hudson heartillv thanked for the clear and adequate manner in which he had drawn up the financial statement. Despite the adverse balance, the committee were unanimously of opinion that the children who took part in the festival, either as characters in the procassion or performers, should be given a tea as an appreciation of their services, and it was de- cided to hold such a tea in the Congregational Sehooknom on Saturday. September r/th, to be 'followed by an entertainment. The committee regretted their inability, owing to the lack of funds, to provide a free tea for the children of the district. Any gift of money or provisions in aid of the tea would be welcomed by the com- mittee.

MARRIAGE OF MISS ETHEL G. MOSTON. Pretty Ceremony at the Wesleyan Church. . The ‘v esleyan Cuurch, Lymm, was the scene, on Wednesday afternoon, or one of the prettiest weddings solemnised in the district for some considerable time, and as both the contracting parties are well known the marriage aroused great deal of interest.. The bride was Miss Ethel Goldsmith Moston, second daughter of the late Mr. F. 0. Moston, and of Mrs. Moston, of Southdene, Lynam. The bridegroom was Mr. Shirley Simister Robinson, son ot the late Mr. Walter gobinson, of Loudon, aid of Mrs. Robinson, of, 260, ,Hawthorn-read, -Booth, and' a grandson of the late Mr. Timothy Simjster, at one time a well-known resident of Runcorn. The bride was given away by her mother, and the...ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. H. 'Corson; ;,tiriWh-aley, Bridge, and the Rev.' Middlewood, Warrington.. The 'orgai2ist was Mr. Harry Brown, and he played appropriate music. The duties o: best man were efficiently performed by Mr. Harold Branson, the Rev. W. A Unsworth acted as groomsman, and the stewards were Messrs. .1. W. Davies, A. Hudson, F. G. Cavanagh, T. P. Corlett and S. W. Win- stanley. The bride looked charming in a pearl white satin dress, trimmed with pearl embroidered lace, while She ivore.a bridal veil of embroidered tulle and orange blossomi Her jewellery con- sisted of an- opal and pearl .necklace; and she carried a pretty bouquet-of white lilies and white heather. She wes- attended.- by three bridesmaids—Miss Muriel Moston ‘sister), Miss Beatrice' Moston and Miss •Maisie Steen Barr (both cousins of the bride). They were daintily gowned in dresses of Sogt pale blue satin, with sleeveless coateee of cream and mauve brocaded silk, and wore black mirror velvet hats, with. clusters of shaded sweet peas. Their jewellery consisted of gold bracelets, the gift of the bridegroom, and they carried shower bouquets of Lady Chatenay roses. The mother of the bride held a reception after the church service in the Eagle Brow School, and during the proceedings vocal am) instru- mental music was rendered by Miss Simpson; Miss B. Moston. and Miss eborley. Later the tta,,pe couple started for the honeymoon, which is being spent hi Switzerlav,d. The bride's travelling dress ennaisted of a navy blue ens. fumes and a- black velours hat with white feather.

div.head: INTERESTING MARRIAGE AT PARISH CHURCH. Wedding of Miss Marion Oldfield.
div.p: INTERESTING MARRIAGE AT PARISH CHURCH. Wedding of Miss Marion Oldfield.

An interesting and pretty wedding was solemn- ised at the Lymm Parish Church on Thursday, when Miss Marion Oldfield, only daughter of Mr. and Mrs.-Charles Oldtield, "South Cliff," Brook- road, LYmm, was Married to Mr. Selwin George Metcalfe, of Knutsford-road, Grappenhall, and formerly of Burton-on-Trent. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attended by three bridesmaids—Miss Crumbleholme (cousin, Bolton),_ and the Misses Metcalfe (sisters of the bridegrootn). She wore a dress of Satin charmeuse, trimmed with Irish lace and pearls, and a wreath of flowers, with a veil of Brussels net. Her ornaments were a diamond and 'sapphire ring, the gift of the bridegroom, and a pendant of pearls and dia- monds. Her bouquet was composed of lilies and white heather. .

Miss Crumbleholme was attired in a dress of mauve satiq charmeuse with gold sash. Her white velour hat was trimmed with feathers and flowers. The Misses Metcalfe's dresses were of helio silk, with hats trimmed with ermine to match. The bridesmaids carried bouquets, the gift of the bridegroom. The Rev. B. Percival (St. Peter's, Warrington) was the officiating elergytuah. The duties of best man were performed by Mr. Alfred Few (Grappenhall). The groomsmen were Mr. Louis Crumbleholme (Bolton) and Mr. Dickenson (Burton-on-Trent). Whilst the party assembled in the church, Mr. W. Cooke played appropriate music on the organ, comprising: Bridal music from "The Birds of Aristophanes " (C. Hubert and IL Parry), military march (Schubert), "Allegretto Cantabile" (William Faulkes). "Festive March" (Calkin). "The Answer" (Wolstenholme). As the bride entered he played the Bridal March from " Lohengrin " (Wagner) and afterwards the "Wedding Pro- cession" (Intro. Act 111. div.head: AN UNSOLVED MYSTERY.
div.p: AN UNSOLVED MYSTERY.

The mystery surrounding the man found drowned in the Bridgewater Canal at Lymm last week has not been solved. Mr. T. Ridgway (the local coroner) held the inquest on Satur- daY evening. John Brazendale, warehouseman, Burford- lane Wharf, and residing at Broom -Edge, said on-• Friday, AUgnst 29th, lie was in the, ware- house, - when the Mate of the. boat • Arizona called to him and said there was a body- in the canal. He got the body to the • side and in- formed the police. He knew nothing about the man_ and had never 'seen him _before._ _

Elson, Broom Edge, said the body b possibly been in the .water three or four days. No hat or coat was found. In one of the pockets were a penknife and a brass stud. No one had been reported missing from the district. The man seemed to have been a better-class labourer.

Dr- Burrows, Lymm, said there were several Wounds on the body, one on the back of the head, another over the hip and one across the back. •There were no signs of the wounds hav- ing been caused before death. They were pro- bably caused by the propeller of a passing boat. A verdict of Found drowned" was returned, there being no evidence to show how the man got into the canal.
