div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

PEESEISZTATION.—Mr. S. G. Metcalfe, cashier of the Grappenhall Tanning Company, was the recipient, on Thursday, of a handsome bronze curb. which was subscribed for by the employes, on the occasion of his marriage to Miss Oldfield, of Lymru.

TAXICAB v. MOTOR CYCLE.—What just escaped proving a serious motor mishap occurred in Grappenhall on Sunday afternoon. A taxicab, owned, by Mr. Paterson, Latchford, driven by his son, was turning out of Victoria-road. GraP- penhall. into Hunt's-lane, when a collision occurred between it and a motor cycle, ridden, by Mr. Marshall, of Cross-lane. The cyclist was somewhat violently thrown from his mount, but fortunately escaped serious injury. The motor cycle, however, was damaged rather badly. Mr. Paterson, jun., made a gallant attempt to avoid a collision,- and: in doing so ran the taxicab on to the footway. with the result that one of the tyres was burst. The incident caused some ex- citement among the spectators,

PARISH COUNCIL—The quarterly meeting of the Parish Council was held on Thursday, Mr. Alan Lister-Kaye presiding. Mr. Wooding aslnd if there was any likelihood of a commencement being Made in the making of Victoria-avenue, Albert-road, and, York-drive.----The Chairman said, the notice had only expired and the matter was adjourned.—On the motion of Mr. J. Brad- ford the Clerk was instructed to write the Che- shire County Council, calling. attention to the dangerous turning in Knutsford-road abutting Cartridge-lane end, and asking them to erect a danger signal.—Mr. Bradford raised the ques- tion of an extra delivery of letters embracing the whole of Cartridge-lane and district, as the pre- sent system was wholly inadequate. . Farmers,, lie said, were put to loss and inconvenience through the present system.--The Clerk was re- quested to bring the matter before the notice of the Postmaster of Warrington.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP Tlrfl.l-:-TATTLE.
It is good to teach the young idea not how to shoot.
But. how to study the beaut!es of nature they can find around them.
This ,was the object of the Garden Society Juniors' expedition on Saturday. The youngsters spent an enjoyable as well as vrolitable time.

How many distinct varieties of wild fruit is it possible to gather? One of the young garden lasses secured no fewer than 34 distinct specimens. What a Garden of Eden this young Eve must have discovered.

But a representative of Adam did better. He got 37 specimens. , • Mankind thus gained another triumph against womankind. The swing bridge across the Ship Canal has received its bi-annual coat of paint. Some of the passer § across the bridge dis covered that they had got their coals. painted: Latest local query: Can one say he is swing- ing along when he crosses the swing bridge?
Mr. Oliver, the next M.P. for the district, told a Stockton Heath audience how he spoke about babies of unknown sex.

'When a child was presented .by proud parent to him he used a little dtplornacy. He did not call the child "it," as some did ; he usually called it "a little angel." • Such tact and diplomacy is rarely met with, and Mr. Oliver's hint ought to prove service- able to other bachelors.. -
FOoTRALL.---Vi7hat the Stockton Heath Associa- tion F.C. contemplate doing. this season will be found describisd by " Linesman " in the sports columns.

A MISSING •GIRL.—Some excitement was occa- sioned in Stockton Heath on Sunday by a rumour that a little girl had been drowned in the Ship Canal. The girl was missing, but fortunately the rumour proved incorrect, and the child was found by her parents later in the day. THE FOWL DISAPPEARED.—The disappearance of a fowl in April resulted in Peter Hall, jun. re- siding at Acton Grange, appearing at an jun., Petty Sessions on Monday on a charge of stealing the bird. It was the property of Thomas G. Williams, Walton Inferior, and was valued at 2s. 6d.—lt was stated by the police that immediately after the alleged theft Hall had disappeared from the district. On Satur- day he was seen in Warrington by the borough police, who effected his arrest, and handed him over to the charge of Inspector Broom at Stock- ton Heath.—After the arrest had been proved, Hall was remanded to the Petty Sessions, to be held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday. CANAL BATHING.—Since the drowning of a War- rington schoolboy in the Bridgewater Canal near Stockton Heath on August' Bank Holiday, and in accordance with the suggestions made by ' the jury at the inquest, notices have been posted at intervals along the canal banks stating that bathing is strictly prohibited. SCARCITY OF SCHOOL Room.—The education authorities in Stockton Heath are finding that the school accommodation is inadequate for the number of children requiring to be educated. The Council School has now some 50 more chil- dren than the number the school was con- structed for, and despite that there are children who cannot find accommodation. It is evident that some extensions will have to be promptly made. even if they are of a temporary charac- ter. This year a considerable number of new houses have been erected in the district and occupied. conseouently the child population has been augmented to a marked extent., The avthorities are aware of the demand, but have hitherto not taken action. The loss in grants ought to cause a scheme for extension to .10 car- ried into fruition.

. WEDDING OF THE REV. E. W. CLARKE. • A Pretty Ceremony at GOole• Parish Church. There was an interesting and. pretty wedding solemnised at the Parish Church; Goolei 'York-- shire, on Tuesday. The bridegroom was the Rev. Ernest Wilson Clarke, curate at Stockton Heath Parish Church, and third son of Major and Mrs. E. L. Clarke, of Brooklands. Cud- dington. The bride was Miss Gwladys Lyth, daughter of Mr. A. S. Lyth. The Bank, Goole. The ceremony was performed bathe Rev. H. R. Everson. vicar of Whinney Bill. Rotherham, and he was assisted by the Rev. J. Collins. vicar of Stockton Heath, and • the Rev. • Edmund Sinker, vicar of Goole. Appropriate Wedding music was played•byMr. Hepworth, the Goole Parish Church organist. The bride, who was given away by her , father, was charmingly gowned in -white satin char- nieuse and she carried an exquisite shower , bouquet of pale .pink carnations. The attendant pages completed what was a very pretty picture. as seen while the bridal Party were at the altar. The pages were Mas- ters Rupert Lyth, Oliver Lvth and Erick Hud- son. cousins of the bride. The pages wore dainty snits ~of white satin of the Kate Greenaway style. The duties of best man were efficiently nerformed" by Mr. E. G. Clarke, brother of the bridegroom. After the ceremony at the church a reception was given at The Bank House. and later in the day the Rev. and Mrs. E. W. Clarke started for the honeymoon, which is being spent in the, Lake district. The bride's travelling drew con.sisted of a Saxe-blne silk moire costume and a-Leghorn hat trimmed with La France roses.

toteresting Speeches at Liberal Meeting. - And are we yet live? • see each other's face. That old Methodist hymn, said Mr. W. H. Sherburn, the chairman at the Liberal meeting held at Stockton Heath on Thursday evening, might well be sung by Liberals after all that had. bedn • said about them. According to the 'calculations of their opponents, the Liberal Government ought to have been dead. The Government, however, was still very much alive, despite the snap divisions of the Tories. There were some young men, representatives for neighboitring:constituencies. who after the failure- to defeat the Govei-ninent by snap sions,did not .13iiite know-- what to tell their canAtitnentei: Ile could' imagine --o tie young: 'Mari, represent-dive for a near neighbonring consti- tuency saying: I have got a-lot •of Tariff Reform women, and as Tariff Reform is very quiet, I must get them something to do. A happy thought strikes me. I'll enlist these women into my great cm- sade. I'll get them to provide, accommodation for the women and children coming from Ulster when the war begins. (Laughter.) I can imagine how that will take on with the women.' The public. said Mr. Sherburn, would under- stand how this young man of Warrington would smile when he talked with his fellows about the scheme. (Laughter and applause.) They in the Knutsford Division had a fairly good repre- sentative, only he persisted in voting in the wrong lobby. They meant, however, to change that in the future, and would send Mr. Oliver to Parliament to vote in the right lobby. (Ap- plause.) _

div.head: Conservative Trickery.
div.p: Conservative Trickery.

. •. Mr. P. M. Oliver, the prospective Liberal Call. didate, spoke about the Conservative trickery over the Insurance Act. When the .Tories saw that the Act was about to Pass, they brought in an amendment that it should not come into operation for another year, That was what they could expect from the Conservative policy of "to-morrow, to-morrow.:and everything in .the far distant future." If that had been.car- ried, the. Act would never have come into opera- tion and the hundred thousands of people who had already received benefits would not have re- ceived a mingle penny of assistance. Colonel Dixon, the chairman of the Cheshire County Council, had said that he lool4d•to the Insurance .Act to greatly lessen disease and death In the future. He thanked Col. Dixon, who was chairman of the Conservative Associa- tion, for that praise he had given to Mr.- Lloyd George and the Insurance Act. Dealing with the land ouestion, Mr. Oliver said it was .necessary that the land interests had not such an unfair advantage in Parliament as it had at present. They had the land plural ,voter in the House of Commons and the great landlords in the House of Lords. and these nowerful interests would have to be removed before they could monerly tackle the land ques- tion. The Plural Voter Abolition Bill was destined to do that. If it was necessary for these,neople to have a rlural vote in defence of their land, it was equally as necessary for the floor man to have a plural vote in defence of his food. but the pluralists would not concede tlytt right to the poor man.

div.head: Democratic Reform.
div.p: Democratic Reform.

Until they did away with the land pluralist, they never could have democratic reform of the land. They also wanted to do away with the land interest in. the House of Lords, and pro- vide a Second Chamber, in which all interests would be fairly and equitably represented. In 33 parishes in the Knutsford Division the

last census showed the population had declined, and if. that happened in a farming county, with the best- markets in the world at its door, what waS happening in other counties?' There. they had one strong case for land reform, to end the depopulation • of the counties and to.. end the crowding of farm servants into cities; when they should be producing the people's food on the land. •
Mr. Jas. Dockett spoke upon the land ques- tion, and argued that farmers must have security of tenure and farm servants must get improved conditions.

BOY AND GIRL NATURALISTS' RAMBLE. It was a bright and happy party of boys and girls who, in charge of Mr. G. A. Dunlop, Mr. E. G. White, Mr. Snaps, Mrs. Morris and Mrs. White, proceeded last Saturday afternoon to investigate the late-summer glories of the Donna, the wild waste-land that lies in the track of the rambler from Hill Cliffs to Hatton. The outing took place under the auspices of the junior section of the Stockton Heath Garden Society, a section that bids fair to find the best sort of recruits for the society of the future. There were just forty present when a move was made from Victoria-square at half-past two, in weather of the most lovely description. If such a thing were possible, zest was added to the proceedings by the offer of prizes for the boys and girls who collected the greatest number of distinct varieties of wild fruit during the afternoon. The rights of private property were rigorously respected, and there was no wanton destruction even of the commonest specimens. Among the specimens collected were: herd's purse, red campion, corn spurrcy, chick- weed, ragged robin, herb Robert, white clover. bramble, dog rose, rowan, willow herb, wild angelica, hogweed, elder, vklerian, marsh cud- wood, mugwort, field thistle, black knapweed, wall lettuce, hair bell, ash, woody nightshade, foxglove, hairy mint, marsh mint, wood sage, marsh woundwort, field °niche, spotted nersi- caria, curled dock, stinging nettle, black bryony. oak, alder. Mr. Dunlop was kept busy explaining where the flowering stage ceased, and the seed or fruit stage began. and every device was employed to induce the children to bring their own powers of observation into play. When collecting came to an end and the proceeds were ustaged" on the roadside, Mr. Dunlop acting as judge, it was found that of the girls Edith Snaps was first with 34 specimens, and that of the boys Stanley- Birrell was first with 37. In the girls Georgina- Lyle-was second and May -White third. Donald -Birrell was second boy, and the third prize was divided between Norman Snaps and Sidney Brayshay. Tea was served on the lane. side, and other diversions, such as chasing rabbits disturbed by the reapers in the adja- cent cornfields, whiled sway the afternoon in the pleasantest possible manner. Before the return journey was begun the children heartily cheered Mr. Minion for his continuous interest In them, and Mt. White promised that the next ramble should be a preparatory one for the children's competition at the Chrysanthemum Show, September 27th, when there will be a prize for the best basket of wild berries.

div.head: THEL WALL.
div.p: THEL WALL.
DROWNED WITHOUT A STRUGGLE.
Mystery of an Irish Labourer.

- - A strange story was narrated at the inquest on Patrick Casey, farm labourer at Oatlands High Farm, drowned in the Mersey on Thurs.; day night. Mr. Ridgway was the coroner, and the inquiry was held at the Pickering Arms on Saturday. Mr. Hankey, the farmer, said he had sly aye known Casey by. that name, and he had kin.wn him for five or six years. Casey bad worked for him since May. He never received any letters, from Ireland in that time, and no papers, wore' in his possession to show from what part of Ire- land he had come. Witness met him on the river bank about 830 an the night of Thursday., 28th August. Casey was sober, but said he had been to the Cheshire Cheese, Latchford, fur a hot whisky, to stop ,toothache.. He had suffered froth his teeth for sentitimay and since the death of a sister-in-law in Ireland, Casey had not Deemed in his right mind. I When witness was lifting his cycl4 over a stile he saw Casey fall into the river. He fell head first into the water. Witness got down the bank, caught hold of Casey's coat, but could not get a proper hold of him before he sank. Casey never spoke or struggled after he fell into the water. The bank was very steep at that part, and there was a straight drop of nine feet. John Green, feriTruan. and. Sergt. Robinson. spoke to dragging for and findilig.the body next day.. It was stick in the Mud. The -police officer said he haa failed to trace any 'friends of .Casey These Irish labourersofteif had one name in one place and another in the next place. The jury, found that Casey had met his death accidentally.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

CHOIR 4ND SCNDAY Senool, SERMONS.—The annual choir and Sunday school sermons at St. Mary's, Orford, were preached on Sunday. The preacher in the morning was the Vicar, the Rev. O. Vale Owen, whose text was "Jesus said, 'Suffer little children to come unto Me, and forbid them not, for of such is the Kingdom of 'Heaven.'" The Vicar said that it was usual to preach in the morning about the Sunday school, and in the evening about the choir. He wanted to talk not only to the children, but to parents4ind adults. He said that to live a godly life they must become as little-children. There was not enough humility in the world; each one wanted to appear as big and as irapottant as possible. A great deal of the drunkenness was I caused through each man wanting to appear as I big as his mate. One stood treat round, and then the Other has to do the-sae,to Show thlit' he was just as good as his friend. -He could give them one example of real humility. The I late Mr. William- Beamont, who- endowed Orford .School, was a great traveller, linguist and scholar. He used to take a class in the. Sunday 'school, and his scholars said that whenever he. I was addressing them they could always sit and I listen to the simple' teachings of that great man. ' lie lived to be an old man, and when his eye- sight began to fail and his hearing was not as good as it had been, and he felt that he had got past his best, he went to the curate and said that he thought he would have to give up his big class, as he didn't feel capable of continuing it, but he would be glad to take one of the infant classes. He thought that was true humility, when a man of .Mr. Beamont's ability, considered that he was only capable of taking an infants' class.—ln the afternoon a children's flower service was held, when the children were addressed by Mr. A rnell, Warrington.—The preacher in the evening was the Vicar. He made .reference to the good work done by the choir. He considered that it was a tremen- dously responsible _position, that of leading the service in God's house. They did not pretend to he a cathedral congregation nor a cathedral but they gave of their best. Sometimes it was a very poor best, but. he hoped they would not criticise too keenly. If anyone had sUggestions to make, whereby they could im- prove the service, he would be very pleased to hear them.—The flowers which the children hronaht to the flower service were afterwards taken to the Infirmary and the Workhouse Hos- pital. The collections were divided between the choir fund and the Sunday school fund-.

QUAINT AND AMUSING.

In accordance with atustom dating from 1656, red rose has been "paid" to the Warden of St. Olave's Grammar School, Tower Bridge, as rent for a field leased from that year to trustees for the benefit of the poor. This!year the rose was presented by Mr. J. W. Oake, an "old boy," who is. now Mayor of Bermondsey.

div.head: TIRED OF. MUSIC.
div.p: TIRED OF. MUSIC.

There are at Montecatini,,a favourite health. resort, the composers Leoncavallo, Mascagni, and Puccini, the tenors Caruso and Bonci and: the conductors 14lugnone, Serail& and Oaleffi. These have formed an anti-musical society, in. which the penalty for speaking either of music or of the theatre when in each other's company is expulsion from the society:

div.head: HOW. TO LIVE LONG
div.p: HOW. TO LIVE LONG

Mr. Horace Fletcher, in his book "Fletcherism: What it is, or how I became .young at sixty," quotes Mr. J. D. Rockefeller's rules for health. They are: "Don't gobble your food. Fletcher- ise, or chew very slowly while you eat. Talk on pleasanl topics. Don't be in a-4Turry. Take time to masticate, and cultivate a cheerful appe- tite while you eat. So' will the demon indiges- tion be encompassed round about, and his slaughter complete."

div.head: DANGER OF TURNED-UP TIIOUSERS.
div.p: DANGER OF TURNED-UP TIIOUSERS.

The ." Medical Officer" condemns the fashion of turning up the bottom of the trousers. "We shudder to think," itsays, "of the accumulation of filth which must be found in these receptacles, and as we believe it is the custom to have the turn-up made as a permanent pocket, it is doubtful whether_during the period of wear any attempt is made to get rid of the accumulation. In the interests of hygiene, we hope this pre- vailing fashion will be but a short madness.'!

div.head: SWALLOWED THE LOOT.
div.p: SWALLOWED THE LOOT.

A burg Air named Louis Nectoux, but better known to the authorities as "Lead Piping," has been operated on for appendicitis at:, Auttm. "Lead Piping" broke into a safe at Autun, and made off with £6—a £4 note and £2 in gold: The alarm was given before he got fairly away. and just as he was .caught he swallowed the note and the gold. He is now suffering such acute pain .from his ill-gotten wealth that an operation was necessary.

div.head: HOME OF MOTOR CAR THIEVES.
div.p: HOME OF MOTOR CAR THIEVES.

Chicago would seem to be maintaining its undesirable record of being the biggest home of motor car thieves, for, according to a report lately issued by the police, no less than 540 cars, val Led at .2162,000, were stolen in the city dur- ing the first half of this year. Out of the num- ber 470 were recovered, leaving 70 unaccounted for. Only fifteen persons were arrested in con nection with the theft-s, most of the cars being found abandoned in out-of7the-way places or in garages in distant towns.

div.head: FEATHERED CENTENARIAN.
div.p: A FEATHERED CENTENARIAN.

One of the minor curiosities of Australia Is a cockatoo whose age is estimated at 121 years. Its present owner has had it for twenty-six years, 'and its former owner, a'sea captain, Mr. George Ellis, had it fOr seventy-eight years. The captain used to say the bird .was seventeen years old when it came into his possession. The bird has an upper beak nearly six inches long, curving towards the chest. The beak, which grow,s about an incli every year, has to be broken off when .it gets too Icing.

div.head: SILENCE 'TORTURE.
div.p: SILENCE 'TORTURE.

In Portugal -there is a- prison called the "Prison of Silence,7,in which nearly everything that human ingenuity. can suggest to terrify the prisoners is done. :The cells are narrow, torah- like,-and, within eactisstands a coffin. The at- tendants creep about in felt ;Uppers. No one is allowed to utter a word. The silence is that of the grave. Once a clay the cell doors are un- locked and the half a thousand wretches march out clothed in shrouds .and with faces covered by masks, for it is part of this hideous punish-' ment Unit none may look upon the. Counten- ances' of' his fellow prisoners. Few of them endure this torture for more than ten years.

div.head: DARING PHOTOGRAPHY
div.p: DARING PHOTOGRAPHY

The daring of the cinematograph operator knows no bounds, and he faces intrepidly the most dangerous task. One of the latest sensa- tions of the profeSsion has been. the extraordin- ary • ascent of the Matterhorn, which was made on the 2nd of July by Mr. Frederick Burling- ham, of London, for the purpose of cinemato- graphing the Zermatt giant. Mr. 'Burlingham took with him three mules and four guides. After a dangerous climb, they succeeded in ob- taining a picture of the shoulder which was then a steep ice slope. So clear was the day that the crowds watching in Zermatt could see Mr. Burlingham turning the. machine on the narrow summit ridge.

div.head: STATUE'S TOILET
div.p: A STATUE'S TOILET

, . . The statue of the Goddess of Freedom on the. top of the dome of the Capitol at Washington has been undergoing a cleansing process. Mtn Freedom, whO stands 19ft. 6in. in her bare feet, is.anything but a'ddinty maiden, judging by the cost of her bath, for Which Congress has appro- priated £3,200 and nearly a carload of soap. Freedom, whose crown contains numerous costly platinum tips, .frequently takes electric 'treatment; and, hardly a Summer passes that some of these • tips are not • melted off by .the lightning, but that does not serve to keep .her clean, and from time to time,it is necessary to erect a seaffording around her and send up a gang of steeplejacks to scrub her with-soap and water.

div.head: TOWER OF PISA.
div.p: THE TOWER OF PISA.

Thrk years ago- a Commission investigated the condition of the Tower of Pisa, and reported that it had increase its inclination from the perpendicular on foot .since it. was last meas- ured in 1829; at which time the inclination was 151 ft. As ,it has, increased since 1910; it must now be nearly 1711., compared with a .height of only 1791 t. The Commission. also examined the foundations, Which proved to be only 10ft. deep, with a circumference no greater than that of the base of the tower. .The discovery of these inadequate foundations has been acceNed as proof that the leaning of the tower was not in- tentional on the part of its builders, but the result of gradual subsidence in the intervening six centuries.

div.head: DOGS AND MOVING incrunEs.
div.p: DOGS AND MOVING incrunEs.

A moving picture show was recently given in London to. determine what effect a cinemato- graph picture had on the intelligence of animals. A series of motion pictures were reeled off in a darkened „room before an audience of prize dogs. First Some pictures of a dog show were run through. The dogs walked up and had a look at it, and turned away, obviously bored and uninterested. Evidently the subject was too familiar. They woke up, however, when an elephant came splashing into a pool of water and. appeared to be walking into the room. A rn4-ssive bulldog niade a dash for the screen. With his head up and ears pricked, he got ready to attack, and the Whole audience barked and bayed in blood-curdling discord. Pictures of birds also ' irritated them, but when other animals were shown they quickly recognised that they were not looking at the real thing, and in a few seconds quietened down com- pletely. The general result of the experiment seemed to be that dogs do not understand still pictures, but that they appreciate motion, though it very largely depends upon the nature of the thing moving.

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE WORLD OF LETTERS.
New Books.
The Bea (*.Wow& 6edrge Edgar. London: Nlills and Boon. 6s.

This is one of. the most interesting novels ever penned by Mr„ George, Edgar, and is just the type of story to peruse upon • a railway journey, or on occasions when thrill is wanted. Around .a plot, about a robbery, the author has woven y. story which grips the reader's attention in the first 'Chapter, keeps hin3 in a thrill all through, and makes hini wish for more when the end is reached.. . •
Love, sensation and romance are cleverly en,
twined. One of the Red Your, the name the :gang of international thieves_ pass Under, de-

frauds his fellows out of their share ht the plunder. Led by the leader of the gang, who IS . a, dual character, posing. one moment as a rnosk respectable, member of, the best society, tt-al the next as the fled Colonel, a. vicious mur-
lerer and robber, they hunt downi We deserter.
Ile has a daughter, and she and a young village doctor are in love. The hunted man gives the girl to her lover and hands over to the doctor
dticuments that are not to be opened' until his death. Ile is murdered the same The documents show that the girl is not his-daugh- ter, but as the murderers, think she and her
over possess the secret of where the plunder is
• . hid, they are dragged into the business.. Both pass through thrilling adventures, and in the end the. young doctor, with the aid of a rmarti-
able journalist-detective, beaks up the survi- vors of the gang.
The book is a splendid bit of imaginary work, _ . _ _
te plot keeps.a hold on one right through, xi 94

the dialogue is crisp and- pointed, with a- sur- priSe for the reader on nearly :every page. .For those who .gloat over intellectual pabulum, the book is not; suitable, but for readers Who like to be-" sensationised " it is just what they desire. The story is narrated with clearness and. point, is excellently printed, and is well worth the. price .asked.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
ROOF GARDENING.
Women of leisure who have to spend .most of ,teir time in town houses have lately seized
apon the idea of roof gardens, and it is spread- ing rftpidly. More than any other city Berlin .-Las encouraged and furthered the progress of ;his decorative work. . All that is wanted is a
.ouse with a flat roof sufficiently solid to sup-

port the made-up soil. that must .be deposjted Upon it. Gradually the green spaces of many cities are passing away, owing to the congestion of buildings, so that this, scheme of utilising, the roofs Of dwellings is worthy of considers-

- hon. stretches of greenery on the tops of houses and round about balconies are refreshing to the eye, and; in. some of the larger examples of the gardener's skill, arbours and seats and shady nooks have been contrived. An American lady, whq was recently in London, (says the 'Telegraph "), had studied garden's on the Con- tinent, and had conic to England for the pur- pose-of Visiting certain grounds in which there are famous old gardens. She is a professional gardener, and has laid out several exceptionally fine and a distic examples. Not flower arrange- ment only is required for these lovely centres, but the woman who makes a success of her

task knows how to group pieces of sculpture; she is an adept in the art of putting up pergolas in certain spots, and of. training over trellis work and arbours creeping flowers and the foliage which in America takes on such wonder- ful colouring. The objection might be made that 'smoke from chimneys, would render those lofty bowers less pleasant than those situated on the level. But it may be pointed out that in summer, when the gardens are , chiefly al); preciated; 'comparatively littlq smoke is 'experi- enced.
THE READING HABIT,. - ,Sooner.-orialer we atl of us tie`ed.sorne kind of consolation 'and diversion; for the world is not taentect to suit any one man's fancy, and
Lie continuous clash of wills is bound to bring

about a certain amount of sorrow to everyone-. Of all 'consolations, the cheapest, Alie easiest, the most effective, is a passion for the printed page. To be able to step out,of .our immediate environment at will, to roam the centuries, to scour the earth, to beckon the spheres, .to have all the best minds ready to serve our need—this is the gift for the reader. ,Reading, like every- thing else, is a matter of habit. Thelittle child, as a rule, finds it painful and certainly less alluring than action. But habit perfectseone in this matter, and the life with books may become as .vital, as real, as consoling as a life with society. Moreover, as soon as one has learned to hive. them, Woks never fail us ; they \ are
lways accessible, always willing to yield up

their secrets, always sympathetic. In life one cannot always cultivate the associations We would like. The peOple you want to know may live at the other ends Of the earth, or their moods may be variable, or their interests other than yours; but in a world of books we can
literally ehoOse just what we want for our Own immediate consolatipn. On the whole, there is nothing in the world, perhaps, so repays a woman as acquiring the habit of reading.

div.head: VENUS TIIE ONLY HABITABLE PLANET.
div.p: VENUS TIIE ONLY HABITABLE PLANET.

Mr. Walter Maunder, the eminent astrontimer, has revived the speculation as to whether the heavenly bodies are inhabited or not by pub- lishing softie careful calculations as to their temperature. Ile shows that the Sun's temper- ature is more than 5,000 C., while the Moon, owing toits lasi: of atmosphere, is At night at about the temperature of liquid air. Mercury, who -always turns one face to the ..Sun; must be far hotter than anything of *Well' we have any knowledge, while Mars must always be at below freezing point. The more distant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune—are so far away from the Sun that they 'receive scarcely any heat from him, while they are still M a nearly incandescent condition, and, ac- cording to Mr. Maunder, have probably no solid nucleus. Venus, however, has a mean tempera- ture of .69 degrees,C., and at the equator one Of 95 degrees. C., so that," allowing.for the differ- ence in pressure, water should 1?6i1 at its equa- tor. This would send forth such vast quantities of sleam.That the clouds would cut off Much of the S'un's heat. Mr. Maunder denies that 4ny planet but Venus Can be habitable,..and as to Venus he reserves judgment. For 'protqplasm, the universal constituent of all living matter, cannot live permaneritlrbelow.o degrees C. nor above 100 degrees C. Therefore the Sun, Mer- Miry, and the, distant-planets would be too hot for it, while Mars and the Moon would be too cold, leaviug only Venus as, a possibility.'

div.head: WHERE VEGETARIANLSM
div.p: WHERE VEGETARIANLSM

• "It is truly ,a murderous diet," says Dr. Arnold. Lorand, of Carlsbad, writing of strict vegetar- ianism. Further on in his chapter he remarks : "1 have never seen a strict vegetarian who did not look pale and thin." A diet of vegetables only is unscientific, for the reason that the most important producer of energy—Lalbumin—is scarcely represented in it. If the vegetables be supplemented by plenty..of eggs, cheese, milk and butter, then the diet becomes almost ideal. But there are vegetarians who will not eat even these. Dr. Lorand censures the . Vegetarian restaurants in Europe, particularly in Germany-, for their apparent .effort to furnish very cheap meals. This necessitates the elimination from their bills of fare of such hluable foods as sago, tapioca, honey, and even rice,, which supply considerable amounts of carbohydrates , that Might take the place of meat. Cows and sheep live on a purely vegetarian diet.. But in order to get enough nutrition cows and sheep have to spend their7entire time eating. Man cannot eat from early morn to late night. His stomach is not big enough. He has only one stomach ; a cow has four. No man on a strictly vegetarian diet can take in enough- food to maintain his I strength. He has to spend most of his waking hours at work and can devote ony a small 'Anil of his time to eating Then, again, to get the full benefit of his vegetable food he must masti- cate it as-thOroughly as a cow does. If his teeth were like a cow's and he had as ,much saliva and pepsin, and could regurgitate the food he had swallowed and then spend hours recheWing it, ike a cow, then he might subsist on vegetable's alone. The small quanti4y of :albumin in vegetables is inclosed in cells of cellulose; which the human teeth are incapable of mashing fine enough, and the human gastric juice incapable of digesting. The result of per- sistence in such a diet is intestinal troublv, owing Jo' the large quantities of food that must be eaten in order to get nutriment, and to the Mile efforts the intestines make to digest it. IloweVer-, there -are Certain diseases—gout, arteriosclerosis, diabetes • and obesity, for example,-Athich :are benefited by a vegetable diet, but it must not be persisted in for 100 long a tinie.
WIT AND HUMOUR OF THE JEWS.
Lucien- Wolf contributes a Very readable
article to the "Sunday, at I-Nme" dealing with Carlyle and Benan!s agegation that "the Jew is not a laughing animal." The writer says a sense of humour is native to the liebrew char-

acter, and it has been neither eNtirpated nor diminished by the much ". laughter on the wrong side of the mouth" to which the kw has been so often driN'en. The optimist view of life which is especially characteristic of Jewish teaching rendered the cultivation of cheerfulness almost a ,religious duty. It is related -in the Talmud that a sage once met the prophet Elijah in a crowded market-place and asked him who would be saved out of all assembled there. The prophet pointed to two ordinary-looking trades- men who were laughing and jesting with one another.
"What are your saving works?" inquired the sage, rushing towards them.

`.-We'are but poor workmen and live by our trade," was the answer.' "All that can he said of us iS that we are always in good spirits, and when we meet a face that is sad or a heart that is downcast, we talk and laugh and cheer away cares and grief."
This high estimqte of the worth of cheerful- n s.s is.characterislically.lewish. Hebrew liter- atare is indeed full of 'practical illustrations of the "saving works" here indicated.

The Rabbis know_ hoW, to enliven the driest and most difficult themes, and their wit does not desert them even in the exposition of profound theological problems. A typical instance occurs in the Talmudic Tracate Sanhedrin in the shape of a discussion between a•Roman Emperor and the famous Rabbi Jehuda Hanai on the subject of the relations of body and soul. "It seems to me," said the monarch, "Mat at pod's footstool body and soul might plead suc- cessfully against punishment. The body has only to point to its own helplessness from the mOffient the soul has.left it in order to prove its incapacity to sin. On the other hand, the soul may lay all the blame on the body and appeal to its own purity when divorced from its material envelope. How can such a defence be withstood?"

• The kiabbi replied: "A 'king once placed his garden under the care of two 'men, one Of whom was lame and the other blind, thinking thus he could no be robbed even by his watchmen. The cripple, however, prevailed upon his blind colleague to take- him on his back, and in this way the two managed .every now and again to pilfer the fruit.. When the king reproached Ahem with their sin the lame watcher pointed out that he could not possibly be guilty, because he was unable to walk, and the blind, with equal posi- ..

tiveness, swore that lie must be innocent, because he could not see. But the king made the cripple mount on the shoulders of the blind man, and then asked them wheth4 they were guilty, and they could not answer. So it is with body and soul."

div.head: LOVE LETTERS OF A CHINESE LADY.
div.p: LOVE LETTERS OF A CHINESE LADY.

, The second series of "Love Letters of a Chinese Lady," in the "Pall Mall Magazine" for. September, have an attraction peculiarly their own. The second of these dainty epistles —there are 25 in all—says : " My Dear One,—Thou -askest: me if I still care for thee, if the remembrance of thy face has grown less dear with the passing of the days. Dear one, thou knowest we Chinese women are not supposed to know of love, much less to speak of it. We read of it, we know it is the song of all the world, but it comes not to us unless by Chance. We go to you as stran- gers, we- have no choice, and if the gods' with- hold their greatest gift, the gift of love, then life is gray and wan as the twilight of a hope- less day. Few women have the joy I feel when I look into my loved one's face and know that I am his and he is mine, and that our lives are twined together for all the days to come. Do I love, thee? I cannot tell. I think of thee by day, and I dream of thee by night. I never want to- hurt thee nor cause a moment's sorrow. I would fill my hands with happiness to lay down at thy feet. Thou art my life, my all, and I am thine to hold through all the years."

div.head: PUZZLE.
div.p: A PUZZLE.

Here is a problem for you. In yobr leading article to-day you write: "By admitting Ger- man Manufactures free of all rates and taxes to this country, the British Government sup- plies wages for millions of Germans." Presum- ably, then, if the British Government did not admit German manufactures free there would be millions of Germans without wages. Mil- lions of starving Germans !—and this in a Pro- tected country! Is Protection, then, NOT a cer- tain _remedy for unemployment, after all?— "A. A. M." to the "Daily Mail" of October 18th, 1911. '

THE DOINGS OF THE MONKS OF ST. WERBURGH.

We opened our article last week xvith a refer- ence to: the ancient Refectory of Chester, one of the half-lost and 41f-forgotten relics of the old city. But we stayed our hand at lhe period of the. Norman invasion, and no account was given of the: cluster of noble buildings which WC. know as Chester Cathedral and its pre- cincts. Perhaps, therefore, another chapter is due dealing with the Abbey and its builders..

the place of the axe for the hewing.. -0E stone, and as monastery buildings- multiplied. they grew in beauty and dimension. Though labour iS cheap,. such work cannot be done save at. large and growing coSt, and so Earl Hugh has given lands and nulls, tithes of corn, chickens, pigs and cheese, and all , the profits of the Fair at. St. Werburghfs Feast. And in this generous attitude his successors have followed him.

The community that lives in the Abbey is sell-supporting. It is a city within a- city, and can hold out and make hostility (as it did more than once) against ,the city without. It had its own lands and mills (the famous one on the Dee and one at the Bache), and a small army of servants ground the corn, cooked and garri- soned normous cellars of wine. • A MONASTERY DINNER.

To witness the community at its happiest (though, perhaps, not at its best), we cannot do better than visit the Refectory at the hour of dinner. The old walls are still there, and the exquisite lectern looks down upon us. Alas! tharwe should see it only as a wreck. Then the sun shone through- coloured glass, tables groaned Under piles of dainties, and the rafters .echoed noisy and .cheery voices. The cook was a mall of substance—an artist in his way. Let us glance •at one of his efforts, monastery dinner.

lie brings from the cook shop peacocks and herons, stewed' pheasants .a•nd cygnets, boiled meats and. sucking rabbits, with brawn, pottage,, almond cream and sage fritters. But this is a' monastery, not a wayside inn. It is a monas- tery, and these are pious men.. And so each course closes . with a huge "device," which is- a set-piece - made from sugar, pastry or jelly, and representing the angel appearing to. Mary or to the shepherds of Bethlehem, each scene being embellished with a Latin text.

These savoury.meSses are duly saturated with choice. red Gascony Wine or white rupell, mus- cadelle or malvoisie. Over the liquors, as over the home-made bread and confectionery, pre- sides the butler, another dignitary of rank and means.

At a later and palmy day, King Edward and Eleanor sat upon the dais among these brave old, gormandisers, and were 'royally entertained. Would that we. could see the Refectory as they saw it that day t Alas the windows are gone, SO also are vestments, chalices and missals,

Yet we are not without some 'eloquent relics. They carved their coarse and grotesque fancies in oak under their misererie seats and upon the corbels of the church. And we have their architecture to show how near to -a heavenly perfection. they could come. Is there anything more beautiful than the lectern in the Refectory? Few visitors see it, but none who would understand the genius of the monk Should miss it. Let us see- it in use! The feast is to begin; small armies of servants bustle with food and wine.; dogs wait to light for bones .amid the. rushes that Strew the floor. g After grace has been recited the reader climbs the ,puly.;it, and. at a sign from the Scripture. Then comes the first course. Athbebsottaibrse in Again the .reading s to recite some passages of and then the second clatter of knives and pewter, .

• • This is monastery.langnage; it declares that man cannot live. 1w bread alone. we may become satirical at. the memory of the army of cooks, yet no ong Can behold the beauty of the reader's lectern and remain. unimprewd.

div.head: COMING OF THE CONQUEROItu
div.p: THE COMING OF THE CONQUEROItu

It -was in the early months of 7the year A.D. 1070 that the Norman warriors entemd Che- shire. Three and a hail years before they had defeated Harold at the Battle of. Scuttle, and now, after years filled with toil and. bloodshed, they .were approaching the completion of -the conquest of England. York had surrendered, and William the Conqueror pierced his way through the snowdrifts or the. Pennine Range to deal with the last city that held out against him.

When Chester Yielded, England' was at his feet, and he marched south to-Salisbury. to hold a review and to. reward his faithful fight- ing men. In the giving or the rewards he was ball shrewd and generous. KnOwing well the importance of Chester. as the city that must keep the untamed Welsh in check„ he bestowed i his o ss nef P.irewiHugh Lupus, giving him the Cheshire and Flint lon g with uiru-nti it, and making Cheshire a County palatine. Durham, also, as the base from which the .Northern tribes must be held back. was made a‘County Palatine, which meant that the rulers were, for all essential purposes, absolute kings In their own sphere. Hugh Lupus, as Earl of Chester, was supreme in his own domain. He had the power of life and death, and could pardon or punish any crime. The sword, which was his symbol of power, can still he Seen in the British Museum, and the charter which confirmed the gift says: "ila libere ad gladium sieut ipse Rex totam tenebat Anglian ad coronam," which we understand to mean that, under the symbol of VIE sword the .Earl was to have in Cheshire the same powers that the king, by his crown; possessed over England.,,

div.head: ENTER HUGH TIIE' WOLF'.
div.p: ENTER HUGH TIIE' WOLF'.

- - Into this heritage stepped Hugh d'Avratiches, familiarly known as Hugh Lulu's 011( Wulf), and he seems to have made the most .of it. Of restraint he knew none. He was cruel, licentious and prodigal, and extracted from his estate as much of Worldly ha.ppiness as.a man well could. Says a chronicler of the period: "He was not abundantly but profusely prodigal, and carried not so -much a family as .an army along with him. He.took no account either of his receipts or disbursements; he daily waSted his estate, and delighted more- in falcons and huntsmen than in the tillers of his land, or Heaven's orators, the ministers.- He was much given to his belly, whereby in time he grew. so fat that he could 'scarc,e crawl." But. Hugh had other qualities. Certainly he was no coward,. and his dealings with the Welsh show him as a man of military skill. His name sent a trernoUr through the Pl'illei- pality. Only once, when he had gone to Nor- mandy in 1094, did they strike an effective blow' at Chester, but they paid dearly fOr that: tem- porary triumph when Hugh" came 'home. He carried sword,- fire and, plunder as .-far as Anglesey, and the stories Of cruelty put a chill into ones blood. Hugh regarded the plague of the Welsh as we should regard a plague of cockroaches, and he had as little uneasiness at measures of wholesale slaughter.

div.head: TIIE FOUNDING OF .THEABBE
div.p: TIIE FOUNDING OF .THEABBE

And -.yet Hugh - Lupus ,was , religious. Had anyone suggested that these wholesale and un- nameable cruelties were irreligious, he would not have understood. If was Li day in Nth" wholesale murder and deep and sincere religion could be the chief marks in al ruler's life. But there were sins (of which torturing Welsh prisoners was certainly not -one) to be dealt with, and it was the Comfortable doctrine. of the day that charity covered a multitude of them. It .was also a useful teaching of the Period that .there was a big account to be settled with' heaven, either in this. world or the next, and that when the balance \VS made lavish gifts to the Chach would be found to weigh heavy in the scale. So Hugh Lupus decided to found a ,monas- tery. Possibly the Church was using pressure, for he had been Earl for twenty years; and done nothing for "Heavens orators, the- min- isters ?'; or the idea may have been 'his own. As friend and adviser, he sent for Ansehn, the Abbot of Bec, in Normandy, and the scheme took shape. Church chroniclers, have spoken in high terms of the huge gifts made by Hugh Lupus in his closing,years. But to a man Who owned two whole counties, and held wide possessions in nineteen, others, it could hardly have been a. sacrifice. • his greatest and most' durable work was the Abbey and Monastery of Chester. Many of the stones that rose under his direction still hold together, and, though much has perished enough remains to enable us to see the scheme as a whole. The rand.thal was to be devoted to the Monas- tery was .about one-fourth of the land inside the walls of the city of Chester, and included a small church which stood upon the site :of the present Cathedral. Here rested the Lones of St. Weiturgh, and as the saint was to give her name to. the monastery, a word had better be said here about her.

div.head: SAINT WERBURGII.
div.p: SAINT WERBURGII.

St..Werburgh was a saint of the seventh cen- tury, a daughter of the Mercian King Wulfere. The story went that she had rejected all lovers, having, as she averred,. chosen Christ as her beloved., Having, with difficulty, obtained per- mission from her father to inter, the Abbey of Ely, she became so distinguished a member that King Ethelred made her ruler oyer all the nunneries Of Mercia. When death overtook her in the midst, of her good works she was buried at Hanbury, but the Danes overran England, and her body was carried to Chester for safety. To this bare record, tradition has added stories of miracles and deeds of mercy, and of a great feast Made by Wulfere to Celebrate the marriage of Werburgh to her Saviour. Such was the reputation or the saint who rested here, and, of course, no other name than hers could be attached to the new abbey and monastery that was to be built.

div.head: WHAT THE ABBEY WAS LIKE.
div.p: WHAT THE ABBEY WAS LIKE.

The reader will, perhaps, • prefer that we should turn on the kaleidoscope, and omitting the toilsome years of buildipg, see the monas- tery in its happiest days. • The first glimpse will cost us no effort. Indeed every reader must have seen it in very deed, for the Abbey gate is still standing. Sombre and strong, it stands as in the days when Benedictines thronged 'under it or came out with naked steel to fight. Not so as we pass beneath into. the Abbey square: We must close our eyes upon the Georgian houses that surround us, and open them if we can upon a different scene. Around Ibis square stood the Monastery brewhouse, bakehouse and limekiln. On the south, massive and fair, had risen the Abbey Church of St. Werburgh. The Master workers who had directed it, and probably its designer had -come from Normandy, but with the passing of the years the local craftsmen had gained much skill. The chisel had taken

div.head: SEAMY SIDE.
div.p: THE SEAMY SIDE.

They are a straiige miXthre, thee .denizens or the-.'AbbeyS. Stains, pitiful and lie upon. -their history. What grim stories belong to. St. Werburgh! ' The monks hold pitched battles in the Streets with the Black and White Friars; wholesale robbery, rape and. plotting; with the-part of. the footpad and highwayman belongs to the record, and these things, vitli the :added crime .Of murder, were no disqualification of the monk aspired to the high'oilice of. Abbot. Clerics are mixed up' in tavern brawls, and, with gowns trussed up, parade the stets with sword in hand. The city authorities- can do nothing with them, for they can ;joie their gates, and,. by the powers given in their. charter, can set thelcormhunity at deillnee. 'St. 'Werburgh's flouts not only the mayor and city, but even the King of: the realm. Good men out of good design ilitVe gifts upon- the monasteries. Their ,glits have gone to feast the monks and inflame their blood with alcohol.
• A- QUAINT RELIC, Yet, on another side, ,how childish and sufc.r- -stitiouS these roystering fellows! Take just one quaint conceit, whtch may be seen in the Cathedral.
Under the second window of the clerestory is a carved figure all huddled together : and bound hand and foot. This. is the expression Of a monkish belief which we will, state lI'S mildly as possible.

The devil was always consumed with a desire to witness the celebration of Mass. lie Could not watch it through the choir windows, be- cause each was guarded by an angel: But the nave windows were not thus Protected against him. Coining from the north,. his own quarter as they believed, he would travel straight to the most easterly Window of the nave, in the hope that by screwing his head close against the glass he might see the altar. But in peeping in the first object he would Re is this•figure all huddled and bound—a pic- tnre.of the fate that awaits him if he ventures to fix his ugly eyes upon the Christian mystery. The devil these men, believed in. was a very genuine character. They studied him and they knew him well. That they felt him very close is proven by a carving under one .of the stalls. Here a small demon (possibly not the (levil-in- chief, but one of, his successful offspring) crouches under the • monk's seat and disturbs his holy meditations with unholy sniggers.

The visitor to Chester .Cathedral should study the misererie seats upon which the •. monks lavished _their art and superstition. The Tomb Of St: Werburgh should also be studied, though to see it as it was in other days we must needs conjure up carved images of Mercian Kings and Queens, and jewels and embroideries that glow in the light of coloured Jumps.

div.head: TWO MEMORIALS.
div.p: TWO MEMORIALS.

It is sufficient, perhaps, for the present article to think •of the -Abbey in connection with its founder. In old age, wrecked in body and impelled by superstition, Hugh Lupus himself took the monk's .gown in his own monastery. But the .sands were fast running out. Three days later he died there- and was laid to rest In the Abbey garden. - • It was an age or rough *Measures . and crude belief. We will, therefore, judge , the Norman Earl as kindly as may be. He left a beautiful Abbey, reared for the glory of -God. Ile left also an example of cruelty 'that bore fruit in his successors.-

There was another pile in Chester.. It was a pile of Welshmen's heads reared in a huge pyramid \in ghastly 'display. Never was savagery over a foe more manifest, than here. It is a fair reading of history to say that Earl Hugh had two me-morial piles in his strong city. One was, the stately monastery the other was a pile of grinning skulls. This last was destined to endure for four centuries.
It was one of history's revenges that, it. stood longer than his Abbey Church, and fastened upon him the grim name by which he NiII be known for ever, [high the Wolf. A. M.

A Clever Canary.

Beatrice" writes: "When I read of: the Brainy•Raccoon,' I thought I would tell you a bit about my canary, that has:just died. We called him Peter, and he was nearly tAv.elve years old. He was five months when I bought him, and, with a little patience, I taught him some amusing tricks. First I trained' him to

hop on the table at meals, telling him to peck at anything that was going, except meat.. At a call he would fly on my head, or shoulder, or finger. He would not only kiss, but also shake hands. He was. very intelligent, and did lots of things 1 should like to tell you about; but I know I must not take up much space. Just this let me say: If I lay in bed in the upper room at the front of the house, and Peter was released from his cage in the lower room at the back, and I whistled to let him know when I was, he would fly upstairs and find me with- out fail every time. I have a capital photograph of him .perched on my forefinger."

A Nice "Chicken " Game.. , One sees the little Chinese children playing this game in the. streets of Hong Kong. A num- ber at straight rows of kindling wood are laid On the ground—as many :rows as there are children—in each row ten. sticks an easy hop- ping,distance apart. The players who are the "chickens" stand at the head of the lines. 'At a given signal each begins to hop over the sticks in his line. Only one foot must touch- the ground at one time, so it is no easy journey. When the end of a row is successfully reached tlw last stick is kicked away, and the "chicken' hops back to his starting point. As soon asshe reaches the first stick, that, too. may be ideked away, and he continues hopning, backward and forward. until only one stick remains :in his row. The player who does this first wins the game.

div.head: BIT THE POLIGEMAN'S HANDS.
div.p: BIT THE POLIGEMAN'S HANDS.

Found in a drunken state by the Runcorn police, John Critchley, no fixed abode, became disorderly when he was Spoken to and the police sought to Jock him up. He behaved-violently, and bit a constable's hands before lie could be locked up. He has since been sent by the local justices to a month in prison with hard labour. •

div.head: POLICE PBESENTATrON ETIQUETTE.
div.p: POLICE PBESENTATrON ETIQUETTE.

At Runcorn Police Court on Monday the Chairman (Mr. F. J. Norman), on behalf of his fellow-justices, and Messrs. Laycock and Steel on behalf of solicitors, congratulated Superin- tendent Ennion upon his promotion to North- .wich. Mr. Shaw asked the Superintendent, to accept a present which the committee of the Mersey Mission Grappling Corps had sub- scribed. -

Superintendent Ennion replied that he was much obliged to Mr. Shaw, but he could not receive any presents without the permission of the Chief Constable. If Mr. Shaw agreed to make such an application, it would give him great pleasure to receive the gift..
The -Chairman said he was su-re that the Chief Constable would give the necessary permission.
THE DOCTOR'S DONKEY.

How a donkey was alleged to have suffered on behalf of scientific research was told at Runcorn Police Court on Monday, when the, R.S.P.C.A. summoned Dr. Warrington Yorke, head of the Research Laboratory of the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, and a well-known expert in sleeping sickness "for unlawfully, cruelly and unnecessarily causing suffering to an -ass by omitting to give the same proper and necessary, care and attention when the animal was in a state of suffering." Dr. Yorke said he was experimenting at the present time on sleeping sickness, and it was necessary to inject certain drugs into animals. In order to treat a disease like sleeping sickness they had first of all to ascertain the maximum dose they could safely give, and it was quite obvious that one could not experiment' on human beings. They must first of all find out the effect of a dose on large animals, such as donkeys and horses, before one could give such a dose to human beings. The object of this chug was to ascertain the dose when the experi- ment was performed. It was absolutely -pain- less, and the animal was lying dead as the result of paralysis. The Bench said the R.S.P.C.A. Society should have made more careful investigation. They dismissed the charge, with two guineas costs against the society, whose solicitor intimated that there would probably be an appeal.

He could recommend very urgently the passing of the scheme. In fact, it recommended itself in saving money , in the administration of the highways. div.head: NO "DEAD" SEASON NOW.
div.p: NO "DEAD" SEASON NOW.

The .ancient city •of • Cologne is to have an exhibition next year, and the committee decided —at a very late hour—that the building to be devoted to women's works, in decorative art, as applied to the home, • statuary, painting, drawing, fashion designing, toys, &c., would be lost fittingly housed in a building designed , carried out by' members of the feminine Accordingly a competition was hastily. ..iounced and limited to candidates of German and Austrian nationality. Tile result is most gratifying to the women who competed, and equally encouraging to those whc; are training as architects. 'Three prizes were offered, and a dozen women competed. The first prize . was awarded to a German„ and her plan is described as well-proportioned and dignified, and requir- ing very little alteration. The second prize, artistic in every curve and line, was won by a, 'Viennese lady, the third by a Berliner. the. judges paid a tribute to the powers of all the competitors to realise the details necessary to the housing and display of exhibition goods, and to the Capacity shown for applying artistic ideas to the building; and its internal decoration. and arrangement. GERMAN WOMEN STUDENTS.
SOX.

German women are availing themselves of te opportunities afforded them of entering the medical and other professions, as well as that Of architecture. At the end of. the summer term there were no fewer than three thousand four hundred and. tliirty7six enrolled women stlidents. and over .one thousand, not yet associated with any of the twenty-one German universities. Of these, nearly eight hundred were medical students. Not all, however, are Germans; at least five. timdred of the total number are foreigners, and quite three-fourths of the German women come from Prussia.

div.head: PROFESSIONS FOR WOMEN.
div.p: PROFESSIONS FOR WOMEN.

Educated women who desire to avoid drift- ing into the overcrowded professions, might well turn their attention to dental or optical work. The National Dental Hospital offers every inducement to women students, but few take advantage of the opportunity to pass the necessary examinations. There are a few suc- cessful women practitioners, but nothing like the number who could find profitable' employ- ment in this profession. It is mainly for women and children patients that there is a growing demand for female professional ser- vices, and in this connection it may be men- tioned that the Queen of Holland has a woman dentist attached to her household. Modern dental surgery is, of course, very different from what it was in former times, when the dentist's operating room was generally regarded as a sort of "chamber of horrors." There may still be occasions when• there is sotnething un- pleasant and disagreeable about dentgl 'clinics( but there is no real objection to women taking up the profession on this score. Even more Suited for women is the profession of an optician, provided an educated. girl can make arrangements for the necessary study and training, as there are no difficulties on the score of sex to. her passing the examinations of ,either the British Optical Association or the Spectacle Makers' _Company:

div.head: LONDON IN. SEPTEMBER
div.p: LONDON IN. SEPTEMBER

To remain in London in the holiday season was, and is still, considered a real hardshiP, by the average native. Yet those who, nolens v.,lens, remain, have not so very much of which It) complain. The • trafficis mu less less gested, the streets are quieter, the, parks are at their Ipbest,)esasnivde. That our Metropolis is in ait is not often that the heat is. very o fair way to become the world's holiday ground is evidenced by the number. of foreigners who crowd the , pavements, and fill to overflowing the omnibuses, restaurants, picture galleries and nuiseums. The provincial long ago dis- covered that London in September was as en- joyable as at any other time, and he will en- dOrse Harriet Martineau's opinion that the evening walks in the parks were a rare pleasure, and that she knew pf 4 few things better than Kensington Gardens in August and September: And the, West End shops are quite alive to the advantages to be derived from attracting th custom of the visitor. The windows are filled with beautiful 'fabrics, chic costumes, charming dresses, delicious millin- ery, and all kinds of alluring accessories. To all appearance. a brisk trade 'is being done, and dollars and sovereigns find their way from the pockets of the holiday-makers to the coffers of the emporiums by quite a natural process. The dead season, as it used to be termed, is Without doubt a thing of the past. COMING MODES.

-- - What is to be worn during the coming autumn and winter is the question that is ex- ercising the fashion-mongers at the present moment, and the new modes that, have made their appearance somewhat early, are eagerly discussed and keenly criticised by the dress- makers and tailors. It ,would seem that the days of the simple frocks are numbered, 'but they are too useful and graceful to be lightly discarded in favour of the voluminous draperies, flounces and frills that are to be in- -troduced this autumn. Fashions are given to extremes, and shapelessness is to be the promi- nent feature of coming .modes, just as the sil- lionette.w6s the other end of the Pole. Skirts have undergone greater . changes than Coats, more especially the tailored types.. These 'latter show gulch fulness in front, and scarcely less at the bapl:. Draperies, are skilfully arranged round the his, in soft lines, that are not un- becoming to sotne figures. However, many fashions launched in the beginning of a season have the most ephemeral existence, and it would not be safe to predict now that radical 'changes are at hand, although some, of Course, are inevitable. THE WIRED FLOUNCE. - - -

The wired tunic lias led to the adoption of the wired flounce, the Precursor, it iS said, of the crinoline. This flounce is seen only on evening dresses, which; in many cases, have three. divisions of colour and material; the corsage, the sash and the flounce, below which an , accordion-pleated underskirt falls limply and skimpily round the ankles. The skirts are full and quite bunchy in the middle, where lhe flounce is wired to keep it from falling fiat at the sides. When not exaggerated, and worn by tall, slim women, the effect is not unpleas- ing. The open neck is still seen, and many corsages are open from the neck ,to the waist, the gap 'being filled pp "With lace or embroidery in a cpntraSting .colour, Or harmonising With tie tones of the dress. Some sleeves are long and tight, and finished at the wrist with a deep fall of lace, others reach the elbow, from which exaggerated frills depend; or, again, 'folds are carelessly arranged and complete the short sleeve just below the elbow. Some evening dresses are quite without sleeves.

div.head: SUFFRAGE NOTES.
div.p: SUFFRAGE NOTES.
Responsibility for the Hooliganism Attending the Pilgrimage Meetings.
WOMEN IN THE COURTS.
BY A CORRESPONDENT,. Mr, McKenna's reply in Parliament to ques-

tions with regard to hooliganism in connection with the Suffrage Pilgrimage Can scarcely be regarded as satisfactory. In answer to Mr. Philip Snowden he stated that no suggestion had been made by the National Union that the disorder was organised from any centre, and
all the evidence he had tended to show

that it was due to outbursts of local hOoligan- ism. This is very misleading. The National Union, in the report- sent to Mr. ,NlcKenna 'On August 14th, produced evidence Which points very strongly to orgtiniseti attempts to stir up the hooligan element in the crowd. The ring- leaders, states this document, were generally men who did not belong to the locality, but pre- ceded the Pilgrims from place to place, and collected bands of rowdy youths to create dis- turbance, and particularly, to pursue the speakers after the meeting and use them roughly. The report also gives a number of specific instances in which the same 'Man, or group of men, stirred up trouble in different places. There is also considerable evidence that the Anti-Suffrage speakers who preceded the pilgrims used language calculated to stir up violence.

div.head: REFORM OF LEGAL PROCEDURE.
div.p: REFORM OF LEGAL PROCEDURE.
We are ,glad to Fe;r—n—That a memorzindum is been addressed to the Horne Secretary_.by

the Women's Freedom League, protesting against the mode Of procedure our Courts in trying cases ,of indecent and Criminal assault. There is great, need for special Courts, presided over by women, fOr trying delinquent girls. No less necessary, in the intereSts of decency and justice, is the influence of women in the trial of certain offences against women and children. The injustice and impropriety of the present cugtom of excluding w9men--2--even relativts of the victim—from such trials, and questioning girls alone in a Court crowded with men, who are often of the lowest type, was admitted by the Home Secretary when his attention was called to it by the Freedom League last Febru- ary; but no steps have been taken to remedy the abuse. _

There is great need for women to serve on juries. There is also great need for women officers with a certain amount of legal training to act in an advisory capacity to magistrates in cases where women and children dre con- cerned. In Russia the special Children's Courts of Justice inquire into eases of physical and moral injury inflicted upon children and young girls, and there is much to be said for the practice. It is certainly in the interests of justice that the woman's point of view shall be represented, both in the case of misdemeanours of this type which can be dealt with summarily, and at the more serious offences under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, which are tried before a jury. The average.man is inclined to regard certain offences far more, lightly than a woman would do; but men are unduly lenient, not out of sympathy with the offender, but because they do not realise to the full the suffer- ing involved. If the women's point of view could be brought home to them it would meet with very little opposition. Rut so long as women are liable to be excluded from the Courts, and take no part in the administration of the law, there is little hope- that, offences against the person will be dealt with more drastically.

div.head: BOTH THE GOODS AND THE MONEY:*
div.p: BOTH THE GOODS AND THE MONEY:*

DID THE POSTCARD COME FROM WARRINGTON?.. A correspondent sends us, as a specimen of Tariff " Reform " propaganda, a postcard bear- ing, within an ornamental scroll, the follow- ing printed text: "I do not know much about the tariff, but I do know this much when we buy goods abroad we get the goods, and the foreigner gets the money; when we buN goods made at home we get both the goods and the money.—ABRAHAM LINCOLN." It seems that this modest yet comfortable -exposition of the glorious gospel of something for nothing is en- joying quite a vogue amongst Tariff " Reformers " as a means of stimulating the cupidity of the unconverted; and, indeed, there is something that we find rather taking in.. its apparently artless simplicity. It reminds us . . of the once-popular conundrum about the shopkeeper who gave a hat and five shillings for a, bad sovereign, which he changed with a neighbouring tradesman, to whom he had sub- sequently to make restitution. There were some people who could never be convinced that the hatter's loss was not two pounds, or at least the hat and twenty-five, shillings,and some of these, or others equally bad at sums, may sus- , pect that hanest Abraham Lincoln discovered a ' - way of ringing the changes' by which buyers could "get both the goods and the money." If there are any such, we suggest, for their benefit, a simple method of testing the statement. Every purchase is also a sale, and therefore what Lincoln said of buying must apply 'equally well to selling. Thus transposed, the golden text would read: " When we sell goods abroad we part with the goods and the foreigner parts with the rnoney ;, when we sell goods at home we. part with both the goods and the money." .The two statements contain exactly the same mea- sure of literal truth and implied .falsehood, the key to the falsehood being, of course, the play made with the word "we."—" Manchester Guardian."

A PROLONGED STRUGGLE. William Marsh, steker, of 34, Woodcock- street, was fined 20s. and costs, on Monday, for assaulting Constable Evans, and ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night in Robins-lane, where he and the officer struggled for a long period.

div.head: LIBERAL PROGRESSION.
div.p: LIBERAL PROGRESSION.
Workers Now Realising Benefits of Compulsory Insurance.
TARIFF REFORM BOGEY.

If the large crowds who assemble to,listen to the speakers at the Progressive Labour League meetings at Bridge Foot be any criterion then the Progressive cause in Warrington is criterion, rapid headway. The tone of the meetings clearly indicate that the, pendulum of public opinion has once more swung round in favour ot the Progressive cause. Mr. JOHN JOHNSON presided at the meeting Oil Monday evening, and there was a crowd of about 1,000, and a most enthusiastic funCtion it proved. Mr. Johnson said -the present Gov- ernment were unique. They had started upon a line which no other Government had ever attempted to travel ; they started along the line of social reform in order to lift the inasses out of 'degradation and poverty. (Hear,. hear.) They had passed some great measures. • The people were now appreciating the bene- fits of the Insurance Act, a measure which the Tories praised at first and then obstructed it wherever they could. The Tories said they believed in national insurance, but not in a compulsory scheme. -flow could there be a national insurance scheme which was not com- pulsory? Suppose two men were out of work. One was insured and the other was not. Both applied for a situation and the employer asked ' if they were insured. One would answer that he was not and he Would get the job, as it would save the employer paying his share. Thus the man who had been thrifty would be always cut out in competition with the un- insured. The Tories had often changed their tune over the Insurance -Act.. • First they said that Mr. Lloyd George was not *paying enouglybenefits. Now they were saying that he was paying too high benefits and that he waS ruining the friendly societies. All through till! Conserva- tive attitude ,to the Insurance Act had been far from creditable. Their criticism had been most unfair and consisted in the main of wilful, dishonest lies. (Applause.)
The Tories' Hopes.

ri. T. MALLALIEU the speaker of the evening, said the Insurance Act was reaching a stage when it could- take care_ of -itself. Ile remembered a well-known Conservative say about the Act, 18_ months ago: "If we can only have a General Election, we can sweep the country, but if this wicked Badical Government can Stay in power ler another two years, until the full benefits of the Act have become known, God knows what chance our party will stand." (Laughter and applause.) That illustrated the attitude of the Tory Party from the first. At first the Act was unpopular amongst some nine million people, who did not under- stand why 4d. should be deducted from their small earnings. The Tories seized upon that and worked the by-:elections for all they were worth upon it. They told the people they were being swindled. If a man paid in 17s. 4cl. a year and received back 335.,- was he swindled? Would not the -.people in Warring- -ton like to be swindled upon these lines. (Laughter, and Voices: "Yes," and. "Very much.") The Insurance Act was not now re- ceiving. the ,attention it once did from the Con- servatives, because people were, beginning to find out its benefits.
Holding Their Own.

That recalled a story about the members of an Irish Urban Council. They had had a little trip into the country, and at night.two of them found the last train to Donegal had gone, and they had, no option but to walk nine miles. "Nine' miles," said. Mike, "Come along, Pat, sure it's only four and a half each." They walked on for hours, met a policeman, and asked, how far they were from Doftek,al. N toe' miles' was the reply. They .walked on all through the night, and in the early morning found a woman lighting her lire, They asked her how far they were frOm Donegal. "Nine miles," was the Answer. " Faith," said Mike, irs mighty queer; but, thank the Lord, We are holding Our own." (Loud Laughter.) 'Well, the Insurance Act was more than holding its own. Bolton election marked the turning point, and Chesterfield had stamped the fact. (Applause.) , There. would now never' come a party in this country who would dare to repeal that Act. They heard some people talking about, this wicked Government. Many were praying night and morning fOr Tory regime. Ilad the country been going to the dogs under the :Liberal Government? (" No.") Was the country worse than it was seven years ago? ("NO.") Were there more unemployment than seven years ago." (" No.") The Tories Could not say the country was worse. and they could not deny that it was infinitely better. (Ap- plause.) The very poor people• who paid a super-tax upon incomes of £5,000 a year still had their motor ears and servants. , These were not signs of national ruin.
Where is Tariff Reform?

'rue working men now knew more about the Tory policy of Tariff Reform than they ,ctid ten years ago. In the interval the Tories had said that their policy of Tariff Reform was,so. simple it did net require demonstration. If that .was .so how Was it the Tory party itself was con- shinny changing itS attitude upon the question of Tariff Reform? (Hear, hear.) They said Tariff Reform meant shifting the taxation bur den. lt,did mean that, and it meant indreasing the burden of taxation borne by , the working class. (Applause.) Mr. Austen'Cheinberlain let tile cat out of the

bag when he said: "With the exeePtion of the National Insurance Act, the present Govern- ment have made no demand upon the working class to contribute towards any of the great social reforms introduced." It was true the Liberals had not made - demands upon the workers, and -where did the .money come from for that purpose? The 1909 Budget provided for it. The money came out of the pockets Of the wealthy._ •(Applause.) The speaker challenged the Conservatives to prOduce one 'State which was better or happier under Tariff Beform than England under' Free Trade. The Tories' could not show one. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: HOW TO PREVENT ACID STOMACHS AND FOOD FERMENTATION.
div.p: HOW TO PREVENT ACID STOMACHS AND FOOD FERMENTATION.
BY A_STOMACH SPECIALIST

, - As a specialiet who has spent many years in the study and treatment of stomach troubles, I have been forced to the conclusion that most people who complain of stomach, trouble possess stomachs that • are ' absolutely healthy and normal. The real trouble, that which causes all the pain and difficulty, is 'acid in the stomach, usually due to, or aggravated by. food fermenta- tion. Acid irritates the delicate lining. of the stomach, and food fermentation causes wind, which distends the stomach abnormally, cans-- ing that full bloated feeling. Thus both acid and fermentation interfere with and retard the process of digestion. The stomach is usually healthy and normal, but irritated almost past endurance. bY these foreign elements—acid and wind. In all such cases—and they comprise over 90 per cent. of all stomach difficulties—the first and only step necessary is to neutralise the acid and stop-the fermentation by taking-in a little warm or cold water immediately 'after eat- ing. half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia, which is doubtless the best and only really effec- tive antacid and food corrective known. The acid will be neutralised and the fermentation. stopped almost instantly, and your stomach will at once proceed to digest the food in a healthy, normal manner. 'Be sure to ask your 'chemist for the bisurated magnesia, as I have found other forms utterly lackinc, in its peculiarly valuable properties.—F.J.Q. °

A 'DANGEROUS PRACTICE. . Levi Whittle .05), 'of Bi—Cambridge-road, was charged at St. Helens, sin Monday, With endan- gering his life by riding on a coal waggon in the Sherdley Colliery on August Ist. Mr. Peace, who prosecuted, said that the matter came to the knowledge of Mr. Kirk, the manager, when the , boy came to the..colliery on August 13th, after having been in hospital. The boy. ex- plained that the injuries to II is head - and shoulders had been caused by his having been jammed between a coal waggon and the roof at a point where it was low: It was an offence to ride on the waggons. unless special permis- sion had been given.-The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs.
