The committee of the League and the secre- tary, Mr. Brandreth, who had a. considerable . influence; have been successful in obtaining the magnificent solid silver Dodds' challenge 'shield, and the club winning the championship, will become holders of it for the following twelve mdliths. ThiS should have a stimulating effect on' the- clubS and players to give of their best form, to prove who, shall have the honour of having their-club's name inscribed on it at the end of the season. All the men have emerged from the practice games with varying degreeS of first-rate merit, and with so much excellent, talent at their dis- posal, it was no easy task for the committee' on Wednesday evening to make n selection of the team. 'ln that chosen, the names of whom appear below, I think they have made a capable selection, and have .given ps a well-balanced side. The defence lines are a powerful lot, just the men who will not allow the most daring of opponents to do too lunch. The attack is equally as capable; and as a whole the team is about the best the club can Produce. Renwick and Skelhorne are absentees. it ,being repotted that they had not yet signed on: Jolley Fhope to see doing big things at full- back. div.head: HUDDERSFIELD MATCH.
div.p: THE HUDDERSFIELD MATCH.

The great match of the month will be, that which- Warrington plays at Huddersfield Monday afternoon. The feast," the Yorkshire equivalent of the Lancashire "wakes," is being celebrated on that day: and this, combined with the fact that Warrington gave Iluddersfield such a close run for the N.U. Challenge Cup last season, should bring out a huge crowd. It is not safe to malce a prediction in regard to the possible result Of a game in which two. such crack sides are involved.

• In the corresponding match last season the score was 187-3 against Warrington, but since then our local " Wirepullers" have improved, and it is very probable that Huddersfield, if 'they do win, will not end the game With a clear lead of 15 points. The team.. it is expected, will_ be much the same as that doing duty to- day-.

div.head: SECOND TEAM AT LEIGH.
div.p: SECOND TEAM AT LEIGH.

The "A" team Make the journey to Leigh, and there they have what. is geographically known as a "stiff bit "to contend with. For the occa- sion they are taking Leigh way a strong team. The thirteen selected are: Brown, back; Baker, -Douglas, Jordan and waywol, threequarter backs; Daintettt and A. Brown, half-backs; Naylor, Harmer. Bradshaw, Boardman, Critch- ley and Bevan. forwards. Brown,, the full-back, has made .great strides gave a most favourable nantrlhaendfuille-dre simincpe lastressio year, ss rehearsal last Sat- urday. Baker, at threequarter, is a new-comer, but this local lad is one who gives much promise of turning out a. crack. He is speedy and gets off the mark quickly. The others are all good men, and should give a first-class account of themselves at Leigh to-day.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

Judging from the poor .show the Warrington cricket eleven Made at Blackpool last Satuoulay, the players must have looked upon the fixture as a holiday picnic. It was, from a Blackpool point of view, for they had quite a day, and at the expense of the Warrington men. On a good wicket the local players, by a huge effort, put together 65 runs, out of which Stafford claimed 20. In response to that total Black- pool mule 190. A last wicket stand between Gillett and Lawton (the latter, by the way, was connected with the Warrington Club many year 9 ago) flogged mercilessly the tired War- rington bowling. Every player on the War- rington side, with the exception of the wicket- keeper, tried his skill with the ball, t,it Hann= had the best average, his five wickets costing 72 runs.

div.head: s-. VA. .
div.p: s-. VA. .
Photograph by But reil. MR. J. MASSEY.

For P 2 years MrAtassey rendered yeoman ser- vice to the Warrington football team, and earned- a splendid reputation as a threequarter back: At 16 .he started with the Warrington Wanderers, and played with the Warrington toam when ilaey .met Asptill at Stanley in the final for the West 'Lancashire Rugby Cup.- It was in this Match that Mr. Massey had his eollar-bone. dislocated. To our .representative's 'remark that' this. was a set-back for a• com- mencement, Mr. Massey chuckled hugely as.he said: "Oh, I was all right again in six weeks. I have been broken and bruised: all over since." This chance statement of his illustrates .quite plainly his thorough good sportsManship, which is well known to Warringtothans. In the "nine" .a side" competitions, he won several prizes, playing remarkably well in Mr. Harry Ashton's team. For a long number of years he held a record for tries, which was beaten by Fish just before that football " hero " retired. It was a very popular appointment when,. in 1891-2' Mr. Mapsey was placed as the skipper of the team, for which he had played so well.

div.head: Life Member.
div.p: A Life Member.

On his retirement, when the Northern Union Rugby League was formed, Mr. Massey was made a life member of the club, and is a regular :Wender at the matches now. He bias only sported the stripes once since his retirement, and that with Crosfield's team, who were beaten in a works competition final by Monks's men. Mr. Massey is 48 years of age, said is full of life and vigour. He looks with pride on the many trophies he has to remind him of his athletic 'days, which include over a score of medals, a 450 shield, silver trays and tea sets, a host of knives and forks, marble clocks and ornaments, tea urns, gold watches, &c. As a trundler, Mr. Massey has won about a dozen mains, but not in recent years. and on one occasion he was the second in Crosfield's main, when J. Barton was a successful corn- -I)etitor. He has been most warmly congratu- lated on his notable win last Saturday. but showers of praise would not turn his head, for he is a genuine English sportsman.

div.head: WITH THE WOODS.
div.p: WITH THE WOODS.
Liberal Association Annual Handicap.
J. MASSEY'S POPULAR WIN.

greater success than. ever has attended the bowling competitions undertaken by the War- rington Liberal Association, and on Saturday the final games in the annual. handicap were played. There were 605 entries, and in addition to being a very popular one, Mr. J. Massey's win was a creditable one, insomuch that he was best of such a great number.

The games were keen from the commence- ment, and that between G. Marshall and P. Middleton was intensely exciting. The players Peeled at 94' but from this juncture Middleton got away to 12-9. Again the players drew even. and there was much speculation as to who would send the winning wood. Middleton's first wood was a yard off, and Marshall managed to beat it. Middleton's next block toucher seemed to decide the issue, but Marshall struck, knocking the winning wood out of the way. Unfortun- ately for him, however, after many turnings and twistings, the block rolled off the green, and a "dead end" was declared. This seemed to dishearten Marshall, who could not beat Mid- dleton's next winning woods.

AS. for the winner. Massey, he had played long lengths in a very skilful manner all the after- noon, whereas his final partner did not seem up to his usual good form. Literally, in the final, Massey "walked home,"'Gleave, although being a very capable trundler on short lengths, not being able to get in at a long run.
Massey has an excellent record in Sporting eireFos. and has won numerous trophies in various branches of sport.

div.head: GAS PROFITS AND THE RATES.
div.p: GAS PROFITS AND THE RATES.
Are the Gas Committee Overcharging Consumers
to Relieve the Rates?

div.head: COUNCILLOR OSBORNE'S STRIKING ANALYSIS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR OSBORNE'S STRIKING ANALYSIS.

gestron, that Osborne succeeded in getting a sugthat the price of gas be reduced by a • penny per. 1,000 'cubic feet, referred back tol the committee for further consideration. His contention was that the Gas Committee, out of the enormous profits they had made, had more than paid for the gas undertaking, including the large amounts paid in relief of the rates; that to overcharge users of gas for the relief of another section of the community was inequitable; and that even a reduction of 3d..Pel I,oooft. could only be regarded in the •light of rc.payment for overcharges. - I

'Gas ,and the part it plays in connection with the valid of the rates was discussed at the meet- ing 4at the Warrington Town Council on Tues- day evening.. The Gas Committee reoora- menaod.: That the price of gas to consumers Other than consumers supplied by means of , prepayment meters) be reduced by Id. per 1,0001 cubic eet. as and from the 31st day oT October ! next, and that the consumers within the borough, supplied by means of prepayment Meters, be ullowed• such additional number of cubic feet as will be an equivalent to the reduc- tion in price to ordinary consumers. , "That, in the opinion of this committee, it is undesirable, if not impracticable, to allow dis- count to the consumers of gas-using slot meters.'" Alderman Tnnoorr moved the resolution with the remark: The _Council have done a stupid and foolish thing in passing the Gough resolu- tion.

A SCENE. Councillor PEMBERTON : Speak for !yourself. :Alderman TINNION : I think"so and I say so. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is not true and you know it. 'Councillor BROADHURST : IS that personal? The MAYOB.: No. Alderman Minos.: I think I was saying the Council had ,done a stupid thing and- Councillor PEmaratzoN:: And I say it is not true. Alderman TINNION : I do not object to what you say. I have the right to my own opinion, and I am not going behind people's backs to tell what I think. I still say it places the Gas Com- mittee in a very awkward position, a position that is almost imposSible. Alderman BOLTON seconded, and said that after what had happened, he could not see any use in passing the minutes. COUNCILLOR OSBORNE CHAMPIONS THE GAS CONSUMERS' CAUSE. Alleged Inequitable Treatment. Councillor Ossonsu moved as an amendment that the recommendation with reference to the reduction of the price of gas be referred back to the committee. He thought a reduction of a penny, considering the enormous profits that had been made out pf the gas consumers, was too small. A reduction of even threepence would be no more than repaying pie consumers for the over charges to which they had been subjected. He found that since the Gas Company was taken over by the Corporation in 1877 no less a Om 'than £136473 had- been applied to the relief of the rates. The total loans taken up amounted to £252,743, of which £107,047 had already been liquidated. That was to say, the gas consumers had paid off in gifts to the rates, and in repayments of loans,, sufficient, together with the amount standing to the credit Of he reserve fund, to wipe out the whole of t.te capital indebtedness of the gas undertaking, and to have handed over to the town, free from debt, an asset worth considerably more than a quarter of it million. In eight years, from 31st March, 1906, to 31st March, 1913, inclusive, the profits, after making the necessary deductions for sinking fund. interest, &c., were £111,098 I.ls. 2d: -.Out of that, £101,937 6s. 3d. had been allOcated to the relief of the rates, or an averai4Q for the past" eight years of £13,117 per annum. A STRONG FINANCIAL: POSITION.

Further, the department was in a very strong financial position. It had the full amount I allowed by Act of Parliament to credit of the reserve fund, viz., £lO,OOO, and had accumulated in the appropriation account the sum of X 26,589 19s. id., which was more than sufficient to -meet all the needs of a working balance. In the light of those figures it did not seem equitable to sug- gest that the rate per 1,000 feet should be reduced by only one penny. That reduction would .mean only ,21,874 155., a small amount to return to consumers, consideiing that the net profit last year was £14,448 16s. sd. The com- mittee would soon have to reconsider the whole question as to whether it was not wrong in principle to overcharge one section of the com- munity in order to relieve another of its re- sponsibilities. Mr. Jaikes Paterson, Mr. Haddock's predecessor, was emphatic on that. point. He said: "The principle so generally adopted by Corporations in supplementing the rates out of the profits realised by the consump- tion of gas is one which cannot, I think, be supported, whether on the grounds of pro- priety or equity. Its operation is simply to tax the gas consumer with a supplementary rate in excess of the general taxes levied upon the town, which, in the case of large consumers, fre- quently becomes a very oppressive burden." ACTS IN A PREJUDICIAL WAY.

And he went on further to say that: "It also acts in a prejudicial way in preventing the natural extension of gas-lighting by reduction in price, which, as we have seen, is almost in- variably the precursor of increased ,progress, together, with maintaining and.securing the con- fidence of the consuiners." Alderman Tinnion had stated that the argument was advanced by some that the general body of ratepayers had their claim to consideration. The Gas Works were their property, and theirs was the ulti- mate responsibility. Personally he did not see where the injustice came in; ratepayers, as rate- payers, had no responsibility. They were not called upon to bear any of the cost of produc- tion; and if, at any time, it was found that gas -could not be 'produced at anything like the pre- sent-cost, the consumers themselves would have to pay the increased" price. If the gas ebh- sumers had to bear the responsibility they should also take the profits. The Water Com- mittee was not asked to make a profit out of its -customers in order . that some thousands might be handed over to reduce the iates, but the rate- payers 'were content with the advantages of cheap water, and cleanliness. tight and heat were quite as necessary, in the home as water, and the Gas Committee would do !well Weinu- late the example of the Water Committee.- The gas consumers were not now asking that all the profits should be returned to them. All that they wanted was to be treated with equity. and that a fair proportion of the profit should

be used to reduce what, after all, they cerisid- ered to be an overcharge. • It did not neces- sarily follow, however, that if the price of gas were reduced the profits would be reduced to the same extent. It is a well-known law of industry that with every increase of the quan- tity produced the relative cost of production was diminished. Whatever tends, therefore, to impede the sale of gas was inimical to the inter- ests of the gas undertaking. Mr.. Haddock had time and again pointed that out in his reports. In 1902 he stated that "to maintain our position it is necessary to sell gas at as low a price as possible. I hope we may soon be able to reduce our price." In 1903 he said: "A lower price of gas invariably leads to a higher consumption, and it would be advisable to reduce the price to ordinary and- slat consumers"; and. he went on .. . to add that a reduction of threepence on ordin- ary meters and an increase of five cubic feet of gas per one penny on the coin meters would reduce their income about £5,000. How did that work out in practice?

- LOWER PRICES CONSUMPTION INCREASES. On November Ist, 1909, gas was reduced a penny per 1,000 cubic feet. The amount handed over to the relief of the rates in 1909— before the reduction—was £13,387 7s. 2d. In 1910 there was a decrease caused, Mr. Haddock stated, by several large works having put down electric plant and generating their own light, but the amount handed over in that year—after the reduction—was £12,000. In the next year, 1911, the sales were up five million cubic ,feet, and the. amount transferred to the -relief of the rates was 40,500. - In -1912, £16,367 ,19s. sd. was handed over. Last year the income' from gas, was over -t.3,100 pp, owing to increased output,. and the year was considered to be the most prosperous on record. When the price was lowered ,to the consumer the consumption went up, and with the reduc- tion there was very little loss of profit, and that for only about a year. A reduction in the price of gas was not unjust to the rate- payers. On the contrary, it was not equitable to tax one section of ratepayers so that another might -be relieved of its responsibilities. A reduction in the price of gas would make many homes brighter and cleaner, and the lot of many •of the poor would be made happier. The results from a hygienic point of view, and in- creased consumption, would soon neutralise any immediate loss made by lowering the price of gas a reasonable amount, and he hoped the committee would see their way to reconsider their decision. Councillor BROADHURST seconded. HAD TO BE SCRAPPED.

Alderman BOLTON said when the undertaking was transferred to the Corporation it had prac- tically to be scrapped because it was obsolete. Owing to the consequent borrowing of money gas could not be supplied at as cheap a rate as would otherwise have been .the case. Gas profits were one means by which the Cor- poration recouped itself from people living c.ut- ' side the borough, who otherwise would cbittri- "bute'practidally nothing to municipal iuiprove.: ments, while deriving considerable benefit hem them: If they reduced the gas 3d., where would

the rates be? Councillor PEMBERTON said the resolutimi only suggested id., and it did not demand 3d. There Was a great deal more behind the question than; appeared. Alderman TINNION You will find it out before you are much older. The MAYOR: What .do- you ,mean? Councillor PEMBERToN : lie means the unfortu- nate ratepayer, who, for private purpose s or business, is called upon to purchase gas, gives to the Gas Committee a profit of is; id. and is thus paying 98-. -id .• instead of Bs. to-the rates. It i really inequitable. (Hear, hear.) It is all very well to have low ratei .at the expeAse Of one section of the toinmunity.-- - The MAYOR: The rates would -go up .to the seine extent if you did not. Councillor PEMBERTON : No, not quite. The greater number of people would have to pay it. DEARER FUEL.

'Alderman BURTON said that this year the cost of fuel to the gas department would be. about ..t3,000 more than last year, while the profit from the sale of by-products was expected to be about £2,000 less. • That meant a difference of £5,000, and, 0..8 the passing of Councillor gough's resolution li-culd involve another £5,000, the whole of their profits. would soon be gone: The proposed further con- cession to slot meter users should have bcen deferred until the end of the .financial year. Councillor PEACOCK expressed the hope that the Gas Committee would shortly transfer the offices of the department to a more, suitable place. He was not in favour of paying off the ' old sinking fund, as those who came after the present generation ought to bear their slare. He believed the price of gas ought to be reduced, as that would be of advantage to those tow on the earth. Councillor GOUGH said the amendment would give the Gas Committee an opportunity of ad- justing affairs. councillor WILKINSON' intimated that the Cor- poration itself was a 'very large customer, of the Gas Department for the lighting of the streets. In' that respect a reduNtion of the price meant taking money out of one pocket and placing it in another.

div.head: "Morality and Religion"
div.p: "Morality and Religion"
Rev. Dr. Mellor and the Subject.

Religion and morality are not identical; said the Rev. Dr. Mellor in the first of a course of sermons on "Morality and the Moral Life," delivered in Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday evening. That view, he added, was contrary to a great mass of popular opinion and to a striking tendency of modern times; and many people were convinced that religion was complete, and realised if a inari tried to lead a good life. It might not do harm to morality that it should be raised to the level of religion, though as a 'fact it Could not sustain itself in that altitude,, but it was 'harmful that religion should be reduced to the level of morality. That was the danger they were in—of losing the true essence of reli- gion in lower things of moral and social practice. The object of religion was eternal. It looked away from things that Nitre seen to things that were not seen. - - . - .

l'instead of what was incomplete kind perfect, religion sought and found completeness and per- fection. In essential quality and character it was as changeless and eternal as God Himself. It was fixed both in its beginning and end, and existed a completed whole, independent f time for fulfilment or completion. Moral' ty meant dissatisfaction, restlessness,' conflict. The essence of religion was satisfaction, rest and joy in a nompleted victory—not their own victory, but God's.

, Alderman TPiNION said that be saw nothing else than for the committee to Withdraw the resolution. It was, however, as well th4t members should give vent to their feelings, as November was drawing near, and "cheaper gas" was a profitable election cry. (Laughter.) If they persisted in the policy which some members were laying down, the rates would be increased by at least is. in. the zC next year. Some of the property-owners would begin to squeal when they found they had to. raise rents above the composition limit. A reduction of 3d. Would mean £5,000, and the cost of production in the 'department was advancing, while the profit from the sale of residuals was falling off. The Gas Committee ouglk to be allowed to work out its own salvation,, without so much interference from members of the Council. it would be much better to make. suggestions to the committee, but that would not mean get- ting into the limelight. " (Laughter.) lie hoped that, as the policy, of the Gas Com- mittee was so bound up with, the financial sta- bility of .the town, the Council would hesitate before doing the many things they were attempt- ing to do. On a vote the 'amendment was declared car- ried, only four members voting against it.

Rev. John Yoage's Golden Wedding. ' Preaching at Wycliffe Church on Sunday even- ing: the Rev. John Ycmge said he wouli like to take the opportunity of expreqiing to the con- gregation, minister and deacons a the church, on behalf of his wife and self, the sincere appro. .ciation for. the kind letters they had received referring to- the event-which occurred on Mon- day, August 25th—the fiftieth anniversary of their married life. They received the earnest and affectionate letter, authorised by the Church meeting and signed by Mr. James and the deacons, containing their congratulations and good wishes for days to come. They had been , much cheered by those communications, and , very glad were they to know that they still lived in the love of their people. Thirty-six years in the Church endeared -the Church to those who 'served if,, and he hoped they would keep that affection alive and green, unto the end.- He' had also received a kind letter from the P.S.A. brethren. He was glad to hear their work was still going on, and he wished it increas- ing usefulness in the years to come.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A

Mr. James Ball spoke at Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday on " Environment?' A great discussion had been going on of late upon this question, he said, but the only conclusion he must come to was'that the great God filled, immensitY in' Min we lived, moved and had our being. Christ was sent as the personification of the great God, and man, at his highest, was the nearest and most like his God, in• the spirit of God, in love, in thodght. His environments were the surround- ings of God around him, and if he used their highest ideals of God they would become more like Him. The jellyfish in its element was beautiful, but as it was cast upon the shore it lost its beauty. There was a fish in a Kentucky cave which had all the organs of sight, but because, these had not been used had become useless. So with our doings and life. If used they became good and beautiful, hut if we used not our powers we became helpless and useless; power to think and work and be, were what we attained in the ser- vice of God and man. Mr. B. Farrar presided and returned thnnks to the brethren for Mr. Yonge for their good wishes sent last week. The brethren sent a message to Mr. Healey, who was laid up with sickness, wishing him a speedy recovery. Mr. Beswick took part in the meeting. Miss Hipkiss gang " Love eternal" in a most impressive man, ner. Mr. Payton presided at the organ.

div.head: Bold Street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold Street Wesleyan Church.

The Rev. H. Williamson occupied the pulpit on Sunday evening, and basing., his, re- marks on the Words "If I, then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another's 'feet," spoke on "Humility." At the outset the reverend gentleman contrasted the treatment meted out to the heroes of the blood-stained- battlefield with that of, the silently heroic mothers, who daily sacrifice their lives in a terrible struggle on behalf .of their children. The _soldier, whose virtues may be few or none, and" whose 'occupation is far from Christian, has his - name enrolled upon a memorial tablet in one of our cathedrals, but the thousands of heroes and heroines scattered throughout the land receive no honours and are buried unnoticed and without sign of pomp. In such a contrast is found the parable of human life. Humanity, ever loving the pomp of earthly splendour, .seems Utterly forgetful of the.nameless and obscureheroines.whose actions reveal the Artily great and the truly' 'heroic. And the, same spirit that hsngs for the meteoric heroism of the athlete Of the soldier, displays itself in our detestation of the narrowness and the monotonous routine of the daily duty. Fool- ishly. and sinfully we pine for the glories which are entirely beyond our reach, :and forget the glorious possibilities that lie within our grasp. The disciples were lovers of the Spectacular. Their conception of the Messiah was of 'a prinee world-conquering and covered with earthly splendour, and their part in His great kingdom was that of rulers judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Even Christ was tempted by the spee- tacular in the wilderness; but He thrust it aside once and for ever, and lived a common- plene life among common People. - The situation at -present occupled by each however commonplace. has its duty and its ideal. To be great and heroic is noS- sible to all, for there is nothing greater than to do one's duty, nor anything more heroic than to -follow Christ. ' If the life is lived according to the spirt of St. Paul's words. "Whatsoever ye do, •do it in the name Of the Lord Jesus," then the common- nla6e dirappears, and every part of the life is full of .God.

HORSE SALE SEQuEL. Watriiiitton Greengrocers Assaulted. A PLUCKY OLD MAN. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesflay, before Mr. F. A. Frost (in the chair) and other magistrates, William Travis and Richard Travis, Old Mill, Houghton Grange, near Croft., were charged with having assaulted and beaten Joseph Cogan, 16, Milner-street, Warrington, on the 19th August. William Travis, the father of Richard, was also charged with assaulting and beating. Denis Dolan, an old man, who was with Cogan.—Mr. Browne prosecuted and Mr. Steel defended. Mr. Browne said that Cogan, who assisted his mother in a greengrocery business, went to St. Helens to sell a pony, and Dolan- accompanied him. At the Red Lion Hotel sale the pony was not sold, because the reserve price was not reached. About seven o'clock at night Richard Travis went to Cogan and said his father wanted to see 'him.
